The following is an addendum to the Integrated Review for NDA 213972 (ORLYNVAH,
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid) signed into DARRTS on 10/24/2024. Table 45 in Section
7.6.1.5 (Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial 310) and Tables 46, 47 and 48 in Section
7.6.1.6 (Laboratory Findings, Trial 310) have been corrected to include subheadings that were
missing in the original Integrated Review.

ITERUM THERAPEUTICS US LTD.
Tablet (500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid)
One tablet orally twice daily for 5 days
ORLYNVAH is indicated in adult women ≥18 years of age for
the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused
by the following designated susceptible microorganisms:
Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis (b) (4)

Approval
One tablet orally twice daily for 5 days
ORLYNVAH is indicated for the treatment of uncomplicated
urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by the designated
microorganisms Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or
Proteus mirabilis in adult women who have limited or no
alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.

ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)

I. Executive Summary
1. Overview
1.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
On April 25, 2024, the 505(b)(2) NDA 213972 for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid oral tablet, a
bilayer fixed-dose combination of the penem antibacterial prodrug sulopenem etzadroxil and
probenecid (500 mg; 500 mg), a renal tubular transport inhibitor, was resubmitted by Iterum
Therapeutics US Ltd. (Applicant) for the proposed indication of treatment of adult women ≥18
years of age with uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by designated susceptible
microorganisms. Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid has Qualified Infectious Disease Product
(QIDP), Fast Track and Priority Review designations. The Prescription Drug User Fee Act
(PDUFA) goal date is October 25, 2024. Throughout this review, the study drug product is
referenced as sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid or oral sulopenem.
NDA 213972 was originally submitted on November 25, 2020, for sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI caused by designated microorganisms proven or
strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone in adult women. The original NDA was
primarily based on Trial IT001-301 (Trial 301), a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, activecontrolled trial comparing oral sulopenem to oral ciprofloxacin for the treatment of uUTI in adult
women. Independent statistical analyses in this trial indicated that oral sulopenem was inferior to
ciprofloxacin for the primary endpoint of overall (or composite) response (including clinical and
microbiological responses) in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacinsusceptible (micro-MITTS) population but achieved statistical superiority in the microbiological
modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacin-resistant (micro-MITTR) population. Data from Trial 302
for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) and Trial 303 for the treatment of
complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAIs) assessing the safety and efficacy of IV to oral
sulopenem formulations versus active comparator regimens were also submitted in the NDA;
however, both trials failed to meet their primary endpoints. The original NDA review team
concluded that results from the single uUTI trial and lack of confirmatory evidence from Trials
302 and 303 were insufficient to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE); thus, the
NDA received a complete response on July 23, 2021. The Division recommended that the
Applicant conduct at least one additional adequate and well-controlled trial in uUTI to support
this indication.
In the current NDA resubmission, data were provided from the new Trial IT001-310 (Trial 310),
a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, noninferiority (NI) trial comparing oral
sulopenem to amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of uUTI caused by designated susceptible
microorganisms in adult women. Oral sulopenem was NI with an NI margin of 10% and
statistically superior to the comparator in the micro-MITTS (amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible)
population. The sample size of patients with isolates that were amoxicillin/clavulanate-resistant
(micro-MITTR) was too small to allow conclusions regarding efficacy.

3
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Safety data from nearly 3000 subjects across the phase 3 sulopenem development program
indicate that oral sulopenem is anticipated to be safe for its intended use. It is expected that
potential safety risks can be adequately mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during
routine pharmacovigilance.
Because sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid will, if approved, be the first oral penem antibacterial
drug on the U.S. market, the NDA was taken to the Antimicrobial Drugs Advisory Committee on
September 9, 2024, to discuss the Applicant’s desired indication and consider the information
that should be conveyed to medical providers to ensure appropriate use of this drug product.
While an oral penem for the treatment of resistant bacteria causing uUTI could potentially
address an unmet need, its use in an ambulatory setting where treatment is most commonly
empiric raises concern for inappropriate use which may contribute to antimicrobial resistance
(AMR). Further, based on the failure of Trials 302 and 303 to meet their primary endpoints, there
was concern for potential off-label use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid as a stepdown
treatment for cUTI and cIAI following initial intravenous (IV) antibacterial treatment.
Based on the totality of evidence and recommendations from the Advisory Committee (see
Section 11), the multidisciplinary review team recommends approval of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid with the following Indication: “ORLYNVAH is indicated for the treatment
of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by the designated microorganisms
Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Proteus mirabilis, in adult women who have limited
or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.” In addition, the required statement
regarding Usage to Reduce Development of Drug-Resistant Bacteria will be strengthened. A
Limitations of Use statement that “ORLYNVAH is not indicated for the treatment of: cUTI or
cIAI or as step-down treatment after intravenous antibacterial treatment of cUTI or cIAI” will be
added. Overall, as delineated in the Benefit/Risk Framework below, the review team concludes
that the benefits of oral sulopenem outweigh its associated risks when used as recommended in
the approved labeling.
The signatory concurs with the review team’s recommendations. There is an unmet need for an
oral penem to provide an oral treatment option for adult women with uUTI caused by certain
resistant bacteria, such as those with infections caused by bacteria expressing extended-spectrum
beta-lactamase enzymes. Trial 301 is considered as two adequate and well-controlled trials based
on the statistical analysis plan (SAP), with separate analyses conducted for the micro-MITTS
(ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population which failed, and the micro-MITTR (ciprofloxacinresistant) population which was successful. The interpretable primary analysis of Trial 310 in the
micro-MITTS (amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible) population was successful. Thus, while the
signatory agrees that substantial evidence of effectiveness has been provided, there is some
element of uncertainty because of the failed Trial 301 primary analysis in the micro-MITTS
(ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population. Consistent with our labeling practices for antibacterial
drug products that address unmet need described in our Guidance document, Antibacterial
Therapies for Patients with an Unmet Medical Need for the Treatment of Serious Bacterial
Diseases – Questions and Answers, (available at (May 2022)) the Indication will read as
described above. This Indication and other labeling will address the need to ensure appropriate
use of the drug, minimize the risk of contributing to penem resistance in the U.S. population, and
avoid use of the drug to treat serious infections such as cUTI or cIAI for which effectiveness has
not been established.

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Microbiological surveillance as a Post-Marketing Requirement (PMR) mandated by 21 CFR
505(o)(3) will evaluate the possible emergence of resistance to oral sulopenem and crossresistance to FDA-approved IV carbapenems with the use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
In addition, FDA will conduct enhanced post-marketing pharmacovigilance to monitor for
potential inappropriate use of the product.

1.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of
Effectiveness
SEE was established with two or more adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations.
Substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the
treatment of uUTI was established based on the results from Trials 301 and 310. For these trials,
the SAP pre-specified that the composite primary efficacy endpoint of overall response
(combination of clinical and microbiological responses) was analyzed independently in the
micro-MITTS (comparator-susceptible) and micro-MITTR (comparator-resistant) populations.
In Trial 301, sulopenem was superior to ciprofloxacin in patients with ciprofloxacinnonsusceptible pathogens (micro-MITTR population) using the primary efficacy endpoint of
overall response. The overall response was 77/160 (48%) for sulopenem and 49/149 (33%) for
ciprofloxacin with a difference of 15% (95% CI, 4.4%, 26.1%; p-value 0.0062). Among patients
with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen (micro-MITTS population),
sulopenem was inferior to ciprofloxacin. The overall response was 218/365 (60%) for sulopenem
and 296/410 (72%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of -12.5% (95% CI, -19.1%, -5.9%). The
failure of sulopenem in the micro-MITTS population in Trial 301 was driven by lower rates of
microbiological success in the sulopenem arm compared to the ciprofloxacin arm.
In Trial 310, oral sulopenem was non-inferior and superior to amoxicillin/clavulanate in the
micro-MITTS (i.e., amoxicillin/clavulanate-susceptible) population using the primary efficacy
endpoint of overall response (clinical response and microbiological response). The overall
response was 296/480 (61.7%) for sulopenem and 243/442 (55.0%) for amoxicillin/clavulanate
with a difference of 6.7% (95% CI, 0.3,13.0; p-value of 0.040). While clinical response was
similar between arms, the rate of microbiological response was greater in the sulopenem arm of
the micro-MITTS population. The sample size of subjects with isolates that were
amoxicillin/clavulanate-resistant (micro-MITTR) was too small to allow conclusions regarding
efficacy in this population.
In summary, SEE for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI caused by the
designated microorganisms E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or P. mirabilis in adult women who have
limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options has been provided by statistical
superiority in the micro-MITTR population of Trial 301 along with NI/superiority in the microMITTS population of Trial 310. To note, there is some element of uncertainty because of the
failed uUTI Trial 301 primary analysis in the micro-MITTS (ciprofloxacin-susceptible)
population. Additionally, as discussed in this review, IV to oral sulopenem did not demonstrate
efficacy for treatment of cUTI and cIAI in Trials 302 and 303, respectively.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common bacterial infections in
the ambulatory setting in the U.S.; 50-60% of adult women will have at least
one UTI during their lifetime (Medina and Castillo-Pino 2019). It is estimated
that 10-12% of adult women in the United States have at least one UTI per
year, with 20-30% of those having a recurrent infection (Kaye et al. 2021).
The incidence of uUTI has a double peak – first in young, sexually active
women aged 15-24 years and then in postmenopausal women (Kaye et al.
2021). Risk factors include sexual intercourse, spermicide use, prior UTI,
new sexual partner within the past year, and history of UTI in a first-degree
female relative (Hooton 2012).
The most common causative bacterial pathogen in uUTI is Escherichia coli
(E.coli) (75-95%). Additional causative pathogens include other species of
Enterobacterales (e.g., Proteus mirabilis (P.mirabilis), Klebsiella
pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae)) and Staphylococcus saprophyticus (S.
saprophyticus) (Gupta et al. 2011).
AMR among urinary isolates is increasing across the U.S., including
resistance related to production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases.

Conclusions and Reasons

Current
treatment
options

•

There are several FDA-approved antibacterial
drugs for the treatment of uUTI. However,
increasing antibacterial drug resistance and
adverse reactions in some patients may limit
treatment options.

•

•
•

Therapy for uUTI is most often empiric. Urine cultures are not typically
recommended for the first incidence of uUTI (Kaye et al. 2021).
The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends the following
antibacterial drugs for the treatment of uUTI: nitrofurantoin, trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (if local resistance rates of uropathogens
causing uUTI do not exceed 20%), fosfomycin, or pivmecillinam.
Fluoroquinolones (including ciprofloxacin) and β-lactams (including
amoxicillin/clavulanate) are considered alternative antibacterials for uUTI
(Gupta et al. 2011).
Some of the recommended antibacterial drugs have known adverse
reactions, including pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, neuropathy,
hypersensitivity reactions, tendinopathy, and QT prolongation.
In the U.S., there is increasing resistance of E. coli to ciprofloxacin and
TMP-SMX and increased prevalence of extended-spectrum β-lactamase
(ESBL) producing E.coli (Kaye et al. 2021). When uUTI are due to
antimicrobial resistant pathogens, treatment may require IV antibacterial
treatment, necessitating placement of an IV catheter and possibly
hospitalization.

Conclusions and Reasons

Risk and risk
management

•

The four phase 3 trials in uUTI, cUTI, and cIAI
provided an adequate safety database for the
proposed dosing regimen of oral sulopenem for
uUTI treatment.

•
•
•
•

•
•
•
•
•

The primary safety population consisted of 1932 subjects with uUTI from
Trials 301 and 310 who received the proposed dosing regimen of
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.
Trial 302 in cUTI and Trial 303 in cIAI, both of which included use of both IV
and oral formulations of sulopenem, provided supportive safety data. A total
of 2962 subjects received sulopenem among the four phase 3 trials.
Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema, were observed in two
subjects from a phase 1 study (IT001-101) and Trial 301 after oral
sulopenem administration.
There were no deaths in Trial 310; the one death in Trial 301 was due to
lung adenocarcinoma and unrelated to sulopenem.
Diarrhea was seen in 10% of subjects who received oral sulopenem, but
most episodes were mild. Five (0.3%) occurrences of diarrhea required
treatment discontinuation. There were no cases of Clostridium difficile
infection (CDI) related to sulopenem.
Elevations in alanine aminotransferase more than three times the upper
limit of normal were seen in 0.4% of uUTI subjects, but in general, were not
treatment-limiting.
One subject in Trial 302 fulfilled laboratory criteria for Hy’s Law but liver
enzyme elevations resolved while still on study drug.
Other treatment-emergent adverse events related to sulopenem included
headache, nausea, vomiting, and vulvovaginal mycotic infection.
Empiric use of oral sulopenem for treatment of uUTI in an ambulatory
setting raises concern for the development of antimicrobial resistance in
general and in particular, for cross-resistance to IV carbapenems.
Based on the failure of sulopenem to demonstrate efficacy in Trials 302 for
cUTI and 303 for cIAI, potential off-label administration of oral sulopenem
as stepdown treatment following IV antibacterial treatment for cUTI or cIAI
raises concern for treatment failure.

The safety profile of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid appears acceptable. The
identified safety risks for sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid can be adequately
mitigated through labeling and further
evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
Given that sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid
will be the first oral penem antibacterial drug on
the U.S. market, effective antimicrobial
stewardship and appropriate positioning of the
drug in the hierarchy of uUTI treatment options
by guidelines committees is critical to mitigate
risk of increased carbapenem resistance
associated with its use. Microbiological
resistance to sulopenem will be monitored for 5
years in a required postmarketing study (PMR).
Limitations of Use to prevent off-label use of
oral sulopenem as step-down treatment
following IV antibacterial treatment of cUTI or
cIAI will be added to the prescribing information
(PI).

2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
Although multiple antibacterial drugs are FDA-approved to treat uUTI, treatment options can be
limited by drug toxicities (e.g., hypersensitivity to β-lactams and QT prolongation, central
nervous system effects or tendinopathies associated with quinolones) and AMR to first-line
drugs including through production of ESBL (Critchley et al. 2019; Dunne et al. 2022).
Carbapenem drugs are the mainstay of treatment for infections caused by ESBL-producers, but
all approved members of this class require IV administration and are generally reserved for the
treatment of culture-proven infections. While an oral penem for treatment of resistant bacteria
causing uUTI could potentially address an unmet need, its use in an ambulatory setting where
treatment is most commonly empiric raises concern for inappropriate use which may contribute
to AMR.
The Applicant submitted data demonstrating safety and effectiveness of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of adult women with uUTI due to designated
microorganisms.
Trial 301 demonstrated that sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is superior to ciprofloxacin for the
treatment of subjects with uUTI caused by ciprofloxacin-resistant organisms (micro-MITTR
population). The overall response at test of cure (TOC) in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid
arm was 48.1% compared with a rate of 32.9% in the ciprofloxacin arm with a treatment
difference of 15.3% (95% CI: 4.4%, 26.1%). Of note, this treatment difference is based on
analysis by the FDA statistical team utilizing the original SAP submitted by the Applicant and
with inclusion of Site 202. After an unblinded interim analysis, the Applicant chose to analyze
the primary efficacy endpoint utilizing an updated SAP and excluding Site 202; thus, the
treatment difference the Applicant obtained was 26.6% (95% CI: 15.1%, 37.4%). Regardless, the
results of both analyses were favorable to oral sulopenem.
Trial 310 demonstrated that sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is non-inferior and superior to
amoxicillin/clavulanate for subjects with uUTI in the micro-MITTS population. The overall
response at TOC in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm was 61.7% compared to 55.0% in
the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm with a treatment difference of 6.7% (95% CI: 0.3, 13.0), which
met the prespecified NI margin of 10%.
The safety database for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, consisting of nearly 3,000 subjects in
the four phase 3 trials and more than 1,000 additional subjects in phase 1 and 2 trials, was
adequate for the proposed dosing regimen and indication. Overall, sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid appears to be safe for its intended use; potential safety risks can be
adequately mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
Based on the review of all available efficacy and safety data, NDA 213972 for sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid provides SEE and a favorable benefit-risk profile for the treatment of
uUTI caused by the designated microorganisms E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or P. mirabilis in adult
women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.

II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
3. Introduction
Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet is a fixed-dose combination of the penem
antibacterial prodrug (sulopenem etzadroxil) and a renal tubular transport blocking drug
(probenecid). Each tablet contains 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid. The
Applicant’s proposed indication is treatment of uUTI caused by designated susceptible
microorganisms in adult women ≥18 years of age. The proposed dose is one tablet orally (PO)
administered twice daily (BID) for 5 days.
Sulopenem etzadroxil, a new molecular entity, is a β-lactam drug closely related to the
carbapenems. On oral administration, sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem
and two other products: formaldehyde and 2-ethylbutyric acid (2-EBA). Probenecid, originally
approved in 1951, is co-formulated with sulopenem etzadroxil to increase the systemic exposure
of sulopenem.
The Division granted sulopenem QIDP designation for the treatment of uUTIs, complicated
urinary tract infections (cUTIs), and complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAIs) on July 29,
2016, as well as fast track designation for these indications on March 15, 2019.
uUTI is the most common bacterial infection in the ambulatory care setting in the U.S. There are
multiple FDA-approved drugs for uUTI treatment (see Benefit-Risk Framework), but their use is
challenged by associated drug toxicities and rising antimicrobial resistance.
The Applicant previously developed an intravenous (IV) formulation of sulopenem and studied
its efficacy with stepdown to oral sulopenem for cUTI and cIAI. Prior to the original submission
of NDA 213972 in 2020, three phase 3 trials were completed - IT001-301 (Trial 301) for uUTI
utilizing oral sulopenem, IT001-302 (Trial 302) for cUTI, and IT001-303 (Trial 303) for cIAI,
each utilizing IV to oral sulopenem. On November 25, 2020, The Applicant submitted NDA
213972 as a 505(b)(2) submission for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenicid for the proposed
indication of treatment of adult women with uUTI caused by designated susceptible
microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone.
The NDA received a complete response on July 23, 2021, due to lack of substantial evidence of
effectiveness (SEE) for sulopenem for the treatment of uUTI. In Trial 301, sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid was superior to ciprofloxacin based on the primary endpoint of overall
response (clinical and microbiological response) in the prespecified subgroup of participants
with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-resistant pathogen in the microbiological modified intentto-treat resistant (micro-MITTR) population. However, in the prespecified subgroup of
participants with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogens [micro-MITTS
(microbiological modified intent-to-treat susceptible) population], sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid was inferior to ciprofloxacin. Also, sulopenem failed to achieve
noninferiority (NI) to the active comparator for the primary efficacy endpoints in the cUTI and
cIAI studies. The safety profile for sulopenem etzadroxil was found to be acceptable.
Given the sole finding of superiority in the micro-MITTR population with inferiority in the
micro-MITTS population in Trial 301 and lack of supportive evidence in the MITT populations
11
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
of the cIAI and cUTI trials, it was concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support the
effectiveness of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI. The Division
recommended an additional trial for uUTI with a different comparator, and that the Applicant
conduct further investigations to determine the optimal sulopenem dosing regimen.
Following the complete response, the Applicant halted further development of the IV
formulation. The current NDA resubmission includes results from the recommended additional
uUTI trial, IT001-310 (Trial 310), in which amoxicillin/clavulanate was chosen as the
comparator. Trial 310 was a phase 3, randomized, multicenter, double-blind, double-dummy
controlled trial of the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid
versus oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of uUTI in non-pregnant adult women.
Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was non-inferior and statistically superior to the comparator
for the primary endpoint of overall response (composite of clinical and microbiological
responses) at test of cure (TOC) in the micro-MITTS population (amoxicillin/clavulanate
susceptible). Based on the statistical analysis plan, NI was first tested and achieved in the
microbiological modified intent-to-treat (micro-MITT) population, but a noninferiority
comparison in this population is not considered appropriate due to the inclusion of patients with
comparator-resistant isolates. No conclusions regarding efficacy could be drawn in the microMITTR population (amoxicillin/clavulanate-nonsusceptible) due to insufficient sample size.
Refer to Sections 6 and 7 for detailed reviews of efficacy and safety for Trial 310.
An Advisory Committee (AC) Meeting was held on September 9, 2024, to discuss the overall
benefit-risk assessment for the use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI
and to consider information that would be most important to convey to medical providers to
ensure appropriate use of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. Details of the Committee’s
deliberations are provided in Section 11. Based on the Committee’s recommendations, the
Indication statement in labeling was narrowed to indicate sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for
the treatment of uUTI caused by the designated microorganisms E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or P.
mirabilis in adult women who have limited or no alternative oral antibacterial treatment options.

initial review cycle for NDA 213972 along with efficacy and safety data from Trials 302 and

5. Pharmacologic Activity,
Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical
Pharmacology
5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
Effectiveness
To support the activity of sulopenem against Enterobacterales, the Applicant conducted in vitro
and in vivo pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) index and target determination studies,
along with a proof-of-concept study in an in vitro hollow-fiber infection model. For uUTI, there
is no established nonclinical model to reliably determine PK/PD targets relevant to the site of
infection. Additionally, significant knowledge gaps surrounding urine-specific PK/PD
parameters and selection of a bacteriologic endpoint predictive of clinical efficacy limit the use
of probability of target attainment (PTA) analyses to predict the efficacy of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of uUTI. Therefore, while the nonclinical data support
sulopenem’s activity against uropathogens, the translational utility of these nonclinical PK/PD
findings is limited.

Pharmacologic Activity
Established pharmacologic Sulopenem is a penem antibacterial, and probenecid is a uricosuric and renal tubular inhibitor. A new established

Mechanism of action
Sulopenem inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to essential penicillin-binding proteins (PBP). Probenecid is a
uricosuric and renal tubular blocking agent that inhibits the OAT3-mediated excretion of sulopenem, thereby providing
increased plasma concentrations of sulopenem
Active moieties

rapidly cleaved to release the active compound, sulopenem.
QT prolongation
At a concentration of ≥40 times the peak sulopenem concentrations associated with the recommended dosing regimen,
clinically significant QTc interval prolongation was not observed. After a single 500-mg dose, sulopenem does not prolong the
QTc interval to any clinically relevant extent. This conclusion was informed by concentration-QTc analysis performed on data
from trial A7371007, a single ascending dose study of sulopenem etzadroxil. The predicted ΔΔQTcF (upper
bounds of 90% CI) value was 0.07(4.34) ms at the geometric mean of the Cmax (i.e., 109.7 μg/mL) associated with the highest
single dose of 2800 mg IV sulopenem administered as a 1 h infusion.
A thorough QTc assessment was not conducted for probenecid either under its original approval in 1951 or as part of the
current application. Nonetheless, QTc prolongation is not described as an adverse reaction in the probenecid labeling.

Distribution
The mean apparent volumes of distribution for sulopenem and probenecid are 134 L and 8.81 L, respectively.
Sulopenem is 10.7% bound to plasma proteins.
Sulopenem is a substrate of OAT3 and sulopenem etzadroxil is a substrate of P-gp. Probenecid is a substrate of BCRP. In a
clinical DDI study with a P-gp inhibitor (itraconazole), the effect on the AUC and Cmax of sulopenem was not clinically
significant.
Elimination
Following oral administration of a 2000-mg dose of [14C] sulopenem etzadroxil, 85.1% of the radiolabeled dose was
recovered in urine (44.3%) and feces (40.8%) as unchanged sulopenem and metabolites. Sulopenem accounted for 26.9%
and 3.1% of the administered dose in urine and feces, respectively.

Clearance

Mean apparent oral clearance values are 77.6 and 2.06 L/h for sulopenem and probenecid, respectively.

Half-life

Mean plasma half-lives are 1.2 and 2.9 h for sulopenem and probenecid, respectively.

Metabolic pathway(s)

Sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed after oral administration to sulopenem in the intestines and in systemic circulation.
Sulopenem and two inactive metabolites formed by β-lactam cyclic amide bond hydrolysis (M1a and M1b) are the major
circulating entities. Sulopenem, M1a and M1b accounted for 32%, 21.8% and 43.6%, respectively, of circulating radioactivity
in the mass balance study. No metabolism of sulopenem was observed in vitro with recombinant CYP or UGT enzymes.

Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as Perpetrator)
In vitro, sulopenem etzadroxil is an inhibitor of CYP3A4/5. However, because it is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem, clinically
relevant DDIs are not expected with CYP3A4/5 substrates.
Probenecid is a known inhibitor of OAT1 and OAT3 and was observed to inhibit BCRP in vitro. Sulopenem etzadroxil is an
inhibitor of BCRP and P-gp. However, because it is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem, clinically significant DDIs are not
expected with BCRP or P-gp substrates.

6. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential
Effectiveness
The Applicant’s proposed dosage of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID
orally was evaluated in two phase 3 uUTI trials (Trials 301 and 310). In Trial 301, the proposed
dosing regimen, 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID demonstrated superiority
to ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID for the treatment of uUTI in patients who presented with a
ciprofloxacin-resistant pathogen at baseline but failed to demonstrate noninferiority to
ciprofloxacin in patients with a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen at baseline. In Trial 310,
500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID was non-inferior to 875 mg
amoxicillin/125 mg clavulanate BID for the treatment of uUTI in the amoxicillin/clavulanate
susceptible population. Despite the limitations of nonclinical PK/PD data (see Section 5.1), the
results of PTA analyses and a 5-day in vitro hollow-fiber infection model study are supportive of
the effectiveness of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID in the treatment of
uUTI. The underlying causes of the mixed clinical trial efficacy outcomes are likely
multifactorial, and PTA analyses are unable to predict the performance of 500 mg sulopenem
etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID against different comparators in an efficacy trial.

6.1.1. Support for Proposed Dose of Sulopenem
Etzadroxil
Probability of Target Attainment Analyses
Urinary drug concentrations are considered important to the successful treatment of uUTIs, while
the relative importance of plasma drug concentrations to efficacy is unclear. The Applicant
conducted PTA analyses for both plasma and urinary drug concentrations using %fT>MIC
targets derived from a murine thigh infection model and an in vitro 1-compartment infection
model to support the proposed dosage of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID
and to support a cutoff value of 0.5 µg/mL for Enterobacterales susceptibility. Due to
deficiencies in the murine thigh infection model study design and limited interpretability of the
findings, the resulting targets (i.e., 16.6 and 20.3% fT>MIC for stasis and 1-log kill, respectively)
were deemed unreliable. Because the in vitro 1-compartment model does not account for bladder
tissue architecture or the complexities of urodynamics, it is unclear whether the derived targets
are reasonable surrogates for the relevant infection site. Nonetheless, PTA based on the median
in vitro targets of 40.9, 50.2 and 62.6% fT>MIC for stasis, 1-log kill, and 2-log kill, respectively,
which numerically offered a more conservative appraisal of efficacy than those determined in the
murine thigh infection model, were prioritized to support the proposed dosage. PTA results
showed that the free plasma concentrations associated with the Applicant’s proposed dose
regimen resulted in achievement of the in vitro targets in ≥90% of simulated subjects at MICs
ranging from 0.031 to 0.25 µg/mL. The Applicant also evaluated the probability of achieving
PK/PD targets in urine by simulating 1 h and 2 h bladder voiding patterns. Based on the urine
concentrations associated with the Applicant’s proposed dose regimen, urine PTA analyses

6.2.2. Trial 310
6.2.2.1. Design, Trial 310
Trial 310 was a phase 3, multicenter, double-blinded, double-dummy, randomized, controlled
study to compare oral sulopenem to oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of uUTI in
adult women. Eligible adult women were randomized 1:1 to receive either oral sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid 500 mg/500 mg BID for 5 days or oral amoxicillin/clavulanate
875 mg/125 mg BID for 5 days. Subjects were followed-up at Day 12 TOC visit and Day 28
(final visit).
6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial 310
Subjects had to meet the following criteria to be eligible for the study:
1. Female subjects ≥18 years of age with ≥24 hours and ≤96 hours of urinary symptoms
attributable to a UTI
2. Two of the following signs and symptoms of uUTI: urinary frequency, urinary urgency,
pain or burning on micturition, suprapubic pain
3. A mid-stream urine specimen with:
a. a machine-read dipstick positive for nitrite AND any positive leukocyte esterase
OR
b. evidence of pyuria alone.
Subjects who met any of the following specified criteria were excluded from the study, for
example, presence of signs and symptoms suggestive of acute pyelonephritis defined as: fever
(temperature >38° Celsius), chills, costovertebral angle tenderness, flank pain, nausea, and/or
vomiting.
See Section 15 for full inclusion and exclusion criteria.
6.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial 310
The primary efficacy endpoint was overall success (combined clinical and microbiologic
success) on Day 12 (±1 days)/TOC in micro-MITT, micro-MITT comparator-susceptible (microMITTS) and micro-MITT comparator-resistant or nonsusceptible (micro-MITTR) populations.
The micro-MITT population included all randomized patients who received at least one single
dose of study medication and had a positive study entry urine culture defined as ≥105 colonyforming units (CFU)/mL of a uropathogen (Enterobacterales or Staphylococcus saprophyticus (S.
saprophyticus) only) and no more than 2 species of microorganisms identified in the study entry
urine culture, regardless of colony count. Comparator susceptibility was based on MIC
[susceptible: MIC ≤8/4 mg/L; nonsusceptible: intermediate (MIC 16/8 mg/L) or resistant (MIC
≥32/16 mg/L)] to the components of the comparator study drug, amoxicillin and clavulanate,
respectively.
26
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
For the definitions of overall success, clinical success, and microbiological success endpoints,
please see Section 15.
Analysis of the Primary Efficacy Endpoint
To control for inflation of the overall type I error rate, the hierarchical testing procedure of
Westfall and Krishen (Westfall and Krishen 2001) was proposed by the Applicant and used to
test the hypotheses of the primary efficacy endpoint in these populations in the sequential order
described below.
•

NI in the micro-MITT population.

•

NI in the micro-MITTS population or superiority in the micro-MITTR population.

•

Superiority test of overall success in the micro-MITT population.

Testing was to proceed to the next comparison only if the null hypothesis in the comparison was
rejected. For pre-specified sequential hypothesis testing, no adjustment to the alpha level was
required. However, in the second step of the hierarchy, the trial did not adjust for multiplicity in
testing in the micro-MITTS and micro-MITTR populations because at the time of study design
the analyses in these populations were considered to address separate questions as if they were
separate studies under a single protocol for logistical reasons.
Two-sided 95% CIs for the treatment difference in success proportions (sulopenem-active
control) would be determined using the method of Miettinen and Nurminen. NI was established
if the lower bound of the CI was greater than -10% and superiority was established if the lower
bound of the CI was greater than 0.
The FDA had communicated the following comment regarding the planned analysis: “We
strongly recommend testing NI in the micro-MITTS population as the primary endpoint. An
alternative is hierarchical testing for (i) NI in the micro-MITTS population followed by (ii)
superiority in the micro-MITT population. It would be an important review issue if the trial is
unable to demonstrate noninferiority in the micro-MITTS population, which is not currently
assessed in the first level of the planned hierarchical testing. We note that the trial is adequately
powered for the analysis of noninferiority in the micro-MITTS population.”
Because the hierarchical testing rejected the null hypothesis in the first level of testing for
noninferiority in the micro-MITT (as will be subsequently discussed), the analysis of the primary
endpoint in the micro-MITTS in the second level of the hierarchy was considered to have the
statistical interpretability of a prespecified primary analysis.
In addition, the FDA finds the NI testing in a population that included patients with isolates that
were not susceptible to the comparator (Step 1), uninterpretable for regulatory purposes.
Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
Clinical response and microbiologic response were analyzed. Overall success, clinical success,
and microbiologic success by baseline pathogen and monomicrobial/polymicrobial infection
were analyzed.
Overall response by baseline uropathogen resistance class(es) were presented.

Interim Analysis
A blinded interim analysis for sample size re-estimation was to be performed when clinical and
microbiologic response data at Day 12 (± 1 day)/TOC were available for approximately 50% of
the subjects (approximately 983 subjects). The sample size of the study would be computed to
ensure that there was sufficient power for the primary efficacy endpoint in the micro-MITTS
population. It was anticipated that this would ensure the study was sufficiently powered to test
the primary endpoint in the micro-MITT and micro-MITTR populations as well.
Following the blinded interim analysis, the Data Monitoring Committee recommended that in
order to maintain 80%-90% power, the trial should continue to enroll to achieve a minimum of
1966 subjects (original sample size in protocol) up to a maximum of 2428 subjects (to achieve
90% power). On October 23, 2023, enrollment was completed with 2222 randomized patients as
the Applicant considered that adequate statistical power had been achieved.
6.2.2.4. Results of Analyses, Micro-MITTS and Micro-MITTR
Populations, Trial 310
The study was conducted in the U.S. between October 18, 2022 and November 21, 2023. The
clinicaltrials.gov identifier for the study was NCT05584657. In the following subsections, the
intent-to-treat (ITT) population will be discussed briefly, followed by results in the microMITTS population and micro-MITTR population. As noted above, because the hierarchical
testing rejected the null hypothesis in the first level of testing, the analysis of the primary
endpoint in the micro-MITTS in the second level of the hierarchy was considered to have the
statistical interpretability of a prespecified primary analysis.
Disposition, Baseline Demographics and Baseline Characteristics
Disposition
The following Table 8 summarizes the disposition of subjects. A total of 2222 subjects were
randomized and included in the ITT population of all randomized subjects. Four subjects in each
arm were excluded from a modified intent-to-treat (MITT) population for not receiving study

subjects completed the study. The primary reasons for study discontinuation were loss to followup (1.8%) and withdrawal by subject (3.0%). The two treatment groups were comparable with
respect to the reasons for treatment discontinuation or study discontinuation.

subjects (53.4%) (Table 13). The most common minor deviation was in study procedures (a
protocol-required visit outside the visit window). The two groups were generally balanced in
protocol deviations.

In the micro-MITTS population, a total of 6.2% of the subjects (comparable in the two treatment

sulopenem group and 2 subjects in the control group were considered as overall successes. A
sensitivity analysis with these successes considered as failures will be provided in Table 30.

Distribution of Baseline Study Uropathogens by Antibiotic Resistance
Distribution of baseline study uropathogens by antibiotic resistance is shown in Table 20. A total
of 8.9% of micro-MITTS subjects had at least 1 baseline Enterobacterales pathogen that was
extended-spectrum β-lactamase-positive, as determined by having a ceftriaxone MIC of >1
μg/mL. A total of 13%, 30.7%, 26.9% of subjects’ isolates were non-susceptible to
nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and quinolones, respectively. Susceptibility was
comparable (not nominally statistically significant) between the two treatment groups.

Primary and Key Secondary Efficacy Results
Primary Efficacy Analysis Results
In the micro-MITTS population, the overall success proportions were 61.7% and 55.0% in the
sulopenem and amoxicillin/clavulanate treatment groups, respectively, with a difference of 6.7%
[95% CI: 0.3%, 13.0%] and a two-sided p-value of 0.040 for superiority. The results
demonstrated NI using a -10% NI margin and superiority of sulopenem to the active control. The
treatment effect for overall success was driven by microbiological success, as the clinical success
proportions were similar between the two treatment groups.

Subgroup Analyses of the Primary Efficacy Endpoint, Micro-MITTS Population
Subgroup analyses were performed to assess the treatment effects among different subgroups
based on age, race, ethnicity, body mass index and diabetes. Breslow-Day tests did not suggest
any heterogeneity of odds ratios in the primary efficacy endpoint. When the sample size was
greater than 90 in each group, the lower limits of the 95% CIs were larger than -10%. In a few
subgroups (age >65 years, Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, and non-diabetes), nominally statistically
significant differences were seen. However, caution is needed to interpret these results because
multiple comparisons were conducted.

Sensitivity Analyses of Primary Efficacy Endpoint
Contaminated Urine Sample Treated as Failure
At TOC in the micro-MITTS population, there were 23 and 24 subjects in the sulopenem and
active control groups, respectively, that were coded by the Applicant as “Eradication” with ≥3
organisms present (indicating contamination at collection). Thirteen and 18 of these subjects
were coded as success for the overall response. If these successes were changed to failures, then
the treatment effect was slightly higher, as shown in Table 30.
Complete Eradication (<100 CFU/mL)
The overall response at TOC when using complete eradication (<100 CFU/mL) as the definition
of microbiologic success was lower in both groups, but the treatment effect was similar to that
observed in the primary analysis (6.5% versus 6.7%) (Table 30).
Concomitant Use of Antibacterial Drugs
Five and two subjects in the sulopenem and the control group, respectively, who received
concomitant antibacterial drugs were considered as successes in the primary efficacy analysis. If
those 7 subjects were considered as failures, the difference between the two groups reduced from
6.7% in the primary analysis to 6.1%, only demonstrating NI.

Study Results, Trial 310/Micro-MITTR Population
Disposition
The study included 67 subjects in total for the micro-MITTR population and failed to enroll the
planned sample size (134 per group). Overall, 95.5% of the micro-MITTR subjects completed
study drug treatment and completed the study, while 4.5% discontinued treatment prematurely
and discontinued the study prematurely. The primary reasons for discontinuation of treatment
and discontinuation from the study were loss to follow-up (1.5%) and withdrawal by subjects
(3.0%).

7. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Nonclinical Data
Nonclinical studies submitted to support the safety evaluation for this NDA include the
following studies with sulopenem etzadroxil: safety pharmacology studies (neurofunctional, in
vitro and in vivo cardiovascular, and pulmonary function assessments), pharmacokinetic and
toxicokinetic assessments (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion), general
toxicology studies (1-month studies in rats and monkeys), in vitro and in vivo genetic toxicology
studies, and developmental and reproductive toxicology studies (male and female fertility study
in rats, embryo-fetal development studies in mice, rats, and rabbits, a pre-postnatal development
study in rats and a juvenile toxicology study in rats). Also, a 14-day combination toxicology
study with orally administered sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid was conducted in rats.
Additional nonclinical safety studies with sulopenem, the active metabolite of sulopenem
etzadroxil, that were evaluated in support of the NDA include an in vitro hERG assessment, in
vitro plasma-protein binding, CYP450 inhibition, mass balance, and metabolite profiling studies,
and a full battery of genetic toxicology studies. Additional information regarding genetic toxicity
findings for probenecid was obtained from historical probenecid product labels previously
approved by the FDA.

7.1.1 Target Organs of Toxicity
Kidney
Adult rats were administered sulopenem etzadroxil in oral doses of 100, 400, and
2000 mg/kg/day in the 1-month toxicology study in rats. Renal effects included minimal
vacuolation of the tubular epithelium, tubular hypertrophy, and a potentially adverse effect, i.e., a
low incidence of tubular degeneration. These effects occurred primarily in high-dose males and
females in the 2000 mg/kg/day group and to a lesser extent in mid-dose males receiving
400 mg/kg/day.
In a definitive juvenile toxicity study, oral administration of sulopenem etzadroxil in doses of 25,
75, and 225 mg/kg/day to juvenile rats for 85 days beginning on postnatal Day 5 and continuing
to postnatal Day 90, was associated with more varied and severe renal histopathology findings

7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
Oral sulopenem etzadroxil is the pro-drug of the penem antibacterial drug, sulopenem and is
hydrolyzed rapidly to sulopenem upon oral ingestion. Penem antibacterials are a class of betalactams structurally similar to carbapenems. If approved, sulopenem would be the first oral
penem on the U.S. market so there are no in-class comparators. In general, carbapenems have a
favorable safety profile and are well-tolerated. Common adverse reactions associated with their
use include headache, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, rash, and injection site reactions. Labeled
Warnings and Precautions for carbapenems (imipenem-cilastatin, ertapenem, meropenem)
include hypersensitivity reactions, seizures and other adverse central nervous system
experiences, Clostridioides difficile-associated disease, severe cutaneous adverse reactions,
thrombocytopenia in patients with renal dysfunction, development of drug-resistant bacteria and
drug-drug interactions (DDIs) with valproic acid resulting in reduction of its plasma
concentrations and increased seizure potential.

50
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Reported postmarketing adverse events (AEs) for carbapenems include anaphylaxis, hepatitis
and hepatic failure, hematologic adverse reactions including pancytopenia and hemolytic anemia,
central nervous system disturbances, muscular weakness, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic
epidermal necrolysis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, erythema
multiforme, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, drug fever, and acute renal failure.
Probenecid has been in use since the 1950s and is generally well-tolerated with a favorable
safety profile. Labeled Warnings and Precautions for probenecid include exacerbation of gout,
increased plasma concentration of methotrexate, severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis,
hematuria, renal colic, costovertebral pain, formation of uric acid stones, and antagonism of the
uricosuric action of probenecid with concomitant use of salicylates. Adverse reactions observed
with probenecid include headache, dizziness, precipitation of acute gouty arthritis, hepatic
necrosis, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, sore gums, genitourinary AEs including uric acid stones
and nephrotic syndrome, hypersensitivity reactions, aplastic anemia, leukopenia, hemolytic
anemia, anemia, dermatitis, alopecia, and flushing.
The risks and safety concerns for oral sulopenem are anticipated to be similar to carbapenems as
summarized above except that because sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is an oral tablet,
injection site reactions would not be expected. Adverse events of special interest monitored by
the Applicant during the uUTI development program included diarrhea and renal disorders;
infusion-related events were monitored in Trials 302 and 303 utilizing sulopenem IV but will not
be discussed further in this review.

Through Postmarket Experience
Not applicable. Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is not approved in the U.S. or in any foreign
market; therefore, no postmarketing experience is available for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.

7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
The primary safety analysis for the resubmitted NDA was conducted on data derived from the
phase 3 uUTI Trial 310. Additional analyses were conducted on the combined phase 3 uUTI
study populations from Trials 301 and 310. During the first review cycle, safety data from Trials
301, 302 and 303 were analyzed, along with phase 1 studies (conducted by the Applicant and
Pfizer) and phase 2 studies (conducted by Pfizer). While specific safety findings from these three
trials (301, 302 and 303) are presented in this review when relevant, please refer to the NDA
Multi-Disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021 for complete
details. Identified safety issues during the previous review cycle included hypersensitivity
reactions (angioedema), elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and gastrointestinal adverse
reactions.
No major data quality or integrity issues were identified for Trial 310. Coding of verbatim terms
to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) preferred terms (PTs) was
generally acceptable. A treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE) was defined by the Applicant
as an AE that newly appeared or worsened in severity following study drug initiation. A TEAE
was considered drug-related if the AE was possibly or probably related to study drug. Safety
evaluations included recording of AEs, vital signs, and collection of laboratory results. While the
TOC visit was Day 12 (+/-1 day), AEs were collected through the final study visit (Day 28 ± 2
days). MedDRA version 26.1 was used for Trial 310 (MedDRA version 21.0 was used for Trials
301, 302, and 303; MedDRA version 22.0 was used for the phase 1 studies). AEs were classified
by investigators as mild (does not interfere with the patient’s usual function), moderate
(interferes to some extent with the patient’s usual function), or severe (interferes significantly
with the patient’s usual function). An AE was defined as a serious adverse event (SAE) if the
event:
•

Resulted in death,

•

Was life-threatening,

•

Required hospitalization or prolongation of hospitalization,

•

Resulted in persistent or significant disability/incapacity,

•

Resulted in congenital anomaly/birth defect,

•

Was assessed as being a medically important event based on medical and scientific
judgement. Such medically important events may not be immediately life-threatening or
result in death or hospitalization but may require medical or surgical intervention to
prevent one of the above outcomes.

The clinical data scientist performed standard safety analyses including FDA medical queries
(FMQs) to identify safety signals. In this review, the terms AE and TEAE are used
interchangeably and sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid is also referenced as oral sulopenem.

Baseline Demographic and Clinical Characteristics
In Trial 310, baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were similar between
treatment arms (Table 38). All subjects were female and from the United States. The
median age in the sulopenem arm was 50 years and 48 years in the comparator arm. In
both arms, most subjects (around 80%) were less than 65 years old. There were slightly
more subjects (7.2%) in the sulopenem arm who were aged 75 years or older compared
to the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (5.8%). In both arms, the majority of subjects were
white and Hispanic or Latino. A greater number of subjects (39.3%) in the sulopenem
arm had a BMI >30 kg/m2 than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (36.5%). The number
of subjects with CrCl >60 mL/min was comparable between arms, but there were more
subjects (1.7%) in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm with a CrCl <30 mL/min compared to
sulopenem subjects (0.8%). There was a higher percentage of subjects with a CrCl of 3060 mL/min in the sulopenem arm (18.0%) compared to subjects in the
amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (15.4%).

7.6.1.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events,

As shown in Table 42, the overall incidence of TEAEs was higher in the sulopenem arm (18.9%)
compared to the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (12.3%). Most TEAEs in both arms were of mild or
moderate severity, but 5 subjects (0.5%) in the sulopenem arm experienced a severe AE

7.6.1.2. Deaths, Trial 310
There were no deaths in Trial 310.
7.6.1.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial
310
There were no SAEs in the sulopenem arm, and 5 SAEs in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. The
SAEs in the comparator arm will not be discussed further.
7.6.1.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment
Discontinuation, Trial 310
The proportion of subjects with TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation was comparable in
both treatment arms (0.7% in the sulopenem arm and 0.4% in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm).
In the sulopenem arm, these included the following PTs, most of which (except chills, headache
and syncope) were related to the Gastrointestinal Disorders system organ class (SOC): nausea (n
= 4), gastroesophageal reflux disease ([GERD] n = 3), diarrhea (n = 3), constipation (n =1),
flatulence (n = 1), abdominal pain (n = 1), chills (n = 1), headache (n = 1), and syncope (n = 1).

7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial 310
TEAEs occurred in 18.9% of the subjects in the sulopenem arm and 12.3% of subjects in the
amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. As shown in Table 44, this difference in TEAEs was largely driven
by diarrhea (8.1% in the sulopenem arm versus 4.1% in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm). The
following TEAEs (listed in decreasing order of frequency) occurred more commonly in the
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm and were seen in ≥1% of subjects: diarrhea (8.1%), nausea
(4.3%), vulvovaginal mycotic infection (3.0%), headache (2.2%), vomiting (1.4%), and
gastroesophageal reflux disease (1.0%). Fatigue (0.5%) and urine odor abnormal (0.4%)
occurred in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm, but not in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.
Abdominal pain occurred in 0.6% of subjects in the sulopenem arm and in 1.0% of subjects in
the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.

As shown in Figure 1, AEs in the sulopenem arm occurred most commonly in the
Gastrointestinal disorders, Infections and infestations, and Nervous system disorders SOCs.

SOCs: Gastrointestinal disorders, Infections and infestations, General disorders and

frequencies of diarrhea (8.1%), nausea (4.3%), and vomiting (1.4%) in the sulopenem arm
compared to the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. The fungal infection FMQ accounted for more
TEAEs in the Infections and infestations SOC in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm
(3.0%) compared to the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (1.2%). Fatigue (General disorders and
administrative site conditions SOC) and somnolence (Nervous system disorders SOC) occurred
only in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm (both 0.5%). Headache also occurred more
frequently in the oral sulopenem arm (2.3%) compared to the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm
(1.5%).

Abbreviations: FMQ, FDA medical query; N, number of subjects in treatment arm; n, number of subjects with adverse event; PT,

Diarrhea
Diarrhea was the most common TEAE in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm and had a
higher incidence (8.1% versus 4.1%) than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm. In most patients
(7.5%), diarrhea was considered to be related to study drug. The mean duration of diarrhea in the
sulopenem group was 2.9 days, and the mean duration from end of sulopenem treatment to
resolution of diarrhea was 4.1 days. There were no cases of Clostridioides difficile infection in
the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm. There was one subject with Clostridioides difficile
infection in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.
Most cases of diarrhea in the oral sulopenem arm were mild or moderate, but there were three
cases (0.3%) of severe diarrhea. The subjects with severe diarrhea were not administered therapy
for diarrhea and did not discontinue study drug. One of the subjects had diarrhea for one day and
the other two subjects had diarrhea for three days. As discussed above in Section 7.6.1.4, three
patients discontinued sulopenem due to mild or moderate diarrhea.
Vomiting
Vomiting was more common in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm, occurring in 1.4% of
subjects compared to 0.4% in the comparator arm. Most cases of vomiting were considered mild,
and none were severe. No patients discontinued sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid due to
vomiting. The mean duration of vomiting in the sulopenem arm was 1.7 days.
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
The incidence of GERD was higher in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm, occurring in
1% of subjects compared to 0.1% in the comparator arm. Most cases of GERD were mild. There
were no severe cases of GERD; however, as described above in Section 7.6.1.4, GERD led to
discontinuation of sulopenem in three subjects. The mean duration of GERD was 3.1 days in the
sulopenem arm.
Fungal Infection
The number of subjects having an AE of fungal infection was higher in the sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid arm (3.0%) than in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm (1.2%). All cases were
under the PT vulvovaginal mycotic infection. AEs were either mild or moderate and did not lead
to treatment discontinuation.

62
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Fatigue
Five subjects (0.5%) experienced fatigue in the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid arm whereas no
subjects experienced fatigue in the comparator arm. Four of the five subjects experienced mild
fatigue and one experienced moderate fatigue. The mean duration of fatigue was 2.7 days. No
subjects discontinued study drug due to fatigue.
Urine Odor Abnormal
The AE of urine odor abnormal only occurred in the sulopenem arm. Four subjects (0.4%)
experienced this AE. All cases were considered mild, and none resulted in treatment
discontinuation. This AE was also seen in Trial 301 and phase 1 studies of sulopenem. Per the
NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021, the
Applicant reported that sulfur-containing sulopenem metabolites are the likely cause of the
abnormal urine odor.
7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial 310
In Trial 310, there were no significant differences between treatment arms in baseline average
chemistry and hematology values or significant interval changes in mean values between
baseline and TOC.
As shown in Table 46, the frequency of patients with one or more chemistry analyte values with
specified elevated or low values was comparable between the two arms.

7.6.1.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial 310
There were no significant differences between the two treatment arms in the proportions of
patients with abnormal liver chemistry values (ALT, aspartate aminotransferase [AST], alkaline
phosphatase [AP], total bilirubin). No subjects in the sulopenem arm had elevations in AP >1.5X
upper limit of normal (ULN) compared to two (0.2%) subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate
arm. One (0.1%) subject in the sulopenem arm had an elevated bilirubin level >2X ULN
compared to 3 (0.3%) subjects in the amoxicillin/clavulanate arm.
Peak post-baseline elevations of ALT and AST among subjects in Trial 310 are shown in Table
49 and Table 50, respectively. In general, the number of subjects with an elevated ALT or AST
were comparable between the two arms. No patients in the sulopenem arm had an ALT ≥5x
ULN. A single patient in the sulopenem arm had an AST ≥5x ULN. No subject in either arm had
an ALT or AST value >10X ULN.

Narratives for subjects in the sulopenem arm with ALT or AST values >3x ULN or Bilirubin
>2x ULN are discussed below. The first three subjects had normal liver function tests at baseline,

•

Subject
was a 74-year-old woman who received five days of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid. On Day 12, ALT had increased to 192 U/L, AST had increased to 87
U/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) had increased to 248 U/L. AP and bilirubin
were normal. At Day 28, AST and ALT had normalized and GGT trended down to 119 U/L
(normal range 7-38 U/L). The subject was asymptomatic but had underlying non-alcoholic
steatohepatitis and was taking Crestor and metformin. Sulopenem may have contributed to
the increase in GGT, AST, and ALT, but attribution of causality is confounded by the
subject’s comorbidities and concomitant medications.

•

Subject
was a 23-year-old woman with ALT and AST elevated at 92 U/L and 231
U/L, respectively, at the Day 12 visit. Additionally, lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at
510 U/L. GGT, AP, and bilirubin levels were normal. On Day 15, ALT and AST were
trending down and lactate dehydrogenase had normalized. Liver enzymes were normal on
Day 22. The subject was asymptomatic and her only other medication was Lo Loestrin Fe.
Investigations included negative viral hepatitis serologies, negative urine toxicology screen,
normal % carbohydrate-deficient transferrin, and normal CK-18 M30 Apoptosense. Given
the time course and lack of an alternative cause, sulopenem was potentially the cause of the
elevation in liver enzymes.

•

Subject
was a 27-year-old woman who received 5 days of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid. On Day 12, total bilirubin and direct bilirubin were elevated at
2.83 mg/dL and 0.49 mg/dL, respectively. ALT, AST, GGT, and AP were normal. Labs were
repeated on Day 37 and the bilirubin had normalized. The subject was asymptomatic and her
only concomitant medication was an oral contraceptive (Yasmine). Urine toxicology screen
and hepatitis serologies were negative. Testing for % carbohydrate-deficient-transferrin was
normal. The etiology of the asymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia is unclear, but Gilbert
syndrome is a consideration.

•

Subject
was a 38-year-old woman who received 5 days of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid. At baseline, ALT (236 U/L), AST (180 U/L), and GGT (123 U/L)
were elevated. At Day 5, these lab values remained abnormal with decreases in ALT and
AST values and slight increase in GGT. At Day 12, ALT, AST and GGT remained elevated.
She had a past history of elevated liver function tests with no clear etiology. As these
laboratory abnormalities were present at baseline, sulopenem was likely not the cause.

Review of mean values and mean changes in vital signs from baseline to Day 12 did not reveal

7.6.1.9. Subgroup Analyses, Trial 310
All subjects in Trial 310 were female. In the sulopenem arm, the frequency of AEs was overall
balanced across age groups. AEs occurred with a similar frequency between white and Black
subjects within both arms. The small number of subjects of other races preclude further

conclusions about race-based AE imbalances. In the sulopenem arm, AEs were less frequent

for this finding is unclear and differs from Trial 301 where AEs were more frequent in Hispanic
or Latino subjects (28.9%) than in non-Hispanic/Latino subjects (22.7%). The frequency of AEs

Sulopenem-treated subjects with a BMI of <25 had the highest frequency of AEs compared with
subjects with higher BMIs; this may be a chance finding as a biologically plausible cause is not
apparent.

7.6.2. Summary of Safety Results, Trial 301
The safety data from Trial 301 were reviewed in the initial review cycle for NDA 213972. The
Agency’s safety database excluded 13 subjects (8 in the sulopenem arm and 5 in the
(b) (7)(A)
ciprofloxacin arm) from Site 218
69
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
(b) (7)(A)

The Applicant included
these subjects in their safety database. For completeness, a summary of safety findings from
Trial 301 is provided below. For detailed analysis, please refer to the NDA Multi-disciplinary
Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021. Identified safety issues during the
previous review cycle included hypersensitivity reactions, elevated ALT, and GI adverse
reactions.
A total of 825 subjects in the sulopenem arm were included in the safety database of Trial 301.
More subjects in the sulopenem arm (25.1%) experienced a TEAE than subjects in the
ciprofloxacin arm (14.0%), largely driven by TEAEs in the Gastrointestinal disorders SOC (17%
in the sulopenem arm, 7.9% in the ciprofloxacin arm) and to a lesser extent by TEAEs under the
SOCs of Infections and infestations (4.6% in the sulopenem arm, 2.6% in the ciprofloxacin arm),
Nervous system disorders (3.8% in the sulopenem arm, 2.8% in the ciprofloxacin arm), and
Renal and urinary disorders (1.5% in the sulopenem arm, 0.1% in the ciprofloxacin arm). The
following TEAEs occurred in 1% or more of subjects in the sulopenem arm and were more
frequent in the sulopenem arm compared to the ciprofloxacin arm (listed in descending order):
diarrhea (12.5%), nausea (3.9%), headache (2.2%), abdominal pain (2.2%), vomiting (1.6%),
vulvovaginal mycotic infection (1.3%), dizziness (1.1%), and urine odor abnormal (1.0%). A
total of 13 (1.6%) subjects in the sulopenem arm had a TEAE leading to study drug
discontinuation compared to 8 (1.0%) subjects in the ciprofloxacin arm. The following TEAEs
led to sulopenem discontinuation: vomiting (n=3), abdominal pain (n=2), diarrhea (n=2),
dizziness (n=2), nausea (n=1), angioedema (n=1), dyspnea (n=1), and hypertension (n=1).
Given that there was a notable imbalance in diarrhea between arms, further analysis was
conducted. Diarrhea occurred in 103 (12.5%) subjects in the sulopenem arm and 21 (2.6%) in the
ciprofloxacin arm. In the sulopenem arm, all diarrhea was either mild (10.2%) or moderate
(2.3%). The FDA reviewer noted that the average duration of diarrhea was longer by about one
day in subjects in the sulopenem arm compared to subjects in the ciprofloxacin arm, and subjects
who took sulopenem with food had a shorter duration of diarrhea (a difference of 2 days on
average) compared to subjects who did not take all their sulopenem doses with food.
There was one death in Trial 301 and this subject is described in Section 7.6.4.2 Six subjects
(0.7%) in the sulopenem arm (described in Section 7.6.4.3 and two subjects (0.2%) in the
ciprofloxacin arm experienced SAEs.
On review of mean chemistry and hematology laboratory values at baseline and Day 12 (TOC),
the proportions of sulopenem subjects with postbaseline abnormalities, including liver enzyme
elevations, were low and no significant differences were noted between treatment arms. There
were no cases meeting Hy’s Law criteria in the sulopenem arm, and no imbalances were noted in
peak AST elevations between arms. The FDA reviewer, Dr. Mukil Natarajan, noted that several
of the subjects with ALT elevations had baseline abnormal ALT values that were likely due to
underlying conditions such as fatty liver disease. Dr. Natarajan concluded that sulopenem may
cause elevation of ALT.
No significant differences in vital signs were seen between the two arms. Electrocardiograms
were not collected in the phase 3 trials as there was adequate data on sulopenem and cardiac
conduction from the phase 1 Study A7371007, which was reviewed by the QT Interdisciplinary
Review Team in 2017.

70
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Subgroup analyses revealed that subjects with Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, BMI>30, and those in
the United States were more likely to have a TEAE compared to the overall population. Among
these groups, the difference in the incidence of TEAEs between the arms was largely accounted
for by diarrhea. Most subjects of Hispanic/Latino ethnicity and BMI>30 were enrolled in the
United States. The FDA reviewer suspected the higher incidence of diarrhea could be due to
different physiological responses based on ethnicity or obesity or could be due to differences in
AE reporting by country/site. The FDA reviewer noted that the rate of TEAEs in Ukraine was
notably lower than in the United States or Russia with no TEAEs of diarrhea reported from
subjects in Ukraine.
The integrated assessment of safety included data from Trials 301, 302, and 303 as well as phase
1 and 2 studies. The following safety issues were identified:
•

Angioedema: As discussed in Section 7.6.4.1, one sulopenem subject in Trial 301
experienced angioedema. In addition, a subject in a phase 1 study experienced angioedema
after a dose of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. Hypersensitivity will be included as a
warning in the labeling.

•

Gastrointestinal AEs: GI AEs, including diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain, were common
among subjects taking sulopenem. Diarrhea was the most common AE among sulopenem
subjects, and in general was mild and not treatment-limiting. Taking sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid with food appeared to shorten the duration of diarrhea. GI AEs are to
be included in Section 6 of labeling.

•

Elevations in ALT: As noted in Section 7.6.4.7, elevations in ALT were more common
among sulopenem subjects compared to ciprofloxacin subjects in Trial 301 and in the
integrated phase 3 population (Trials 301, 302, and 303). Please refer to Section 7.6.4.7.
Elevated transaminases will be noted in Section 6 of labeling.

The safety findings from Trial 310 were consistent with the safety findings from Trial 301. No
new safety signals were identified in Trial 310.

7.6.3. Summary of Safety in Phase 1 and Phase 2
Clinical Studies
The phase 1 and 2 studies were reviewed during the initial review cycle (see the NDA Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated July 22, 2021). Safety signals
identified in phase 1 studies were diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash,
and abnormal urine odor. Additionally, as noted above, one subject who received oral sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid experienced angioedema of the face and lips and discontinued study drug.
The safety signals in the phase 3 trials were consistent with the observed AEs in the phase 1
studies.
In the Pfizer-conducted phase 2 studies, there were three deaths in subjects who received
sulopenem. Dr. Natarajan reviewed the narratives. Two deaths were due to underlying
malignancy and not related to sulopenem. The third death was related to myocardial infarction
and pneumonia which were unlikely to be related to sulopenem.

related to complications of the underlying cancer and not to study drug as it occurred months

sulopenem exposure.

7.6.4.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Pooled
Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
In the uUTI ISP, six subjects (0.3%) who received sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid experienced
SAEs compared to five (0.5%) and 2 (0.2%) in the amoxicillin/clavulanate and ciprofloxacin
arms, respectively. All six sulopenem subjects were enrolled in Trial 301. In the sulopenem arm,
the SAEs included angioedema, lung adenocarcinoma, presyncope, small intestinal obstruction,
abdominal pain upper, chest pain, pyelonephritis acute, and urosepsis. Only the SAE of
angioedema was attributed to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. As presyncope, small intestinal
obstruction, abdominal pain and chest pain occurred on Day 21 or later, the clinical reviewer
judged these events as less likely to be related to sulopenem. The SAE of lung adenocarcinoma
was not related to sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid as discussed above. Pyelonephritis and
urosepsis were attributed to an obstructing kidney stone rather than to study drug. For further
details, please refer to the NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972} dated
July 22, 2021.

7.6.4.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment
Discontinuation, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
TEAEs resulting in treatment discontinuation were reported in 21 (1.1%) subjects in the pooled
sulopenem group of the ISP with the majority of these TEAEs falling under the Gastrointestinal
disorders SOC, including nausea (0.3%), diarrhea (0.3%), abdominal pain (0.2%),
gastroesophageal reflux disease (0.2%), vomiting (0.2%), constipation (0.1%), dyspepsia (0.1%),
eructation (0.1%), and flatulence (0.1%). Three (0.2%) subjects experienced dizziness leading to
treatment discontinuation. Non-gastrointestinal AEs leading to treatment discontinuation in 0.1%
of subjects treated with sulopenem were angioedema, syncope, chills, fatigue, dysgeusia,
headache, dyspnea, pruritus, and hypertension.

On review of Trials 302 and 303 during the initial NDA review, the clinical reviewer identified 5

7.6.4.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Pooled
Analyses, Trials 301 and 310
In the ISP (Trials 301 and 310), the most common AE in subjects treated with sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid was diarrhea, which occurred in 194 (10%) subjects, compared to 4.1%
and 2.6% of subjects treated with amoxicillin/clavulanate and ciprofloxacin, respectively. The
second most common AE in subjects treated with sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was nausea,
which occurred in 80 (4.1%) of subjects. In addition to diarrhea and nausea, the following AEs
occurred in >1% of subjects treated with oral sulopenem: vulvovaginal mycotic infection (2.4%),
headache (2.2%), vomiting (1.5%), and abdominal pain (1.1%). Gastroesophageal reflux disease
(0.7%) and urine odor abnormal (0.6%) occurred infrequently in subjects treated with sulopenem
but in more sulopenem subjects than in the comparator groups.

In the integrated phase 3 population from the initial NDA review consisting of the combined
safety population of Trials 301, 302, and 303, 397 (21.4%) out of 1855 subjects in the sulopenem
arm experienced at least one TEAE compared to 305 (16.5%) out of 1852 subjects in the
comparator arm. The following TEAEs occurred in ≥0.5% of subjects in the sulopenem arm:
diarrhea (7.4%), nausea (2.9%), headache (2.2%), abdominal pain (1.5%), vomiting (1.2%),
dizziness (0.8%), vulvovaginal mycotic infection (0.8%), and hypertension (0.7%). The clinical
reviewer noted that much of the imbalance in TEAEs between sulopenem and the comparator
was accounted for by PTs in the gastrointestinal SOC, mainly diarrhea and abdominal pain. For
further details, please refer to the NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA
213972} dated July 22, 2021.
7.6.4.6. Laboratory Findings, Pooled Analyses, Trials 301 and
310
No major laboratory abnormalities were noted in the sulopenem arm of the ISP. Distribution of
abnormal chemistry laboratory findings as shown in Table 59, are similar between the sulopenem
and comparator arms. There was a slightly higher percentage of subjects with level 2
(≥200 mg/dL) glucose elevation in the sulopenem arm (4%) compared with the
amoxicillin/clavulanate (3.3%) or ciprofloxacin (2.7%) arms. However, the percentage of
subjects with level 3 (≥250 mg/dL) glucose elevations were balanced among the three arms.
While elevations in potassium were balanced between the sulopenem arm and ciprofloxacin
arms, a higher percentage of sulopenem subjects had Level 1 (>5.5 mEq/L) and Level 2 (>6

likely to be significant in the context of uUTI treatment.

All subjects in Trials 301 and 310 were female. Within the sulopenem arm, TEAEs were evenly
distributed across age groups, but occurred more frequently than in comparator arms. In contrast,

among treatment arms. The small number of subjects of other races preclude further conclusions
based on race. The frequency of AEs in subjects from Ukraine compared to the frequency of AEs
in subjects from the United States or Russia was markedly lower in both the sulopenem and
