ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)

7.7. Key Safety Review Issues
None.

8. Therapeutic Individualization
8.1. Intrinsic Factors
8.1.1. Hepatic Impairment
The effect of hepatic impairment has not been evaluated for either IV or oral sulopenem. Sixtyfive patients across all 4 phase 3 trials (301, 302, 303, and 310) had a history of hepatic disease,
including hepatic steatosis and nonspecific liver disorder. However, none of these patients had a
Child-Pugh categorization of the severity of their hepatic impairment and the safety of
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in these patients was comparable to the rest of the phase 3 trial
population. In vitro, sulopenem is not metabolized by recombinant CYP or UGT enzymes.
Additionally, the mass balance study (Study A8811006) indicated that biliary excretion does not
play a role in sulopenem elimination. Therefore, hepatic impairment is not expected to have a
clinically significant effect on sulopenem exposures, and no dosage adjustment is recommended
based on hepatic impairment.

8.1.2. Renal Impairment
The Applicant did not propose any alternative dosage recommendations for the use of sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid in patients with renal impairment. In the mass balance study,
approximately 26.9% of total radioactivity was recovered in urine as unchanged sulopenem
following oral administration of a 2000 mg dose of [14C] sulopenem etzadroxil. In the dedicated
renal impairment study (A8811009), when compared to subjects with normal renal function,
sulopenem plasma AUC0-∞ increased 2.0-, 3.0- and 7.4-fold in subjects with mild (CrCl 60 to
<90 mL/min), moderate (CrCl 30 to <60 mL/min) and severe (CrCl 15 to <30 mL/min) renal
impairment, respectively, following administration of a 1000 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil.
Because sulopenem exhibits dose proportionality within the dose range of 400 to 2000 mg,
similar fold increases in AUC are anticipated for the Applicant’s proposed 500 mg dose of
sulopenem etzadroxil. Although assessment of the effect of renal impairment on sulopenem PK
was conducted in the absence of probenecid, the observed exposure changes with sulopenem
etzadroxil are expected to approximate the fold changes in exposure with administration of the
bilayer tablet due to the decline in probenecid’s effectiveness as an OAT3 inhibitor as renal
function declines.
From an efficacy perspective, there is theoretical concern for a reduction in efficacy with
declining renal function given that renal impairment is associated with decreases in renal
clearance and ultimately, urinary concentrations of sulopenem. In Trial 301, overall response at
the TOC visit was lower in subjects with CrCl <60 mL/min compared to those with CrCl
≥60 mL/min. However, in Trial 310, overall response was comparable for subjects with CrCl
above and below this threshold (Table 69). Of note, CrCl <60 mL/min was not a pre-specified
86
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
criterion for treatment group randomization, and thus, other confounders may have contributed to
the observed outcomes in Trial 301. Therefore, the totality of information is inconclusive on the
effect of renal impairment on sulopenem’s efficacy in the treatment of uUTI and the need for an
alternative dosage strategy.

Source: Table 60 of the Applicant’s Individual Study Report IT001-310 and Statistical Reviewer’s analysis
Abbreviations: CrCl, creatinine clearance; micro-MITT, microbiological modified intent-to-treat; N, number of subjects; TOC, test of
cure

From a safety perspective, data from trial A8811009 and phase 3 Trials 301 and 310 did not
associate mild, moderate or severe renal impairment with a higher incidence of TEAEs as
compared with subjects with normal renal function. Given these observations, sulopenem’s short
plasma half-life of 1.2 h and the proposed 5-day duration of therapy, 500 mg sulopenem
etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid BID is expected to be safe in patients with CrCl ≥15 mL/min.
However, there are no PK or safety data in patients with CrCl <15 mL/min or those on
hemodialysis to inform dosage recommendations in these subpopulations. Moreover, uUTI in
patients on hemodialysis may not be considered uncomplicated. Therefore, use of 500 mg
sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid bilayer tablet is not recommended in patients with
CrCl <15 mL/min and those on hemodialysis.

8.1.3. Other Intrinsic Factors
Population PK analysis involving PK data from phase 1 trials and phase 3 Trials 301, 302 and
303 indicated that sex, body weight (38.8 to 140 kg) and age (18 to 91 years) did not have a
clinically significant effect on the PK of sulopenem.

8.2. Extrinsic Factors
8.2.1. Food Effect
Following administration of the to-be-marketed sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet
formulation to healthy adult volunteers, area under the concentration-time curve estimated to
infinity (AUC 0-∞) and maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) increased 48% and 45%,
respectively, with a high fat meal (800-1000 calories; 50% fat) compared to fasted conditions.
(b) (4)
The Applicant proposes that the bilayer tablet should be taken with food
because food increases the oral bioavailability and tolerability of sulopenem. This
recommendation is consistent with the instructions provided to Trial 301 and 310 participants.
Because neither trial recorded the type of food consumed, caloric content or timing of food
intake, fed status was poorly defined. Study 310 only provided a comparison of efficacy
outcomes based on fed status. Nonetheless, Trial 301 did provide a comparison of safety and
efficacy outcomes under fed and fasted conditions. In this trial, while the incidence of clinically

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
significant treatment-emergent diarrhea was comparable under fed (7.1%) and fasted conditions
(7.4%) (Table 70), food appeared to decrease the mean duration of treatment-emergent diarrhea
from 5.6 days to 3.7 days. The lack of a notable difference in the incidence of diarrhea is
consistent with the safety findings from the dedicated food effect Study 105, where the incidence
of GI-related TEAEs following administration of the bilayer tablet were identical (7.1%) in the
fed and fasted states. In both Trial 301 and 310, food did not appear to significantly impact
efficacy as administration of the bilayer tablet in the fed or fasted states resulted in comparable
overall response rates of 63.5% and 62.8%, respectively, at the TOC visit for the entire
microbiologically-evaluable population. Additionally, in PTA analyses, simulated sulopenem
exposures under fed conditions yielded target attainment at MIC values that were either
comparable or a single-fold dilution higher than under fasted conditions. Based on the findings
that food increases bioavailability and may improve tolerability by shortening the duration of
clinically significant treatment-emergent diarrhea, the clinical pharmacology review team
recommends administering the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet with food.

8.2.2. Summary of In Vitro Drug-Drug Interaction
Studies
In vitro studies indicated that sulopenem is a substrate of OAT3, and the prodrug sulopenem
etzadroxil is a substrate of P-gp and inhibitor of CYP3A4/5, P-gp, breast cancer resistance
protein (BCRP), OAT1 and OAT3. No clinical studies of sulopenem etzadroxil as an OAT1/3,
88
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
CYP3A4/5, BCRP and P-gp inhibitor were conducted by the Applicant. Given that sulopenem
etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed upon oral administration and was undetected in plasma in the
human mass balance study (A8811006), the potential for clinically relevant DDIs with OAT1/3
is considered to be low. Because sulopenem etzadroxil is administered orally, it has the potential
to inhibit CYP3A4/5, BCRP and P-gp in the gut. The sulopenem etzadroxil half-maximal
inhibitory concentration (IC50) for inhibition of CYP3A4/5 could not be calculated within the
concentration range studied in vitro and was estimated to be >150 μM. Although the IC50 values
for BCRP (IC50 = 20.4 μM) and P-gp (IC50 = 1.91 μM) are likely to be exceeded by more than
10-fold in the GI tract following administration of a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil,
the Applicant’s in vitro stability and release studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil is
rapidly degraded in simulated intestinal fluid. Therefore, sulopenem etzadroxil’s inhibition of
BCRP and P-gp is expected to be transient. Similarly, regardless of the magnitude of the in vitro
IC50 for CYP3A4/5 inhibition, sulopenem etzadroxil’s effect as a CYP3A4/5 inhibitor is also
expected to be transient and not to result in clinically significant DDIs with CYP3A4/5
substrates.
Probenecid is a known OAT1/3 inhibitor and was found to be a substrate and inhibitor of BCRP
in vitro. No clinical evaluations of probenecid as a BCRP substrate and inhibitor were
performed. The in vitro IC50 of probenecid as a BCRP inhibitor was 814 μM, resulting in an Igut
to IC50 ratio of 10, which is the threshold for characterizing an orally administered drug as a
BCRP inhibitor in the 2020 FDA Guidance for Industry, In Vitro Drug Interaction StudiesCytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions (January 2020).
However, because of probenecid’s low aqueous solubility (0.06 mg/mL), the probability of
clinically significant BCRP-mediated DDIs with probenecid is low.

8.2.3. Summary of Clinical Drug-Drug Interaction
Studies
8.2.3.1. Effect of P-gp Inhibitors on Sulopenem PK
Because sulopenem etzadroxil was identified as a P-gp substrate in vitro, the Applicant
conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the effect of P-gp inhibitors on sulopenem exposure
using oral itraconazole. In Study IT001-103, administration of a clinical dose of 200 mg
itraconazole (2 x 100 mg capsules) daily for 3 days in the fasted state, followed by concomitant
administration of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid on Day 4 in the fed state resulted in a nonclinically significant increase in sulopenem exposure. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is
required for coadministration of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with P-gp inhibitors.
8.2.3.2. Effect of Antacids and Proton Pump Inhibitors on
Sulopenem PK
Results of in vitro solubility studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil is a Biopharmaceutical
Classification System Class IV drug (i.e., low permeability and low solubility) that does not
exhibit pH-dependent solubility within a pH range of 1.2 to 6.8. Based on this information,
coadministration of gastric pH modifiers would not be expected to impact sulopenem’s exposure.
However, per the Applicant, in vitro stability studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil was

8.1 Pregnancy
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
Sulopenem etzadroxil was orally administered during organogenesis in
embryo-fetal studies in mice, rats, and rabbits. In pregnant mice, an
increased litter incidence of a fetal malformation, cleft palate, was
observed with an oral dose of sulopenem etzadroxil associated with a
sulopenem exposure approximately 23 times the clinical sulopenem
exposure for the MRHD of 1000 mg/day sulopenem etzadroxil. No
maternal toxicity or fetal malformations occurred in mice with doses
≤400 mg/kg/day (approximately 3 times the clinical sulopenem exposure
for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC
comparison).
In pregnant rats and rabbits, orally administered sulopenem etzadroxil
was not associated with fetal malformations at any dose, but in rats,
maternal toxicity and reduced fetal body weights occurred at sulopenem
etzadroxil doses associated with sulopenem plasma exposures
approximately 2 and 6 times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem
exposure for the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil. The doses at which no
maternal toxicity or fetal toxicity occurred in rats were, respectively,
100 mg/kg/day and 400 mg/kg/day (less than or equal to and
approximately 2 times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for
the MRHD of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).
In rabbits, maternal toxicity, reduced numbers of viable fetuses, and
reduced fetal body weights occurred at sulopenem etzadroxil doses
associated with sulopenem plasma exposures approximately 0.1 and
0.2 times, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD
of sulopenem etzadroxil. Maternal body weight gain and food
consumption were decreased in all the sulopenem etzadroxil dose
groups. The dose at which no fetal toxicity occurred was 5 mg/kg/day
(approximately 0.1-times the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD
of sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).In a prepostnatal study in rats, sulopenem etzadroxil was administered by oral
gavage to pregnant females from gestation day 6 through the lactation
period to LD 20 in maternal doses of 100, 300, and 1000 mg/kg/day. No
adverse effects on the survival, growth, behavior, or reproduction of firstgeneration offspring occurred with any of the sulopenem etzadroxil
doses up to the high dose of 1000 mg/kg/day (approximately 10-times

8.2 Lactation

Nonclinical Data

Probenecid
Available published data over several decades of probenecid use in
pregnant woman have not identified a drug-associated risk of
miscarriage, major birth defects, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes.
No embryo-fetal development studies with probenecid have been
conducted in animals. Probenecid crosses the placental barrier and
appears in cord blood.
Human Data
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
There are no data on the presence of sulopenem etzadroxil or its
metabolite in human milk, the effects on the breastfed infant, or the
effects on milk production.
Probenecid
Probenecid is present in human milk based on a case report. There are
no reports of adverse effects in infants associated with probenecid
exposure through breastmilk. There is no information on the effects of
probenecid on milk production.

13.1 Carcinogenesis,
Mutagenesis,
Impairment of Fertility

Animal Data
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
The active metabolite of sulopenem etzadroxil, sulopenem, was present
in rat milk after oral dosing of sulopenem etzadroxil to lactating female
rats. When a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely that the drug will
be present in human milk.
Impairment of Fertility
Sulopenem Etzadroxil
Male and female fertility and early embryonic development were
examined in rats (20/sex/group) orally administered sulopenem
etzadroxil in daily doses of 100, 400, or 2000 mg/kg beginning 28 days
prior to mating and throughout the mating period in males and for 14
days before mating, throughout the mating period, and until GD 7 in
females. There were no treatment-related effects on estrous cycle
length, mating and fertility rates, implantation, conceptus viability, sperm
concentration and motility, or accessory male sex gland weights. No
adverse effects on male and female fertility or early embryonic
development in female rats were observed at doses up to
2000 mg/kg/day (approximately 10- and 12-times in male and female
rats, respectively, the clinical sulopenem exposure for the MRHD of
sulopenem etzadroxil based on plasma AUC comparison).

Human Pregnancy Data
Pregnant women were excluded from all clinical studies of sulopenem. However, one pregnancy
(b) (6)
occurred in the sulopenem arm of Trial 310. A 22-year-old woman (Subject
) received
5 days of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid. The baseline urine pregnancy test was negative as
was a urine pregnancy test on Day 28. On Day 41, a serum pregnancy test was positive. Possible
conception dates were determined to be 12-22 days after the sulopenem course was completed;
therefore, it was unlikely the subject was pregnant while receiving sulopenem. The subject gave
birth to a full term healthy female baby.
There was also one pregnancy in the sulopenem arm of Trial 301. A 26-year-old woman had a
negative screening urine pregnancy test at the trial site but three days later, the central laboratory
reported the pregnancy test as positive. Study drug was stopped. The subject had an uneventful
pregnancy and gave birth to a healthy male baby 8 months later.
During the initial review of NDA 213972, DPMH was consulted to assist with the Pregnancy and
Lactation subsections of labeling. In their consult response dated May 4, 2021, DPMH noted that
as a penem antibacterial drug, sulopenem is very similar to carbapenems, and teratogenic risks
and adverse maternal and fetal outcomes have not been identified with carbapenem use during
94
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
pregnancy. Additionally, based on decades of experience with carbapenems, sulopenem is not
expected to cause harmful effects in breastfed infants. DPMH also observed that available
published studies over several decades of probenecid use in pregnancy have not identified a
drug-related risk of miscarriage, congenital malformations, or adverse maternal or fetal
outcomes. Therefore, DPMH did not recommend a postmarketing pregnancy study or
postmarketing lactation study for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid.

9. Product Quality
Approval
This NDA was recommended for approval from the Product Quality perspective in the first
review cycle (refer to the Office of Pharmaceutical Quality (OPQ) Integrated Quality
Assessment # 1, dated June 1, 2021, in the Document Archiving Reporting and Regulatory
Tracking System. The drug product is a pink, oval-shaped, film coated, immediate release,
bilayer tablet, containing 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid, and
conventional excipients of compendial grade. With the current NDA resubmission (SDN# 71,
dated April 25, 2024), several changes and updates have been proposed in Module 3, such as
removal of blister packaging originally proposed for the drug product. The OPQ review team has
assessed the NDA 213972 resubmission with respect to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls
and has determined that it meets all applicable standards to support the identity, strength, quality,
and purity that it purports. The currently proposed commercial packaging configurations for the
drug product include high density polyethylene bottles only (10-count and 30-count) with childresistant caps. Based on the overall stability data package submitted in the original NDA and the
resubmission, the proposed expiration dating of 60 months is granted for the drug product to be
stored at room temperature (20-25°C). All proposed commercial manufacturing and testing
facilities have been found acceptable and an overall “Approve” recommendation was entered
into Panorama by the Office of Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Assessment on September 6,
2024. As such, OPQ recommends approval of this NDA from a quality perspective (refer to the
OPQ Integrated Quality Assessment # 2, dated September 25, 2024, in DARRTS).

The following discussion questions were posed to the AC:

The Applicant is seeking an indication for sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid in adult

microorganisms. Discuss the overall benefits and risks for the use of sulopenem

Although there were no voting questions, the AC members discussed concerns for potential
downstream risks to both individual patients and to society from antimicrobial cross-resistance to
carbapenems arising from unrestricted empiric use of oral sulopenem for uUTI in an ambulatory
setting. The potential lack of mechanisms for effective antimicrobial stewardship in an
ambulatory setting in general was discussed. Given the totality of evidence presented in the FDA
Briefing Document and the concerns outlined above, the AC members recommended restricting
the indication and providing limitations of use statements.

12. Summary of Regulatory History
On March 1, 2016, Iterum Therapeutics US Ltd. (Sponsor) submitted IND 129849, for
sulopenem etzadroxil (PF-03709270 sulopenem oral prodrug) tablets.
A type C Guidance meeting was held on February 27, 2017, to discuss the development program
for PF-03709270. The Sponsor stated that following completion of the ongoing phase 1 clinical
program the Sponsor would select the prodrug to move forward into clinical development.
An End of Phase 2 meeting was held on July 21, 2017, to discuss the design of Trial 301 for the
treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infection (uUTI). During this meeting, the Division
emphasized that the clinical response component of the overall response endpoint (combined
clinical and microbiological responses) should be defined as the resolution of all urinary tract
infection (UTI) symptoms present at trial entry. Discussion also included considerations of
evaluation of sulopenem versus ciprofloxacin based on assessment of non-inferiority (NI) in the
micro-MITTS (ciprofloxacin-susceptible) population and assessment of superiority in the microMITTR population (ciprofloxacin-resistant population). The Division noted that the primary
analysis population in an NI analysis should only include patients with pathogens susceptible to
the proposed comparator.
A type B, chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) meeting was held on August 28, 2017.
During this meeting the data needed to demonstrate comparability between the sources of the
drug substance, frequency of microbial testing, impurity testing, dissolution methods, suitability
of batch manufacture and the overall CMC-development program to support NDA submission
was discussed.
On September 19, 2017, the Sponsor submitted their initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) to IND
129849 and an Agreed iPSP letter was issued on February 26, 2018.
On October 27, 2017, PF-03709270/probenecid (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid) bilayer tablet
was granted Qualified Infectious Disease Product (QIDP) designation for uUTI, complicated
urinary tract infection (cUTI), and complicated intra-abdominal infection (cIAI) and Fast Track
designation for these same indications on March 15, 2019.
On December 8, 2017, in follow-up to a meeting request to discuss the statistical analysis plan
for study IT001-301, the Division provided the Sponsor with comments on the proposed
framework for hypothesis testing and interim analysis. The Division commented that discordant
results in the two primary analyses (assessment of NI in the microbiological modified intent-totreat ciprofloxacin- susceptible (micro-MITTS) population and assessment of superiority in the
microbiological modified intent-to-treat ciprofloxacin-resistant (micro-MITTR) population)
could be problematic and that there would need to be an understanding of the reasons for
discrepant findings. Further, such results may also have labeling implications.
On December 27, 2017, the Sponsor submitted a Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) for
Protocol IT001-301, entitled: “A prospective, Phase 3, randomized, multi-center, double-blind

302 (for cUTI) and 303 (for cIAI) were submitted as supportive data only, as both trials failed to
meet their primary endpoints.
On February 25, 2021, the Division provided an update on the NDA review during the MidCycle Communication teleconference; on May 26, 2021, the Late-Cycle Meeting was held with
the Applicant to discuss substantive review issues. No Advisory Committee meeting was held
during the first cycle review.
The NDA received a complete response action on July 23, 2021, due to lack of substantial
evidence of effectiveness (SEE). While sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid demonstrated
superiority to ciprofloxacin for the overall (clinical and microbiological) response rate in the
micro-MITTR population, the product was inferior in the micro-MITTS population.
Additionally, the cUTI Trial 302 and cIAI Trial 303, conducted with IV sulopenem followed by
oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid stepdown therapy, failed to meet their primary endpoints
and thus, were not considered to provide supportive evidence of effectiveness. FDA
recommended that the Applicant conduct an additional trial for uUTI using a different
comparator.
On September 23, 2021, a type-A, Post Action meeting was held to discuss and clarify the
deficiencies outlined in the complete response letter and on December 21, 2021, a type B,

Nonclinical PK/PD Studies
Identification of PK/PD Index for Sulopenem
PK/PD index and target determination for sulopenem were previously conducted using
neutropenic and immune-competent murine thigh infection models. As with other beta-lactams,
the percent of time that free drug concentrations remain above the minimum inhibitory
concentration (%fT>MIC) was expected to be the PK/PD driver of sulopenem’s efficacy.
However, the Applicant’s dose fractionation studies failed to illustrate definitively the index
most relevant to efficacy, instead suggesting that the relevant index is pathogen-specific.
Because the relevant PK/PD index for antibacterial drugs is typically pathogen independent, the
discordance between pathogens was partly illustrative of the complexities of sulopenem’s PK/PD
properties. However, ambiguities within the study methodology and inconsistences with data
analysis raised concerns about the reliability and interpretability of study findings. Refer to NDA
213972 Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021, for further details. As a
result of these observations, the Applicant was asked to conduct additional dose fractionation
studies to better understand sulopenem’s PK/PD behavior. Because sulopenem has a short
murine half-life of ~5 min, completion of PK/PD studies in the murine model of infection is
technically challenging. Therefore, the review team agreed that the Applicant may conduct
subsequent PK/PD studies in an in vitro model of infection.

101

Using a wild-type strain of E. coli (NCTC 13441), a series of duplicate dose-fractionation studies
were conducted in a 1-compartment in vitro infection model using 5 different total sulopenem
daily doses of 62.5, 125, 250, 500 and 2000 mg divided equally according to q4h, q8h or q12h
dosing regimens. To approximate oral absorption, sulopenem was infused into the in vitro
system over 2 h. A Hill-type model was fit to the resulting PK and PD (i.e., changes in bacterial
burden) to determine which of the 3 traditional PK/PD indices best correlates with sulopenem’s
activity. %fT>MIC held the strongest correlation with sulopenem’s activity based on r2 values
(Figure 4), followed closely by free-drug maximum plasma concentration/MIC. These findings
suggest that sulopenem exhibits both time and concentration-dependent bacterial killing.

Reviewer’s comment: %fTime>MIC was selected as the PK/PD index for sulopenem as it is the
index typically attributed to the beta-lactam drug class. However, the fact that free-drug
maximum plasma concentration/MIC is also highly correlated with bacterial killing suggests
sulopenem’s dosing could be also optimized by maximizing maximum plasma concentration.
Determination of PK/PD Targets for Sulopenem
Instead of a separate set of dose-ranging studies dedicated to target determination, the Applicant
relied upon the results of the dose fractionation studies against a set of Gram-positive and Gramnegative pathogens to determine the magnitude of %fT>MIC (the assumed PK/PD index for
sulopenem) required for stasis and 1-log kill. The atypical approach to target determination and
concerns with reliability of data precluded use of this data to inform probability of target
attainment (PTA) analyses.
Dose-ranging studies were conducted in duplicate in the 1-compartment in vitro infection model
against a panel of 10 Enterobacterales (i.e., 6 E. coli and 4 K. pneumoniae) with sulopenem
MICs of 0.03 to 0.5 µg/mL. Free sulopenem exposures associated with doses ranging from 7.81
to 2000 mg q12h were simulated in the model to determine the magnitude of sulopenem
%fT>MIC required to achieve stasis, 1-log and 2-log kill. Similar to the dose fractionation
studies, sulopenem was infused into the in vitro system over 2 h to simulate oral absorption, and
a Hill-type model was fitted to the resulting data to determine individual as well as pooled targets
for each of the bacteriologic endpoints of interest. 1-log kill was achieved in all but 1 isolate,

while 2-log kill was achieved in only 4 of the 10 isolates. The median %fT>MIC targets were
40.9, 50.2 and 62.6% for stasis, 1-log and 2-log kill, respectively.
Proof-of-Concept Study in a Hollow Fiber Infection Model
In a series of studies conducted in a hollow fiber infection model, sulopenem urinary exposures
associated with 500 mg q12h regimen were simulated against 4 extended-spectrum β-lactamase
(ESBL)-positive E. coli isolates with sulopenem MICs 0.03 to 0.06 µg/mL. The selected isolates
were resistant to levofloxacin and susceptible to meropenem to allow for the use of levofloxacin
750 mg q24h and meropenem 2 g q8h as negative and positive controls, respectively. For all 4
isolates, sulopenem exposures associated with 500 mg q12h produced a sustained reduction in
bacterial burden from baseline and suppressed the development of resistance. Representative
results for 1 of the isolates, E. coli 845741, are shown in Figure 5.

14.5. Pharmacometrics Assessment
14.5.1. Review Summary
The Applicant previously developed a population PK (PopPK) model using plasma PK data from
nine phase 1 and three phase 3 trials, in which sulopenem etzadroxil was administered either as a
monolayer tablet, the to-be-marketed bilayer tablet and a powder-in-bottle (PIB) formulation
with or without probenecid. Briefly, the PopPK model was previously reviewed in detail and
found to reasonably describe the concentration-time profiles of sulopenem in healthy subjects
and subjects with uUTI. Additionally, the PopPK model was considered acceptable in generating
exposure parameters (i.e., area under the concentration-time curve during the dosing interval and
maximum plasma concentration) to support labeling statements. However, potential correlations
between intrinsic and extrinsic factors (i.e., renal function, food effects, and formulations) (with
or without probenecid) may confound the evaluation and interpretation of covariate effects on
sulopenem PK, and as such, careful consideration should be exercised when interpreting
simulations (e.g., PTA) based on the correlated covariates. Refer to the NDA 213972 Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021, for details on the PopPK model
evaluation and utility.
In the current submission, the PopPK model was extended to describe the disposition of
sulopenem in urine (i.e., fraction of elimination from the central compartment to urine
compartment) based on urinary exposure data obtained from a subset of the studied PK
population (i.e., healthy subjects). Additionally, urine PTA was conducted to predict the
proportion of subjects achieving specified target exposures in the urine. Although the updated
PopPK model is generally acceptable for characterizing sulopenem urine PK in phase 1 Trial 101
and phase 3 Trial 302, the model did not reasonably describe the phase 3 Trial 301 urine data. It
is unclear whether this is due to a difference in sulopenem urine PK between healthy subjects
and those with uUTI. Further, there are uncertainties regarding the assumed bladder voiding
frequencies that limit the interpretability of the urine PTA results. Nonetheless, the plasma-based
PTA results support a susceptible breakpoint of up to 0.5 mcg/mL.

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)

14.5.2. Introduction
The objectives of the PopPK analysis were to:
•

Develop a PopPK model to describe the disposition of sulopenem in plasma and urine

•

Evaluate the impact of clinically relevant covariates on the PK of sulopenem

•

Predict the probability of PK/PD target attainment in plasma and urine

14.5.3. Model Development
The clinical Pharmacology Review Team previously reviewed the model development,
evaluation of model performance and covariate analysis; refer to NDA 213972 Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22, 2021. Briefly, the PopPK model is based on
data from 12 studies as summarized in (Table 73); there are no PK data available from Trial 310.
A summary of the number of observations from each trial and demographic information are
provided in Table 74, Table 75 and Table 76. Phase 1 studies included rich PK sampling while
sparse samples were obtained in the phase 3 trial participants. A graphical illustration of the
initial model, which was a 3-compartment model with non-linear elimination developed using
only plasma PK data, is shown in Figure 6.
For urine observations, urine concentration and volume data were collected for 243 subjects in
Trials 101, 301, and 302 (Table 76). The final and updated PopPK model was based on urine
measurements results from Day 1 of Trial 101, where the urine collection process was wellcontrolled and yielded reliable urine concentration and volume data (i.e., with sampling at 2 h
intervals through 12 h post dosing in 32 subjects) in healthy subjects. In total, 32 unique subjects
contributed 159 urine concentration and urine volume observations. Because urine PK data were
available for only a subset of subjects in the PK population, the Applicant limited their analyses
to estimation of urine-specific parameters (i.e., urine fraction, inter-individual variability in urine
fraction, and a residual error of the urine concentration data) by fixing the plasma PopPK model
parameters to individual’s empirical Bayes estimates.

Table 77 and Table 78, respectively. Parameters were generally estimated with precision

Using the final model parameter estimates and assuming no difference between healthy
volunteers and patients, urine PK was simulated for Trials 101, 301 and 302 population.
Prediction-corrected visual predictive check plots for the sulopenem urinary concentrations in
the presence or absence of food and probenecid indicate that although the updated model tends to
reasonably capture the central tendency for data in Trials 101 and 302, there are underpredictions
for the respective 95th percentiles of the observed urine data in these two studies. Furthermore,
the relatively wide 95% CI of the predicted 5th percentiles for the observed urine data in Trials
101 and 302 are likely due to small sample size and high variability (Figure 8). For Trial 301, the
updated PopPK model underpredicts the urine exposures, and it is unclear which factor(s) (i.e.,
potential difference in urine PK between subjects in Trial 101 and Trial 301, shorter urine PK
collection period in Trial 301, or relatively higher variabilities of the nominal urine concentration
compared to those of Trials 101 and 302) may account for the underpredictions. Because of these
limitations, the urine PTA findings based on the updated PopPK model should be interpreted
with caution.

14.5.4. Probability of Target Attainment in Plasma and
Urine
The final PopPK model was subsequently used to simulate and estimate PTAs for both plasma
and urine using Monte Carlo simulations. Patient covariates incorporated in the PopPK model
(i.e., body weight, sex, and creatinine clearance [CrCl]) were obtained by re-sampling
111
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
individuals, with replacement, from the analysis dataset (from Trials 101, 301, and 302),
resulting in the covariate distributions summarized in Table 79. Although in the current
regulatory setting, uUTI is generally considered to occur in women with normal genitourinary
anatomy inclusion of data from male trial participants (who are expected to exhibit lower
sulopenem exposures than females based on model predictions) was reasonable to allow a more
conservative estimation of PTA (Section 2.1). To account for the impact of bladder emptying,
two voiding frequencies (i.e., 1 h and 2 h) were evaluated. However, it is unclear whether these
voiding patterns are readily generalizable in clinical settings. The urine production rate (L/h)
used in the simulations was based on literature reports indicating normal urine production rates
of 0.5-1.5 mL/kg/h. A value of 1 mL/kg/h appeared to best align with observed urine production
rates in 101, 301, and 302 (calculated as measured urine volume (L) divided by time in between
observations).

A total of 5000 subjects were simulated where each subject had one MIC value drawn from the
distribution for Trial 301. Probability of achieving the %fT>MIC targets derived from
nonclinical PK/PD studies was then assessed for a 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg
probenecid dose. Typically, PTA analyses rely upon the epidemiological MIC distribution, but
this alternative was acceptable given that the MIC distribution from Trial 301 mirrors the
epidemiological values (see Section 19.1). Given the review team’s finding that the murine thigh
infection model-informed PK/PD targets are unreliable (see Section 5.1), PTA results in plasma
and urine are only presented for the in vitro PK/PD targets.

15. Study/Trial Design
Inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, analysis populations, and efficacy endpoints of Trial 310 are
described below.
Inclusion Criteria
Patients had to meet the following criteria to be eligible for the study:
•

Female patients ≥18 years of age with ≥24 hours and ≤96 hours attributable to a UTI

•

Two of the following signs and symptoms of uUTI: urinary frequency, urinary urgency, pain
or burning on micturition, suprapubic pain

•

A mid-stream urine specimen with:
– a machine-read dipstick positive for nitrite AND any positive leukocyte esterase
OR
– evidence of pyuria alone as defined by either:
▪

a machine-read dipstick positive for large leukocyte esterase

▪

at least 10 white blood cells per cubic millimeter on microscopic analysis of unspun
urine

▪

white blood cell count ≥10 cells/HPF in the sediment of a spun urine

OR

OR
•

Has given written informed consent to participate in the study

Exclusion Criteria
Patients who met any of the following criteria were excluded from the study:
•

Presence of signs and symptoms suggestive of acute pyelonephritis defined as: fever
(temperature >38° Celsius), chills, costovertebral angle tenderness, flank pain, nausea, and/or
vomiting

•

Receipt of antibacterial drug therapy potentially effective as treatment of uUTI within the
prior 7 days

•

Concurrent use of non-study treatments that would have a potential effect on outcome
evaluations in patients with uUTI, including analgesics (e.g., non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs, aspirin, paracetamol etc.), phenazopyridine, and cranberry products. Note: Patients
could be included if these medications were previously taken and had ceased at the time of
Screening onward.

•

Any anatomical abnormality of the urinary tract, including surgically modified urinary tract
anatomy, and obstructive uropathy due to nephrolithiasis, stricture, tumor, or fibrosis

•

Ongoing urinary retention

•

Neurogenic bladder

•

Current resident of a long-term care facility

Instrumentation of urinary tract in the previous 30 days

•

An indwelling urinary catheter, ureteral stent or other foreign material in the urinary tract

Any history of trauma to the pelvis or urinary tract

Current urine culture, if available while evaluating eligibility, that was positive for more than
2 microorganisms regardless of colony count (contaminated), or confirmed a fungal UTI

Urine samples, including results from urine tests, collected as part of routine standard of care,
prior to obtaining informed consent, may have been used to assess eligibility for enrollment into
study and/or for baseline urine culture.
Analysis Populations
Intent-to-Treat (ITT): all randomized patients regardless of whether or not the patient received
study drug.
Modified ITT (MITT): randomized patients who received at least a single dose of study
medication.
Micro-MITT: all MITT patients with a positive study entry urine culture defined as ≥105
colony-forming units (CFU)/mL of a uropathogen (Enterobacterales or S. saprophyticus only)
and no more than 2 species of microorganisms identified in the study entry urine culture,
regardless of colony count.
The primary comparisons for regulatory approval were in two mutually exclusive subpopulations
of the microbiological modified intent-to-treat (micro-MITT) population defined by a baseline
characteristic, the micro-MITTS and micro-MITTR populations:
•

Micro-MITTS population: the subset of patients whose baseline pathogens were
determined to be susceptible (MIC ≤8/4 mg/L) to the comparator study drug,
amoxicillin/clavulanate.

•

Micro-MITTR population: the subset of patients whose baseline pathogen was determined
to be non-susceptible [intermediate (MIC 16/8 mg/L) or resistant (MIC ≥32/16 mg/L)] to the
comparator study drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate.

Efficacy Endpoints
Primary Efficacy Endpoint
The primary efficacy endpoint was overall success (combined clinical and microbiologic
success) on Day 12 (±1 days)/test of cure (TOC) in the micro-MITT, micro-MITTS and microMITTR populations.
A patient was defined as an overall success if the following criteria were met:
•

The patient was alive

•

The patient received no rescue therapy for uUTI
– If an antibiotic active against the urinary tract pathogen was given for other reasons, then
the patient would be considered indeterminate

•

The patient had resolution of the symptoms of uUTI present at trial entry and no new uUTI
symptoms (based on the Patient Symptom Assessment Questionnaire)

•

Urine culture taken on Day 12 (± 1 day)/TOC demonstrated <103 CFU/mL of the baseline
uropathogen based on results of quantitative cultures performed on collected urine
specimens.

All other patients would be considered as failures unless data were unavailable to determine
whether the patient was a success or a failure. In this case, the patient would be considered as
having an indeterminate response. Patients with an indeterminate response were included in the
denominator for determination of the overall success rate.
For overall response, if the urine culture was contaminated, baseline pathogen(s) was/were
considered eradicated. For microbiologic response, contaminated results were considered a
negative culture and therefore an eradication. We will conduct additional analysis to address the
effect of contamination coded as eradication for the primary efficacy endpoint.

denominator for determination of the response rate.
Investigator-Determined Clinical Response
The following clinical response definitions were used by the investigators:
•

Clinical success: all pre-therapy signs and symptoms of the index infection had resolved
such that no additional antibiotics were required.

•

Clinical failure: patients who met any one of the following criteria:
– Death related to uUTI prior to end of trial (EOT), TOC, and final visit (FV), respectively
– Persistence or progression of any pre-therapy uUTI signs and symptoms or use of
additional antibiotics for the current infection
– Patient previously met criteria for failure and received rescue antibiotics

•

Indeterminate: Data not available for evaluation of efficacy for any reason, including but
not limited to:
– Patient lost to follow-up or assessment not undertaken such that a determination of
clinical response could not be made at either the EOT, TOC or FV, respectively
– Death prior to EOT, TOC, or FV, respectively, where uUTI was clearly non-contributory

16. Efficacy
The results from Trial 301, the micro-MITT and ITT populations of Trial 310, Trial 302 for
cUTI, and Trial 303 for cIAI are included in this section. Trials 301, 302 and 303 were included
in the initial NDA submission; therefore, only a brief summary of these three trials is included in
this review.

16.1. Summary of Trial 301 in uUTI
A total of 1660 adult women with uUTI were randomized and received trial medications in this
multinational, randomized, double-blind clinical trial comparing oral sulopenem etzadroxil
500 mg and probenecid 500 mg twice daily (BID) for 5 days to oral ciprofloxacin 250 mg BID
for 3 days. The micro-MITT population, which included all patients who had at least one
uropathogen isolated at baseline (≥105 CFU/mL), consisted of 1105 patients; the median age was
53 years; median weight in the randomized population was 70.4 kg. Patients were enrolled from
the United States (55%) and Eastern Europe (45%). Patients were Caucasian (90%), African
American (9%) or of other races (1%).
Composite response (combined microbiological response and clinical cure) was determined by
comparing the response rate of sulopenem to ciprofloxacin at the TOC visit (12 days after
randomization) in two primary populations: Micro-MITTS (micro-MITT population with
baseline pathogens susceptible to ciprofloxacin, MIC ≤1 μg/mL) and Micro-MITTR (microMITT population with baseline pathogens non-susceptible to ciprofloxacin, MIC ≥2 μg/mL).

ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Clinical cure was defined as the resolution of patient-reported uUTI symptoms and no new uUTI
symptoms. Microbiological response was defined as a reduction of all baseline uropathogens to
less than 103 CFU/mL in the urine.
Sulopenem demonstrated efficacy in the micro-MITTR population but did not demonstrate
efficacy in the micro-MITTS population.

16.2. Study Results, Micro-MITT Population, Trial
310
The Applicant listed the micro-MITT population as Step 1 in the hierarchical testing procedure
and reported the results. Therefore, we include the results from this population in the review. As
the micro-MITT population was mainly composed of micro-MITTS subjects, the results were
very similar to those in the micro-MITTS population.
Disposition
Overall, approximately 96% of the 990 micro-MITT subjects completed study drug treatment,
while 4% discontinued treatment prematurely. The primary reasons for discontinuation of
treatment were non-compliance with study drug (1.1%) and withdrawal by subject (1.2%). The
primary reasons for discontinuation of study were loss to follow-up (2.0%) and withdrawal by
subject (2.3%).

16.4. Trial 302 for cUTI
Trial 302 was a phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial designed to compare the
efficacy, tolerability, and safety of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid with that of IV ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin or
amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of cUTI in both men and women.
Subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive either IV sulopenem 1000 mg once daily for at least
5 days (five doses) followed by oral sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg co-administered with oral
probenecid 500 mg BID to complete 7 to 10 total days of treatment versus ertapenem IV
1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg or
129
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
amoxicillin/clavulanate 875 mg BID to complete 7 to 10 total days of therapy. Duration of
treatment could be extended up to a total of 14 days for patients with bacteremia at baseline.
The primary efficacy endpoint was overall response (resolution of symptoms and clearance of
the baseline uropathogen) at Day 21 (TOC). The primary analysis population was the microMITT, defined as subjects who received at least a single dose of study medication, had the
disease under study (with two of the five baseline cUTI symptoms), and a positive study entry
urine culture within 48 h prior to the first dose. The study entry urine culture had to have no
more than two species of uropathogens (Enterobacterales only, susceptible to sulopenem [MIC
≤1] and ertapenem [MIC ≤0.5]) at ≥105 CFU/mL, except in the situation where one of the
organisms cultured from the urine was also isolated from blood cultures drawn at baseline.
Patients with a study pathogen isolated from baseline blood cultures were included in the microMITT population regardless of the patient’s baseline urine culture result.
The Applicant’s efficacy results were based on definitions of microbiological responses using the
same definition for “persistence” as in Trial 301, i.e., a uropathogen present in baseline urine
culture which grew at ≥103 CFU/mL at TOC with further specification as follows: “The
genus/species and susceptibility profiles need to match. For the Baseline and TOC visits,
additional molecular testing by pulsed field gel electrophoresis or whole-genome sequencing
may be performed for confirmation.” FDA requested reanalysis of the data for Trials 301, 302,
and 303 (for cIAI), based on definitions of microbiological response without using additional
molecular testing. The results from the two analyses from the initial and updated reports were
consistent, but only the results using the initial statistical analysis plan (SAP) are reported here.
The two treatment groups were comparable with respect to demographic characteristics. The
majority of subjects were female (about 55%). The mean age was about 59 years (range 18 to
94 years). The majority of subjects had acute pyelonephritis (57.1% in the sulopenem arm;
56.9% in the ertapenem arm). E. coli was the most common organism isolated (76.1% on
sulopenem; 78.6% on ertapenem).
As shown in the following Table 96, Trial 302 failed to show noninferiority using a -10%
noninferiority margin. IV sulopenem followed by oral (PO) sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid
was significantly worse than the active comparator, IV ertapenem followed by PO ciprofloxacin
or amoxicillin/clavulanate.

Efficacy Conclusions From Trial 302
Trial 302 did not provide evidence for the efficacy of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid for the treatment of cUTI. In the primary efficacy analysis of overall
clinical and microbiological response at the TOC visit, IV sulopenem followed by oral
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid did not demonstrate noninferiority compared to the control
group treated with IV ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin or oral amoxicillin/clavulanate.
Further, the sulopenem group was statistically inferior to the control group. Results for overall
response in the two treatment groups were similar at Day 5 (the minimum duration of IV
therapy) and the EOT but differed by the TOC visit on Day 21. The efficacy decrement was
driven by a difference in microbiologic response rates, as clinical response rates were similar
between the sulopenem and ertapenem treatment groups. There was remaining uncertainty
regarding whether any efficacy decrements were due to the intravenous or oral sulopenem
because while the randomized comparisons were designed to evaluate intravenous-to-oral
regimens, results were suggestive of an efficacy decrement of stepdown sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid compared to stepdown ciprofloxacin in subjects with ciprofloxacinsusceptible pathogens. Such an efficacy decrement is consistent with the Trial 301 results seen
for uUTI where the noninferiority of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid to oral ciprofloxacin
in ciprofloxacin-susceptible isolates was not demonstrated.

16.5. Trial 303 for cIAI
Trial 303 was a phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial designed to compare the
efficacy, tolerability, and safety of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid with that of IV ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin and
metronidazole or amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of cIAI.
A total of 674 subjects were randomized (1:1) to receive either IV sulopenem 1000 mg once
daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg co-administered
with oral probenecid 500 mg twice daily to complete 7 to 10 total days of treatment or ertapenem
IV 1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (five doses) followed by oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg
twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg four times a day or amoxicillin/clavulanate 875 mg twice
daily to complete 7 to 10 total days of therapy. Duration of treatment could be extended up to a
total of 14 days. The results are shown in Table 101. After initial unblinding of the study,
imbalances in outcome by treatment were identified by the Applicant. Subsequently, the
Applicant conducted a post hoc analysis by re-examining and re-analyzing the data. FDA did not
agree with the Applicant’s post hoc analysis after the study data were unblinded. Trial 303 failed
to show NI using a -10% margin, either based on the primary analysis or the post hoc analysis.

19. Clinical Microbiology
19.1. Nonclinical Microbiology
Please refer to the previous Multidisciplinary Review dated July 22, 2021, for the evaluation of
in vitro and in vivo microbiology data presented in the initial NDA submission. No new in vitro
and in vivo studies were conducted for this resubmission.
Clinical Studies for the uUTI Indication
The Applicant conducted two phase 3 uUTI clinical trials (IT001-301 or Trial 301 and IT001310 or Trial 310) to determine the safety and efficacy of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid
for this indication. For the treatment of adult women with uUTI, oral sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid was compared with oral ciprofloxacin in Trial 301, while in Trial 310, oral
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was compared with oral amoxicillin/clavulanate.
Data from Trial 301 were reviewed for the initial NDA submission and are not included in this
review. Please refer to the previous Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22,
2021. There are no pooled analyses, as only one phase 3 trial, Trial 310 is included in this
resubmission. Therefore, this review only covers the uUTI Trial 310 and the Agency’s
recommendation on sulopenem broth microdilution MIC and disk diffusion breakpoints (BPs)
for the uUTI-indicated Enterobacterales species.
uUTI Phase 3 Clinical Study: IT001-310 or Trial 310
In Trial 310, oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid was compared with oral
amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of adult women with uUTI. The primary endpoint was
overall response on Day 12 (±1 day) which was the TOC visit.
Definitions of Analysis Populations
Intent-to-Treat: The ITT population included all randomized patients regardless of whether the
patient received study drug.
Modified ITT: The MITT group included all randomized patients who received at least a single
dose of study medication. Patients were analyzed according to the treatment group to which they
were randomized.
Microbiologic-MITT (or micro-MITT): Micro-MITT patients were MITT patients with a
positive study entry urine culture defined as ≥105 CFU/mL of a uropathogen (Enterobacterales
or S. saprophyticus only) and no more than two species of microorganisms identified in the study
entry urine culture, regardless of colony count.
Micro-MITTS: The micro-MITTS population comprised micro-MITT patients with a baseline
uropathogen susceptible to the comparator drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate (defined as MIC
≤8/4 mg/L per Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [CLSI] breakpoints [CLSI M100]),
and no baseline pathogen non-susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanate.

141
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
Micro-MITTR: The micro-MITTR population comprised micro-MITT patients with a baseline
uropathogen non-susceptible (intermediate [MIC 16/8 mg/L per CLSI M100] or resistant [MIC
≥32/16 mg/L per CLSI M100]) to the comparator drug, amoxicillin/clavulanate.
In the ITT populations, a total of 522/1111 (47%) and 468/1111 (42.1%) patients were in the
micro-MITT populations of the sulopenem arm and amoxicillin/clavulanate arm, respectively.
The micro-MITT population included both micro-MITTS (patients with a baseline pathogen
susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanate) and micro-MITTR (patients with a baseline pathogen
non-susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanate) populations. In Trial 310, the micro-MITTR
population was very small (3% total in both arms) compared to the micro-MITTR (18%) in Trial
301.
Microbiological Sampling
Methods for Microbiological Collection, Culture, and Identification
For microbiological culture and analysis, mid-stream clean-catch urine specimens were collected
from patients at Screening (Baseline), Day 3, Day 5 (EOT), Day 12 (TOC), Day 28, and for any
study-related visits. Urine samples were received at International Health Management Associates
in boric acid tubes within 48 hours of collection, either ambient or refrigerated.
Baseline/screening urine samples were cultured on blood agar plates, and MacConkey plates
using a 1 µL loop. Samples from all other visits were cultured on blood agar plates, CAN, and
MacConkey plates using a 1 µL and a 10 µL loop. All culture plates were incubated at 35°C for
18 to 24 hours in non-CO2 incubators.
Target Pathogens
For Study IT001-310, the following organisms were considered a uropathogen when isolated
from an acceptable urine culture specimen:
Monomicrobial or polymicrobial infections caused by:
•

Enterobacterales

•

Staphylococcus saprophyticus

•

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

•

Enterococcus spp.

The latter two organisms were considered non-target pathogens. All target and non-target
pathogens were identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization–Time of Flight
(MALDI-TOF), had aspartate aminotransferase testing by broth microdilution, and were saved
when considered significant. Disk diffusion testing was performed on only Enterobacterales and
S. saprophyticus. The micro-MITT population for this study only included patients with uUTIs
caused by Enterobacterales. A study urine culture that was positive for more than two species of
microorganisms was considered contaminated, regardless of colony count.
Microbiological Outcome Measures
The microbiological definitions used in the assessment of the per-pathogen microbiological
response at baseline and post-baseline are summarized in Table 104 and Table 105.

As mentioned earlier, the Applicant also conducted two additional phase 3 trials to evaluate the
safety and efficacy of sulopenem for the treatment of cUTI and cIAI; both failed to meet their

treatment of uUTI, were reviewed in the Multidisciplinary Review and Evaluation dated July 22,
2021.

Correlation of Microbiological Success to MIC Values of Baseline E. coli, K. pneumoniae,
and P. mirabilis Isolates From uUTI Trials 301 and 310
Microbiological success at the TOC visit, in relation to MIC values of total baseline E. coli, K.
pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis isolates from the sulopenem treatment group in the micro-MITT
population of both uUTI clinical trials (301 and 310), are summarized below:
•

Among a total of 876 baseline E. coli isolates from Trials 301 and 310, the MIC range was
≤0.008 to 1.0 mcg/mL; the MIC90 values against E. coli isolates from surveillance and
clinical studies were 0.03 and 0.06 mcg/mL, respectively. Overall microbiological
eradication/success at TOC was achieved in 661/876 (75.5%) isolates. While the cumulative
microbiological success rate of 75.4% (660/875) was achieved up to the highest MIC
0.25 mcg/mL, 5/7 (71.4%) isolates were eradicated at this MIC. No baseline E. coli isolates
with MIC 0.5 mcg/mL or ≥2 mcg/mL were available; only one baseline E. coli isolate with
sulopenem MIC of 1 mcg/mL was available and eradicated. Therefore, we recommend a
susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL as more appropriate to cover most of the E. coli population.

•

Among a total of 108 baseline K. pneumoniae isolates from Trials 301 and 310, the MIC
range was 0.015 to 8.0 mcg/mL; the MIC90 values against K. pneumoniae isolates were
0.12 mcg/mL and 0.06 to 0.12 mcg/mL from surveillance and clinical studies, respectively.
Overall microbiological eradication/success at TOC was achieved in 81/108 (75%) isolates.
While the cumulative microbiological success rate of 74.5% (79/106) was achieved up to the
highest MIC 0.25 mcg/mL, 1/2 (50%) isolates were eradicated at this MIC. No baseline K.
pneumoniae isolates with MIC 0.5 and 1.0 mcg/mL were available. However, 2 baseline
isolates with MIC 4 mcg/mL and 8 mcg/mL were available and eradicated. Therefore, we
recommend a susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL as more appropriate to cover most of the K.
pneumoniae population.

•

Among a total of 31 baseline P. mirabilis isolates from Trials 301 and 310, the MIC range
was ≤0.015 to 0.5 mcg/mL; the MIC90 values against P. mirabilis isolates from surveillance
and clinical studies were 0.5 and 0.25 to 0.5 mcg/mL, respectively. Overall microbiological
158

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
eradication/success at TOC was achieved in 20/31 (64.5%) isolates. While the cumulative
microbiological success rate of 67.9% (19/28) was achieved up to the highest MIC
0.25 mcg/mL, 13/14 (92.9%) isolates were eradicated at this MIC. Three baseline P.
mirabilis isolates with MIC 0.5 mcg/mL were available but only one isolate was eradicated.
No baseline P. mirabilis isolates with MIC ≥1.0 mcg/mL were available. Therefore, we
recommend a susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL as more appropriate to cover most of the P.
mirabilis population.
PK/PD Data and PTA Predictions in Plasma
The lack of an established nonclinical model for uUTIs and uncertainties surrounding: 1) urine
specific PK/PD parameters, 2) appropriate bacteriologic endpoint for use in PTA analyses, and
3) the relative importance of plasma versus urine drug concentrations limited the Agency’s
reliance on the Applicant’s PK/PD package to support the proposed STIC. Because of concerns
with the reliability of the results of the murine thigh infection model PK/PD studies, results of
the in vitro PK/PD target determination studies were prioritized in the Agency’s PTA
evaluations. PTA analyses showed that the free plasma concentrations associated with the
proposed dose regimen resulted in achievement of the in vitro targets in ≥90% of simulated
subjects up to an MIC 0.25 mcg/mL. In urine, PTA analyses showed achievement of the in vitro
targets in ≥90% of simulated subjects up to an MIC of 8 mcg/mL. Given the aforementioned
knowledge gaps and their implications for the translatability of nonclinical PK/PD findings to
clinical efficacy, the Agency prioritized the more conservative findings from plasma-based PTA
analysis in support of a sulopenem susceptible BP of 0.25 mcg/mL against Enterobacterales.
In summary, the FDA review team recommends sulopenem Susceptible (S)/Intermediate

20. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance
20.1. Mechanism of Action
Sulopenem is a penem antibacterial drug that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to
penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). A competitive binding assay was conducted with 3Hpenicillin in E. coli strain W-7 that showed sulopenem (CP-65,207) had the highest affinity for
PBP2, with concentrations as low as 0.004 mcg/mL (Gootz et al. 1989). The assay also showed
that the relative order of affinity for PBPs of sulopenem in E. coli was PBP2 >PBP1A >PBP1B
>PBP4 >PBP3 >PBP5/6. Additionally, it was determined through a hydrolysis study that
sulopenem (CP-65207) was highly stable to some cephalosporinases, including plasmid-encoded
enzymes TEM-1, SHV-1, and PSE-2.
Similar to other carbapenems, sulopenem showed bactericidal killing by time-kill assay at
concentrations ≥4X the MIC against E. coli and K. pneumoniae.

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)

20.2. Drug Resistance
In general, the mechanisms for β-lactam resistance in gram-negative bacteria include the
following:
•

Hydrolysis by penicillinases, cephalosporinases, oxacillinases and carbapenemases;

•

Reduced uptake across the outer membrane due to decreased expression or loss of porin
channels;

•

Extrusion of drugs by multidrug resistance efflux pumps;

•

Mutation of PBP targets (e.g., PBPs).

High-level ß-lactam resistance is achieved when multiple mechanisms are combined in a single
cell, e.g., production of a carbapenemase in a cell that lacks porin(s) and has overexpressed
efflux pumps.
In vitro, development of resistance to sulopenem was evaluated in spontaneous mutation
frequency studies using two E. cloacae isolates and in serial passage studies using clinical
isolates of E. coli and K. pneumoniae.
In spontaneous mutation frequency studies, sulopenem resistant mutants were selected in vitro at
a frequency of 1 × 10-8 with a ≤2-fold MIC increase from the parent E. cloacae strain. In the
serial passage mutation studies, MIC values increased 16-fold during 15 serial passages in two
out of the three tested E. coli isolates and were unchanged for the third isolate. MIC values
increased 8-fold during serial passage for one of the two K. pneumoniae isolates tested, and MIC
values increased from 0.5 to 256 mcg/mL for the other isolate.
Similar to other carbapenems, resistance to sulopenem occurs primarily due to enzymatic
inactivation by carbapenemases, but also can be caused by β-lactamase production, efflux pump
165
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5468170

NDA 213972
ORLYNVAH (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid)
expression, and changes in porins and/or PBPs (Papp-Wallace et al. 2011; Harting 2019; PappWallace 2019) Aside from the β-lactam class of antimicrobial drugs, sulopenem is not expected
to demonstrate cross-resistance to any other class.

Please refer to Section 10 for a summary of findings from the clinical site inspections. Details of

appears to have been conducted adequately, and the clinical data generated by these clinical sites
appear to be reliable in support of this NDA.
The clinical sites were chosen using a risk-based approach primarily based on numbers of
enrolled subjects, treatment effect, and prior inspection history. The three sites were Dr. Jodi
Sanson (Site 129), Dr. Peyman Banooni (Site 115), and Dr. Moises A. Issa (Site 251).

not always obtained within the protocol-specified timeframe, and (2) the specific method of
ongoing contraception was often not recorded. All subjects were contacted as needed to
retroactively obtain and record the missing information about the specific contraception
method. No subject became pregnant during the study.

(ANC)of 0.99 x 103/uL, just under (at) the protocol-specified minimum of 1.0 x 103/uL.

23. Labeling: Key Changes
This Prescribing Information (PI) review includes a high-level summary of the rationale for
major changes to the finalized PI as compared to the Applicant’s draft PI submitted on April 25,
2024 (Table 126). The PI was reviewed to ensure that PI meets regulatory/statutory
requirements, is consistent (if appropriate) with labeling guidance, conveys clinically meaningful
and scientifically accurate information needed for the safe and effective use of the drug, and
provides clear and concise information for the healthcare practitioner.
Based on discussions with the Office of New Drug Policy (ONDP), Regulatory Policy Advisors
Team and Labeling Policy Team (email from ONDP dated 9/30/2024), it was noted that due to
the specific concerns regarding ORLYNVAH use and possible increase in antimicrobial
resistance, ONDP agreed with DAI/OID’s position that parts of the language under 21 CFR
201.24 (Labeling for systemic antibacterial drug products) are not appropriate to include in the
ORLYNVAH PI. Omission and/or revision of parts of the language under 21 CFR 201.24 seems
particularly critical from a public health standpoint for ORLYNVAH given the concerns about
inappropriate use of ORLYNVAH (which could lead to drug resistance) and antibacterial drug
stewardship. See Table 126 below for descriptions of omissions/revisions made to the language
under 21 CFR 201.24 in Section 17 (Patient Counseling Information) and subsections 1.2 (Usage

{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}

1. Executive Summary
1.1. Product Introduction
Sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet is a fixed-dose combination of a penem
antibacterial prodrug (sulopenem etzadroxil) and a renal tubular transport blocking drug
(probenecid). The role of probenecid is to increase the systemic exposure of the antibacterial
drug, sulopenem. Each tablet contains 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid.
Sulopenem etzadroxil is a new molecular entity while probenecid was approved in the 1950s.
The Applicant’s proposed indication is the treatment of adult women ≥18 years of age with
uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by designated susceptible microorganisms
proven or strongly suspected to be nonsusceptible to a quinolone. The proposed dose is one
tablet orally (PO) administered twice daily (BID) for 5 days.

1.2. Conclusions on the Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
The Applicant has not provided substantial evidence of effectiveness for sulopenem for the
treatment of uUTI. In the prespecified subgroup of subjects with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacinnonsusceptible pathogen in Study 301, sulopenem was found to be superior to ciprofloxacin
based on the primary endpoint of overall response (clinical response and microbiological
response). However, in the prespecified subgroup of subjects with uUTI caused by a
ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen in Study 301, sulopenem was inferior to ciprofloxacin. As
clinicians usually do not obtain urine cultures when treating uUTI, it may be difficult to identify
patients who may benefit from therapy with sulopenem. Additionally, in the related indications
of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) (Study 302) and complicated intraabdominal
infections (cIAI) (Study 303), sulopenem was not noninferior to the active comparator based on
the primary efficacy endpoints in each trial. Of note, sulopenem was inferior to the active
comparator in Study 302. Nonclinical PK/PD data suggest that the Applicant’s proposed dose of
sulopenem is suboptimal which may provide an explanation for the Phase 3 study results.
In order to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness, the Applicant should conduct at least
one additional successful study in uUTI and consider using a different active comparator drug in
the study(ies) that is more reflective of currently recommended treatment for uUTI.
Additionally, the Agency recommends that the Applicant conduct further investigation to
determine the optimal sulopenem dosing regimen for the proposed treatment indication(s).

1.3. Benefit-Risk Assessment
Benefit-Risk Summary and Assessment
In this NDA, the Applicant seeks approval of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet for the treatment of adult women ≥18 years of
age with uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) caused by designated susceptible microorganisms proven or strongly suspected to be
nonsusceptible to a quinolone. uUTI is a common infection that affects most women at least once in their lives. Although there are many
antibacterial drugs approved to treat uUTI, antimicrobial resistance may limit their use in certain patients. In addition, many of the antibacterial
drugs available to treat resistant pathogens are only available for intravenous administration while oral therapy is preferred in the treatment of
uUTI.
In uUTI Study 301, sulopenem was found to be superior to ciprofloxacin with respect to overall response (clinical response and microbiological
response) in the prespecified subgroup of subjects with a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogen. Overall response was attained by 77/160
(48%) of sulopenem subjects and 49/149 (33%) of ciprofloxacin subjects with a difference of 15% (95% CI, 4.4% to 26.1%; p-value 0.0062).
However, among subjects with a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen, sulopenem was found to be inferior to ciprofloxacin. The overall response
was 218/365 (60%) for sulopenem and 296/410 (72%) for ciprofloxacin with a difference of -12.5% (95% CI, -19.1% to -5.9%). Of note, clinicians
usually do not obtain urine cultures when treating uUTI. As a result, the role of sulopenem in treating uUTI is unclear and also raises concerns
about how to distinguish an appropriate patient population. In addition, in the related indications of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI)
and complicated intraabdominal infections (cIAI), sulopenem was not noninferior to the active comparator based on the primary efficacy
endpoints in each trial. Nonclinical PK/PD data suggest that the Applicant’s proposed dose of sulopenem is suboptimal which may explain the
results of the Phase 3 studies. Overall, there is insufficient evidence to support the findings of benefit for sulopenem in patients with a uUTI
caused by a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible pathogen.
The primary safety database for this NDA consisted of 825 sulopenem subjects with uUTI from Study 301. This database was supported by the
safety findings from the cUTI Study 302 and the cIAI Study 303; a total of 1855 subjects were exposed to sulopenem in the three Phase 3 trials.
Taken together, there was an adequate safety database for this NDA. In Study 301, gastrointestinal adverse reactions, including diarrhea,
nausea, and abdominal pain, were common among subjects taking oral sulopenem/probenecid. In particular, diarrhea occurred in 12% of
sulopenem subjects in Study 301. However, the diarrhea and other GI adverse events were generally mild and not treatment-limiting.
Elevations in ALT, generally less than 5x the upper limit of normal, occurred more commonly among sulopenem subjects compared to
ciprofloxacin subjects in Study 301. However, there were no cases that met Hy’s Law criteria in Study 301. Hypersensitivity reactions, including
angioedema involving the face, were noted uncommonly in the studies. The identified safety issues (e.g., hypersensitivity reactions, GI adverse
26
Version date: October 12, 2018

Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
reactions, and elevations in transaminases) can be addressed through labeling and do not preclude approval. Overall, there is an acceptable
safety profile for sulopenem/probenecid.
In summary, while the safety profile for sulopenem is acceptable, there is insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of sulopenem for
the treatment of uUTI. In order to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness, the Applicant should conduct at least one additional successful
study in uUTI and consider using a different active comparator drug in the study(ies) that is more reflective of currently recommended
treatment for uUTI. Additionally, the Agency recommends that the Applicant conduct further investigation to determine the optimal
sulopenem dosing regimen for the proposed treatment indication(s).

Conclusions and Reasons

uUTI is an acute infection of the bladder in women with normal anatomy
of the urinary tract and is characterized by symptoms of lower abdominal
discomfort, dysuria, and urinary frequency.
Progression of the infection to the kidney (pyelonephritis) is uncommon,
but if it occurs could necessitate hospitalization.
The most common bacterial cause of uUTI is Escherichia coli (75-95%);
other less common pathogens associated with uUTI are Staphylococcus
saprophyticus, Klebsiella species, and Proteus species.
uUTIs are common; up to 80 to 90% of women will have at least one uUTI
during their life. Risk factors for uUTI include recent sexual intercourse,
use of spermicides, and history of prior UTI.

uUTI is a common infection with more than
80% of women experiencing a uUTI at least
once in their lives.

There are many FDA-approved antibacterial drugs for the treatment of
uUTI including trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin,
fosfomycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins.
Some of the available antibacterial drugs have known adverse reactions
including hypersensitivity reactions, QT prolongation, tendonitis, and
neuropathy.

There are many approved antibacterial drugs
available for the treatment of uUTI. Therapy is
typically chosen empirically since cultures are
not usually obtained. Of note, antibacterial
drug resistance may limit treatment options.

Conclusions and Reasons

The decision of which antibacterial drug to use to treat uUTI is often made
empirically as cultures are not usually obtained when treating uUTI.
Antibacterial drug resistance in urinary pathogens has been increasing
over time. If a patient is found to have a uUTI caused by a drug-resistant
pathogen, clinicians may need to change the chosen treatment. In some
cases, an IV drug may be needed which would necessitate placement of
an IV catheter and may require hospitalization.
The efficacy of sulopenem for the treatment of uUTI was only
demonstrated in a prespecified subgroup of a single adequate and wellcontrolled trial (Study 301).
Sulopenem was superior to ciprofloxacin in patients with ciprofloxacinnonsusceptible pathogens using the primary efficacy endpoint of overall
response (clinical response and microbiological response). The overall
response was 77/160 (48%) for sulopenem and 49/149 (33%) for
ciprofloxacin with a difference of 15% (95% CI, 4.4% to 26.1%; p-value
0.0062).
Among patients with uUTI caused by a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen,
sulopenem was not noninferior to ciprofloxacin. The overall response was
218/365 (60%) for sulopenem and 296/410 (72%) for ciprofloxacin with a
difference of -12.5% (95% CI, -19.1% to -5.9%). Sulopenem was inferior
compared to ciprofloxacin based on the overall response.
In the related indications of cUTI and cIAI, sulopenem was not noninferior
to the active comparator based on the primary efficacy endpoints in each
trial.

compared to the active comparator (IV ertapenem with step down to oral

In the cIAI trial (Study 303), sulopenem (IV to oral step down) was not
noninferior compared to the active comparator (IV ertapenem with step
down to oral ciprofloxacin/metronidazole or amoxicillin/clavulanate)
based on the primary endpoint of clinical response. The clinical response
was 204/249 (82%) for sulopenem and 233/266 (88%) for the comparator
with a difference of -6.0% (95% CI, -12.2, 0.2).
There are inadequate data to support the use of T > MIC in target
attainment analyses to justify the dose selection and susceptibility
breakpoint determination.
The results of the nonclinical PK/PD studies are not definitive but suggest
that sulopenem exhibits concentration-dependent killing against
pathogens relevant to uUTI, cUTI, and cIAI.
