2. Therapeutic Context
2.1. Analysis of Condition
Uncomplicated urinary tract infections are characterized by local signs and symptoms including
lower abdominal discomfort, dysuria, and urinary frequency that is associated with pyuria and a
microbial pathogen on urine culture. uUTI, also referred to as acute cystitis, occur in females
with normal anatomy of the urinary tract and are not accompanied by systemic signs or
symptoms, such as fever greater than 38 degrees Celsius or costovertebral angle
pain/tenderness. Urinary tract infections associated with systemic signs or symptoms, such as
fever, and those occurring in males are referred to as cUTI.
uUTIs are common in women with normal genitourinary tracts. Up to 80 to 90% of women will
have at least one uUTI during their life. Risk factors for uUTI include recent sexual intercourse,
use of spermicides, and a history of prior UTI.
The most common bacterial cause of uUTI is Escherichia coli (75-95%); other less common
pathogens associated with uUTI are Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella species, and
Proteus species. Rates of antibacterial drug resistance for E. coli have been increasing
worldwide (see Section 2.2). It is important to note that in clinical practice uUTIs are often
diagnosed based on symptoms and, if available, a dipstick urinalysis positive for leukocyte
esterase or nitrites; urine culture is not regularly obtained unless there are risk factors for a
drug-resistant pathogen.
Although baseline or follow up urine cultures are not usually obtained in the treatment of uUTI,
clinicians generally expect that antibacterial drug treatment will result in eradication of the
causative pathogen and sterilization of the urine. The goal of treatment in uUTI is to resolve the
acute symptoms but also to reduce the risk of infection progression, including the development
of pyelonephritis. Persistent bacteriuria following treatment is generally considered treatment
failure. In two randomized studies of antibacterial drugs compared to NSAIDs, the rate of
pyelonephritis in patients with uUTIs who were not treated with antibacterial drugs was
between 2 to 5% compared to 0 to 0.4% in patients treated with antibacterial drugs (Gagyor et
al. 2015; Kronenberg et al. 2017).
The association between bacteriuria, even when asymptomatic, and infectious complications
has been shown in pregnant women. In studies from the 1960s and 1970s, between 20% to
30% of pregnant women with untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria developed pyelonephritis
later in the course of pregnancy (Nicolle 2015). In a more recent study from the Netherlands
(Kazemier et al. 2015), pyelonephritis occurred in 2.4% of pregnant women with asymptomatic
bacteriuria who were not treated with antibacterial drugs, and in only 0.6% among pregnant
women who did not have asymptomatic bacteriuria. Among the patients who were treated for
asymptomatic bacteriuria, there were no cases of pyelonephritis. A similar finding is noted in
the renal transplant literature. In a study of renal transplant patients from a transplant center in
New York (Lee et al. 2013), having >10 bacterial colony forming units (CFU)/mL in the urine
32
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
during the 3 months post-transplant was an independent risk factor for subsequent bacteremia
(hazard ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.2-4.8).

2.2. Analysis of Current Treatment Options
The decision of which antibacterial drug to use to treat uUTI is often made empirically.
However, if culture results are available, they are used to guide treatment choice. When making
an empiric treatment choice, clinicians need to consider the local rates of antibacterial drug
resistance. Determining the local rate of resistant pathogens for uUTI may be challenging as
resistance rates obtained from passive surveillance may overestimate resistance as cultures are
obtained more often from patients with risk factors for having a resistant pathogen (Ti et al.
2003). Still, passive surveillance from microbiology laboratories can be helpful, especially in
detecting changes in resistance patterns. Two studies found that drug-resistant E. coli are
becoming more common. In a U.S.-based study from 2000 to 2010, rates of E. coli resistance
from outpatient urine cultures increased for ciprofloxacin (3% to 17%), TMP/SMX (18% to 24%),
nitrofurantoin (0.8% to 1.6%), and ceftriaxone (0.2% to 2.3%) (Sanchez et al. 2012). In Olmsted
County, Minnesota from 2005 to 2009, the rate of E. coli resistance identified from urine
cultures increased for ampicillin (39% to 43%; P=.02), cefazolin (4% to 7%; P<.001),
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (17% to 25%; P<.001), fluoroquinolones (7% to 16%; P<.001),
fluoroquinolone plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (4% to 10%; P<.001), gentamicin (3% to
7%; P<.001), and extended-spectrum cephalosporins (1% to 3%; P<.001). The rate of
nitrofurantoin-resistance did not increase (Swami et al. 2012).
Table 1 below summarizes the currently available treatment options for uUTI. Clinical efficacy
for all the listed treatment options are generally high if the pathogen is susceptible to the
antibacterial drug. Current treatment guidelines recommend trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole,
nitrofurantoin, or fosfomycin as first-line options for the treatment of uUTI.

3. Regulatory Background
3.1. U.S. Regulatory Actions and Marketing History
Sulopenem is a new molecular entity and has not been approved in the United States or any
other country.

3.2. Summary of Presubmission/Submission Regulatory Activity
The development program was conducted under IND 129834 (intravenous [IV] sulopenem;
opened 02 Mar 2016), IND 129849 (sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid; opened 02 Mar 2016),
(b) (4)

The Division
granted sulopenem qualified infectious disease product designation for uUTI, cUTI, and cIAI on
29 Jul 2016 and fast track designation for these same indications on 15 Mar 2019.
The Division and Iterum met in July 2017 to discuss the clinical trial design for Study 301 for the
treatment of uUTI. The Division emphasized that the clinical response component of the overall
response endpoint (combined clinical and microbiological responses) should be defined as the
resolution of all UTI symptoms that were present at baseline. The Division also noted that for a
noninferiority trial it is essential that only patients with pathogens susceptible to the
comparator (ciprofloxacin) be included in the efficacy analysis. The Sponsor was concerned that
excluding patients with a ciprofloxacin-resistant pathogen would remove a significant
population from their study. In November 2017, Iterum submitted a proposal for statistical
hypothesis testing for the uUTI trial in which there would be two analysis populations, one for
subjects with a ciprofloxacin-susceptible pathogen at baseline (microbiological modified intentto-treat susceptible [MMITTS]) and another for subjects with a ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible
pathogen at baseline (microbiological modified intent-to-treat resistant [MMITTR]). Superiority
testing would be used in the MMITTR population while noninferiority testing using a 10%
margin would be used in the MMITTS population. The following comment was sent to Iterum in
response to this study design.
We agree with the proposed framework for hypothesis testing and interim analysis.
Because the analyses in the MMITTS and MMITTR populations can be viewed as
answering separate research questions, we agree that it is not necessary to use alpha
sharing or hierarchical testing to control the overall Type I error rate for the two
primary analyses at the one-sided alpha =0.025 level. However, it is important to note
that discordant results in the two primary analyses, for example, if the trial is only able
to demonstrate that sulopenem is superior to ciprofloxacin in the MMITTR population,
but is not able to demonstrate that sulopenem in noninferior to ciprofloxacin in the
MMITTS population can be problematic. We will need to understand the reasons for
the discrepant findings. Also, the discordant results may have significant labeling
implications, such as, limited use language, limitation of use/warning regarding
35
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
empiric use. For a clinical condition such as uUTI, where therapy is generally empiric,
the utility of a product for which efficacy is not demonstrated in the MMITTS
population could be limited.
A pre-NDA meeting was held on 28 Sep 2020. The Division reiterated their concern regarding
the discordant results between the MMITTS and MMITTR populations and that the results did
not support the use of sulopenem for uUTI caused by ciprofloxacin-susceptible isolates. In
addition, the Division noted that there are limitations to exploratory analyses of studies that
failed to meet their primary endpoint and that the data from Study 302 could not support a
labeled indication for cUTI.

4. Significant Issues From Other Review Disciplines Pertinent to Clinical
Conclusions on Efficacy and Safety
4.1. Office of Scientific Investigations
Routine PDUFA surveillance inspections were conducted for four clinical investigators, Drs.
Fernandez, Sorkin-Wells, Rodriguez de la Torre, and Thomas, and the study sponsor, Iterum
Therapeutics International, in support of NDA 213972. In addition, combined PDUFA/for-cause
inspections were conducted on two clinical investigators, Drs. Oporta and Terrelonge. All of the
inspections covered one clinical study, IT001-301.
The source records documenting the overall response criteria (i.e., survival status, concomitant
non-study antibacterial therapy, urine culture and susceptibility testing results, and Patient
Symptom Assessment Questionnaire [PSAQ] responses) and the investigator’s assessment of
clinical response (i.e., resolution of pre-therapy signs and symptoms of the index infection and
whether additional antibacterial drugs were required) were reviewed and verified against the
Applicant’s data line listings, with only minor discrepancies noted. The data generated by Site
219 (Dr. Fernandez), Site 103 (Dr. Sorkin- Wells), Site 150 (Dr. Rodriguez de la Torre), and Site
200 (Dr. Thomas) appear acceptable in support of the uUTI indication. However, data reliability
concerns were identified during the routine PDUFA inspection of the Applicant as follows:
1. The statistical analysis plan (SAP) was amended after a pre-planned interim analysis
conducted by an unblinded statistician. The SAP amendment specifically changed overall
response criteria to state that the genus/species and susceptibility profiles of the urinary
isolate needed to match [to incorporate results from whole genome sequencing (WGS) and
pulse-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE)].
2. WGS and PFGE test results (which were used to place subjects in subgroups of susceptible
and resistant populations and to determine overall response) were incorporated after the
study was unblinded (i.e., study was unblinded on 19 June 2020; WGS and PFGE were
incorporated on 29 June 2020).

multiple subjects.

4.2. Product Quality
The NDA, as amended, has provided sufficient Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls
information to assure the identity, strength, purity, and quality of the proposed drug product,
sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid tablets. The drug product is a pink, oval-shaped, filmcoated, immediate release, bilayer tablet, containing 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg
probenecid. The drug product formulation contains conventional excipients of compendial
grade. The proposed commercial packaging configurations for the drug product include high
(b)
density polyethylene bottles (10-count and 30-count) and aluminum foil blisters ( (4) -count). The
stability information submitted in the NDA supports the 24-month expiration dating for the
drug product to be stored in the proposed commercial packaging systems at room temperature
(20-25°C). Overall, the information provided in the NDA for the drug product (sulopenem
etzadroxil and probenecid tablets) and both drug substances (sulopenem etzadroxil and
probenecid) was found to be adequate. The manufacturing and testing facilities for this NDA
are deemed acceptable and an overall “Approve” recommendation was entered into Panorama
by the Office of Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Assessment on May 4, 2021.

please refer to the Office of Pharmaceutical Quality Integrated Quality Assessment dated June

4.3. Clinical Microbiology
Microbiological response analyses related to pathogen isolation, identification, and
susceptibility testing with standard culture methods are covered in Section 16.5 of this review.
A summary of the clinical microbiology review and recommendations is presented below:
4.3.1. Mechanism of Action
Sulopenem, a penem antibacterial drug, inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to
penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) resulting in cell death. In Escherichia coli, the relative order of
affinity towards PBPs was PBP2>PBP1A > PBP1B > PBP4>PBP3>PBP5/6. Similar to other
carbapenems, sulopenem showed bactericidal killing by time-kill assay at concentrations ≥4X
the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against E. coli and K. pneumoniae.
4.3.2. Antimicrobial Spectrum of Activity
Sulopenem demonstrates in vitro activity against both aerobic and anaerobic gram-positive and
gram-negative bacteria. The in vitro MIC50/90 values (inhibits the growth of ≥50% and ≥90% of
the isolates) were determined for sulopenem against isolates of relevant pathogens from 3
recent surveillance studies (North American and European isolates) and a single uUTI clinical
study (IT001-301). Against E. coli isolates, sulopenem had MIC50/90 values of 0.03/0.03-0.06
µg/mL; against K. pneumoniae isolates, sulopenem had MIC50/90 values of 0.03-0.06/0.06-0.12
µg/mL; and against P. mirabilis isolates, sulopenem had MIC50/90 values of 0.12-0.25/0.25-0.5
µg/mL reported.

43
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
4.3.3. Resistance
Sulopenem resistant mutants were selected by conducting in vitro spontaneous mutation
frequency studies using two E. cloacae isolates at a frequency of 1 X 10-8 with a ≤2-fold MIC. In
serial passage mutation studies, MIC values to sulopenem were observed to increase 16-fold
during 15 serial passages in two of the three E. coli isolates tested and were unchanged for the
third isolate. MIC values increased 8-fold during serial passage for one of the two K.
pneumoniae isolates tested, and MIC values increased from 0.5 to 256 µg/mL for the other
isolate. Resistance occurs primarily due to enzymatic inactivation of carbapenems by
carbapenemases, but also can be caused by β-lactamase production, efflux pump expression,
and changes in porins and/or PBPs. No instance of antagonism was observed in vitro between
sulopenem and other routinely used antibacterial drugs against tested E. coli and K.
pneumoniae isolates.
4.3.4. Clinical Study
A single Phase 3 clinical study (IT001-301) was conducted to determine the safety and efficacy
of a 5-day course of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid versus a 3-day course of oral
ciprofloxacin (comparator arm) for the treatment of women (≥18 years of age) with uUTI. The
microbiological modified intent-to-treat (mMITT) population comprised all subjects who had at
least one or a maximum of two baseline urinary bacterial pathogen(s) identified from urine
with ≥105 CFU/mL. Bacterial urinary pathogens were identified from microbiological culture of
acceptable urine specimens collected at baseline, and subsequent visits.
In the mMITT population, uUTIs were predominantly caused by E. coli (56.0% in sulopenem
treatment group and 58.4% in ciprofloxacin treatment group), K. pneumoniae (6.5% in
sulopenem treatment group and 6.0% in ciprofloxacin treatment group), and P. mirabilis (2.2%
in sulopenem treatment group and 2.1% in ciprofloxacin treatment group).
4.3.5. Breakpoints or Susceptibility Test Interpretive Criteria (STIC) for
Sulopenem
The following is a summary of the Clinical Microbiology team’s proposed breakpoints (BPs)
rationale and labeling recommendations:
For setting the MIC BPs for sulopenem against E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis, the
Clinical Microbiology team relied primarily on microbiological eradication rates at each MIC
dilution of clinical isolates, and the in vitro MIC data from clinical and surveillance isolates. The
pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) target index for sulopenem was predicted to be
either T > MIC or Cmax/MIC based on plasma concentration; however, the results are not
definitive. Typically, beta-lactam drugs exhibit T > MIC. The Clinical Pharmacology team has
concerns with the validity of PK/PD study results. The microbiological success in relation to MIC
values of baseline E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis isolates from the sulopenem
treatment group in mMITT population at test-of-cure (TOC) visit are summarized below:



Among 437 baseline E. coli isolates with an MIC range of 0.015 to 1.0 µg/mL, the overall
microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 76.4%. The highest sulopenem MIC
corresponding to microbiological success was 0.25 µg/mL and 3/5 (60%) isolates were
eradicated. There was only one baseline E. coli isolate with sulopenem MIC of 1 µg/mL and
it was associated with microbiological persistence. No baseline isolate with an MIC ≥2
µg/mL was observed. The MIC50/90 was 0.03/0.06 µg/mL against all E. coli isolates from both
surveillance and clinical studies. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL appears
reasonable and will cover most of the E. coli population.
Among 48 baseline K. pneumoniae isolates with an MIC range 0.015 to 8.0 µg/mL, the
overall microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 77.1%. The highest sulopenem MIC that
corresponded to a favorable microbiological outcome was 0.12 µg/mL and 7/8 (87.5%)
isolates at this MIC were eradicated. No baseline isolates were observed with MIC values
between 0.25 to 2.0 µg/mL. However, 2 baseline isolates with MIC values of 4 and 8 µg/mL
were identified and eradicated. The MIC50/90 was 0.03/0.12 µg/mL against all K. pneumoniae
isolates from the surveillance and clinical studies. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL
appears reasonable and will cover most of the K. pneumoniae population.
Among 17 baseline P. mirabilis isolates with an MIC range of 0.03 to 0.25 µg/mL, the overall
microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 82.4%. The highest sulopenem MIC that
corresponded to microbiological success was 0.25 µg/mL and 10/10 (100%) isolates at this
MIC were successfully eradicated. No baseline isolate was available with MIC values ≥0.5
µg/mL. Against P. mirabilis isolates from both surveillance and clinical studies, the MIC50/90
values were between 0.12/0.25 to 0.25/0.5µg/mL. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25
µg/mL appears reasonable and should cover most P. mirabilis isolates.

In summary, microbiological success was observed in patients with baseline isolates of E. coli
and P. mirabilis that had MIC values of ≤0.015 to 0.25 µg/mL. No baseline E. coli isolate had an
MIC of 0.5 µg/mL but a single isolate at an MIC of 1.0 µg/mL was associated with
microbiological failure. No baseline P. mirabilis isolate had an MIC ≥0.5 µg/mL. Microbiological
success was observed in patients with baseline K. pneumoniae isolates that had MIC values of
≤0.015 to 0.12 µg/mL. No baseline K. pneumoniae isolates with MIC values between 0.25 to 2
µg/mL were observed; however, two isolates at MIC 4 and 8 µg/mL were observed and
eradicated. Therefore, susceptible (S)/intermediate (I)/resistant (R) MIC BPs of ≤0.25/0.5/≥1.0
µg/mL against all three uUTI pathogens appeared to be reasonable and will cover most isolates.

5. Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology
5.1. Executive Summary
The proposed product is a bilayer oral tablet that consists of a fixed dose combination of
sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid. Sulopenem etzadroxil (PF-03709270) is a prodrug that is
rapidly cleaved upon intestinal absorption to generate its active metabolite, sulopenem (CP70429) which is a penem antibacterial drug. Penem antibacterial drugs are known to be
degraded quickly by human renal dipeptidase, and an inhibitor of this enzyme, probenecid, is
included in the fixed dose combination to prolong the actions of sulopenem. The product if
approved is intended for the treatment of uUTI with a treatment regimen of one bilayer tablet
containing 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid administered twice a day for 5
days.
Pivotal toxicology studies that were conducted in support of the NDA in adult animals included
1-month toxicology studies in rats and monkeys with sulopenem etzadroxil and a 14-day
combination toxicology study with sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid in rats. There were no
46
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
toxicity findings of concern, but renal changes were observed in rats. The primary finding
observed in adult rats in the 1-month toxicology study was a low incidence of regeneration of
proximal tubular epithelium in the kidney accompanied by minimal vacuolation of the renal
tubular epithelium, renal tubular hypertrophy, and increased kidney weights. The renal findings
are not considered to be clinically relevant due to the limited scope and severity of the findings.
The lowest sulopenem etzadroxil dose in rats associated with the kidney findings was 400
mg/kg/day which was associated with a mean plasma area under the curve (AUC) exposure for
sulopenem of approximately 9 times the mean clinical AUC exposure for sulopenem following a
single oral administration of the bilayer tablet. In the combination sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid toxicology study, kidney weights were increased with an oral sulopenem
etzadroxil dose of 800 mg/kg/day administered for 14 days to adult rats, but renal
histopathology findings were not observed. These results suggest the duration of sulopenem
etzadroxil dosing may influence the severity of renal findings.
In the definitive juvenile toxicity study, oral administration of sulopenem etzadroxil to juvenile
rats for 85 days beginning on postnatal day 5 and continuing to postnatal day 90, was
associated with more varied and severe renal histopathology findings compared to the findings
in adult rats in the 14-day and 1-month toxicology studies. Renal histopathology in juvenile
male and/or female rats included slight degeneration of tubular epithelium, renal infarcts, and
intratubular concretions. The findings in juvenile rats occurred at lower sulopenem etzadroxil
doses and exposures than the doses associated with renal findings in adult rats in the 1-month
study, and the findings were poorly reversible or, in the case of tubular concretions, irreversible
after a 2-week recovery period. The renal toxicology results in juvenile rats suggest longer
durations of repeated sulopenem etzadroxil dosing may result in more varied and severe renal
toxicity with potential clinical relevance. The results are also consistent with a potential for
more severe renal toxicity in juvenile rats compared to adults. The sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet will not be approved for pediatric patients until clinical
trials in this population are completed. The results from the juvenile toxicology study suggest
increased monitoring of renal toxicity should be considered for future clinical pediatric studies.
Additional sulopenem etzadroxil-related findings were observed in gastrointestinal (GI) tissues
in the 14-day combination toxicology study in rats (mixed cell infiltrates, hyperplasia of
glandular epithelium and edema in the large intestine) and the 1-month study in monkeys
(minimal mucosal hyperplasia). These effects were reversible and are not considered to be a
likely source of serious adverse events (SAEs) for clinical dosing for 5 days with the bilayer
tablet. Monkeys also exhibited positive Coombs test results that tended to increase with
sulopenem etzadroxil dose and likely contributed to antibody mediation of minimal erythrocyte
loss and compensatory erythropoiesis in monkeys. Should a similar reaction to sulopenem
etzadroxil occur in humans, it is not expected to produce serious adverse effects over a short 5day course of treatment with the bilayer tablet, but more concern may be warranted for
repeated courses of treatment.
Both sulopenem etzadroxil and sulopenem were shown to inhibit hERG potassium channels in
vitro with estimated IC50 values of 33.4 mcM (15.9 µg/ml) and 300 mcM (104.8 µg/ml),
47
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
respectively. However, concern for inhibition of hERG potassium channels and possible QT
prolongation in the clinic is minimal because the 2.64 µg/ml plasma Cmax for sulopenem
associated with administration of a single bilayer tablet containing 500 mg sulopenem
etzadroxil in fed patients is approximately 6-fold and 40-fold lower than the hERG IC50 values
for sulopenem etzadroxil and sulopenem, respectively. Also, in a Phase 1 study where no QT
prolongation was observed, a single IV dose of 2800 mg sulopenem was associated with a mean
plasma Cmax value (109.7 µg/ml) for sulopenem that was approximately 40 times greater than
the expected clinical sulopenem Cmax associated with oral administration of a single bilayer
tablet.
In vitro and in vivo genetic toxicology testing was conducted with sulopenem etzadroxil and
sulopenem with a similar pattern of results for both compounds. Both compounds were shown
to be negative for mutagenicity in Ames assays and sulopenem was negative for mutagenicity in
an in vitro CHO HGRPT forward mutation assay. However, both compounds produced positive
results for clastogenesis in several in vitro assays in mammalian cells including an in vitro
micronucleus assay and human lymphocyte assay with sulopenem etzadroxil and a
chromosome aberration assay with sulopenem. These results were balanced by negative results
for both compounds in vivo in micronucleus assays in bone marrow cells from rats (both
compounds) and mice (sulopenem). Based on the negative results in the in vitro mutagenicity
assays and the in vivo micronucleus assays, the weight of evidence supports a negative
potential for genotoxicity for sulopenem etzadroxil.
Sulopenem etzadroxil did not inhibit fertility in male and female rats and was not associated
with fetal malformations in embryo-fetal studies in rats and rabbits. However, in mice, a higher
litter and fetal incidence of cleft palate in fetuses occurred at a sulopenem etzadroxil dose
associated with sulopenem exposures approximately 46-times the mean clinical exposure
following a single oral dose of the bilayer tablet. In a pre-postnatal study in rats, sulopenem
etzadroxil was not associated with changes in the viability, physical development, neurological
development, or reproductive capacity of first-generation offspring.
Sulopenem and 2-ethylbutyric acid (2-EBA) are released by hydrolysis of sulopenem etzadroxil,
and during hydrolysis the formation of formaldehyde is anticipated. However, measurable
quantities of formaldehyde were not observed in any of the rat or monkey toxicology studies,
(b)
although the lower limit of quantitation for formaldehyde in these studies was high, (4) µg/ml.
According to the Applicant, the theoretical maximum amount of formaldehyde expected to
(b)
form with a 1000 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil is (4) mg which is substantially lower than
the daily body burden of 36 g/day formaldehyde expected to be ingested and formed
endogenously. Because the amount of formaldehyde formed through hydrolysis of sulopenem
etzadroxil is expected to be much smaller than the normal body burden, the formation of
formaldehyde is not a safety concern. The other major metabolite of sulopenem etzadroxil, 2EBA, had plasma exposures in the nonclinical toxicology studies that often exceeded exposures
for sulopenem. 2-EBA is considered to be qualified for safety by its substantial exposures in the
general toxicology studies, in vivo genetic toxicology studies, and developmental and
reproductive toxicology studies with sulopenem etzadroxil. Similarly, two metabolites that
48
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
occur disproportionately in humans, M1a and M1b, are considered qualified for safety in the
rat toxicology studies based on their high percentages in rat plasma.
Probenecid was first approved in 1951 as BENEMID followed by a number of generic
probenecid drug products including the listed probenecid product referenced by the Applicant,
PROBENECID by Actavis Pharma, Inc., which is approved for oral doses of up to 1000 mg/day for
chronic treatment of gout. In the 14-day combination toxicology study, increasing doses of
sulopenem etzadroxil were associated with proportional decreases in probenecid exposure
when the two compounds were administered concomitantly. In the same study, probenecid
was not associated with notable toxicity and coadministration of probenecid with sulopenem
etzadroxil did not substantially change sulopenem AUC exposures in plasma or augment
sulopenem etzadroxil-related toxicity. The general toxicity of probenecid is further qualified by
its extensive use in FDA-approved products. Information on the product label for the listed
probenecid product including warnings, drug interactions, and adverse reactions for probenecid
will be included in the labeling for the current product. Information that is missing from the
product label for the listed product including information on the nonclinical fertility, embryofetal, and pre-postnatal effects of probenecid will also be absent on the product label for the
current product.
Considering the nonclinical results as a whole, NDA 213972 is considered approvable from a
Pharmacology/Toxicology perspective.

maximum recommended dose of sulopenem etzadroxil in humans.

Major Findings
One female and one male Cynomolgus monkey were administered a single dose of
200 mg/kg [14C]CP-70429 by intravenous injection. Urine, feces, and plasma were
collected at different timepoints over a total period of 88 hours. Approximately 78.5%
of the dose was recovered in urine with less than 3% recovered in feces. Four
metabolites were identified in plasma from both males and females with similar
percentages in both sexes (Table 12). The primary metabolite in plasma was M2
which comprised more than 30% of the total radioactivity in plasma in both sexes.

sulfoxide reduction, and sulfide cleavage.

Type of Study
A 14-Day Oral
Gavage Toxicity
Study of PF03709270 With
and Without
Probenecid in
Rats with a 14Day Recovery
Period/ Study No.:
18IT001- (b) (4) 417503-02

Major Findings
Sprague-Dawley rats were administered vehicle or PF-03709270 with and without
probenecid in the following groups in daily oral gavage doses for 14 days: Group 1
(vehicle for PF-03709270), Group 2 (vehicle and 200 mg/kg probenecid), Group 3
(100 mg/kg PF-03709270), Group 4 (800 mg/kg PF-03709270), Group 5 (100 mg/kg
PF-03709270 and 200 mg/kg probenecid), Group 6 (800 mg/kg PF-03709270 and
200 mg/kg probenecid).
CP-70429 Plasma Toxicokinetics (Table 18)
Dose Proportionality: Plasma AUC values for CP-70429 increased in an
approximately dose-proportional manner and plasma Cmax values increased in a less
than dose-proportional manner.
Plasma Accumulation: AUC values were relatively similar after the first dose
compared to after 14 days of dosing consistent with limited plasma accumulation
with repeated dosing.
2-Ethylbutyric Acid (2-EBA) Plasma Toxicokinetics (Table 19)
Dose Proportionality: Plasma AUC values for 2-EBA increased in a more than doseproportional manner and plasma Cmax values increased in a less than doseproportional manner.
Plasma Accumulation: AUC values were relatively similar after the first dose
compared to after 14 days of dosing suggesting a limited plasma accumulation of 2EBA with repeated dosing.
Ratio of CP-70429 to 2-EBA: Plasma AUC values for CP-70429 were as much as
2-fold lower than those for 2-EBA.
Probenecid Plasma Toxicokinetics (Table 20)
Plasma Accumulation: Probenecid Cmax and AUC values were generally similar on
Days 1 and 14 with little evidence of plasma accumulation.
Effect of Concomitant Probenecid on CP-70429 Exposures:
Plasma AUC exposures to CP-70429 in males and females were approximately 1.5
higher for both sexes in the 800:200 mg/kg/day PF-03709270:probenecid group
(Group 6) compared to the 800 mg/kg/day PF-03709270 group (Group 4). However
the AUC exposure for the lower-dose combination group, 100:200 PF03709270:probenecid (Group 5) was the same or less than comparable exposures
for males and females in the 100 mg/kg/day PF-03709270 group (Group 3). This
pattern is consistent with probenecid having a slightly more pronounced effect on the
renal elimination of higher plasma exposures of CP-70429.
Effect of Concomitant PF-03709270 on Probenecid Exposures: Probenecid
exposures reduced in a PF-03709270 dose-dependent manner. This pattern
suggests PF-03709270 may have increased the plasma clearance of probenecid.

5.5. Toxicology
5.5.1. General Toxicology
Study title/ number: 1-Month Oral Toxicity and Micronucleus Study of PF-03709270 in Rats/
Study No: 06GR278





Based on minimal vacuolation of the renal tubular epithelium, renal tubular hypertrophy,
and a low incidence of tubular regeneration that occurred primarily in high-dose males and
females and to a lesser extent in mid-dose males, the low-dose of 100 mg/kg/day was
identified as a no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) in this study.
The plasma AUC0-24h for CP-70429 (sulopenem) associated with the NOAEL dose of PF03709270 on Day 30 was 7240 ng•hr/ml.
The oral administration of PF-03709270 to rats did not induce micronuclei in the
polychromatic bone marrow erythrocytes at ≤2000 mg/kg.

Table 37. Observations and Results: Changes From Control (Study No.: 06GR278)
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
One HD male was euthanized on Day 23 due to body weight loss and clinical
signs including rough fur, stained fur, decreased skin turgor, and noisy labored
respiration observed on Days 19 to 23.
Clinical Signs
In the HD group, clinical signs included stained fur of the muzzle, urogenital
and/or anogenital region in 7/20 animals, noisy respiration in 3/20 animals, and
loose stools in 1/20 animals. The observations were observed sporadically with
low incidence throughout the study.
Body Weights
No PF-03709270-related effects on body weight were observed.
Feed Consumption
Except on Day 8 where slight decreases in mean food consumption (-11% to 12%) were observed in MD and HD females and HD males, no changes in food
consumption occurred.
Ophthalmoscopy
No PF-03709270-related ophthalmoscopy findings were observed.
Hematology
Day 31
HD males: +40% mean prothrombin time**
The increased mean prothrombin time occurred only in HD males and was not
considered to be toxicologically important.
Clinical Chemistry
No toxicologically relevant changes in serum chemistry were observed. Mean
values for ALT and AST were statistically significantly decreased compared to
control values in HD and/or MD males and HD females.
Urinalysis
No toxicologically relevant urinalysis findings were observed
Gross Pathology
Gross pathology findings included enlarged cecum and/or pale multi-focal
discoloration of the kidney in 1/10 LD males, 4/10 MD males, 2/10 MD females,
and 9/10 HD males. In 9/10 HD females, enlarged cecum was observed
including one female with dilation of the duodenum.
Organ Weights
Kidney: Relative kidney weights (relative to body weight) were increased
approximately 10% and 40% in both sexes in the MD and HD groups
respectively compared to control values. The increased kidney weights
correlated with renal tubular hypertrophy observed microscopically.
Liver: Mean absolute and relative liver weights were increased 10% -20% in
both sexes in the HD group compared to control values.
Spleen: Absolute and relative spleen weights were significantly decreased by
13-14% in HD females compared to control values.
Prostate: Absolute and relative prostate weights were decreased approximately
20% in MD and HD males.
In the absence of histologic correlates, the changes in liver, spleen, and
prostate weights were not considered to be toxicologically important.

Histopathology
Minimal focal vacuolation of segmental tubular epithelial cells in the renal cortex
Adequate battery: Yes occurred in 5/10 HD males and 5/10 HD females and in 1/10 MD females. All

hypertrophy of the outer stripe of the medullary zone of the kidney. The tubular
hypertrophy was characterized by mild dilation of the tubular lumina with
increased amounts of epithelial cytoplasm sometimes accompanied by multiple
foci of epithelial regeneration. The severity was minimal to mild in HD males and

correlated with the increased kidney weights for males and females at the two
highest dose levels. Immunohistochemical staining for P450 enzymes 3A1, 2B6,
and 2E1 in kidney sections from one control male and one HD male showed
increased intensity of staining in the hypertrophic outer stripe zone in the HD

Table 39. Observations and Results: Changes From Control (Study No.: 06GR263)
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
No mortality occurred during the study period.
Clinical Signs
PF-03709270-related clinical signs included loose/liquid stools and emesis, and
with a lower incidence, distended abdomen. Loose/liquid stools were observed
beginning on Day 1 in all dose groups and persisted with dose-dependent
increases in incidence and severity throughout the dosing period. Sporadic
emesis was observed in all dose groups between Day 1 and 26. Abdominal
distention was observed in one MD male (Days 30-31), and two HD males (Days
5-12 and 16-31 for one animal and Days 2-12 for the other) and one HD female
(Days 28-30). Hunched posture was observed in one HD male (Days 8-9 and 1112) and one HD female (Day 10) possibly secondary to the gastrointestinal
observations.
Body Weights
Body weights were decreased at the end of the dosing period in HD males and
females by approximately 16% and 9%, respectively, compared to control values.
Feed Consumption
Delays in eating and decreases in food consumption (qualitatively assessed)
were observed beginning on Day 2 in MD and HD males and females.
Ophthalmoscopy
No PF-03709270-related ophthalmoscopy findings were observed.
ECG
No PF-03709270-related changes in any ECG parameters, blood pressure, or
heart rate were observed.
Hematology
On Day 15, minimal to mild decreases in RBC, HGB, and/or HCT (reduced 15%
to 19% compared to pretreatment values) were observed in individual HD
monkeys. On Day 30, slightly greater, but generally mild, decreases in group
mean values for these parameters (reduced 14% to 23% compared to
pretreatment values) were noted in HD monkeys and in MD females as well as
increased RDW (red cell distribution width, 10-20% higher than pretreatment
values) and absolute and percent reticulocytes (240% to 550% increases
compared to pretreatment values). Direct Coomb’s testing on Days 15 and 30
demonstrated positive reactions for polyspecific anti-human globulin and antiIgG, but not anti-C3b/C3d, in all MD and HD animals and the strength of the
reaction tended to increase with dose. These results were consistent with
antibody-mediated red blood cell loss with compensatory erythropoiesis. Slightly
increased platelet counts (40% to 60% increase compared to pretreatment
values) on Days 15 and 30 in male HD monkeys was consistent with
thrombocytosis secondary to antibody-mediated red cell turnover.
Clinical Chemistry
In HD males and females, slight reductions in mean serum albumin (reductions
of 14% to 18% compared to pretreatment values) were observed. The reduction
in serum albumin coupled with slightly increased serum globulin in HD females
(+10% compared to pretreatment values) resulted in a decreased albumin/
globulin ratio (-24% compared to pretreatment). These systemic responses may
have been associated with immune-mediated red cell turnover.
Urinalysis
On Day 31, urine pH was slightly decreased to ≤8.0 in 0/6, 1/6, 4/6, and 3/6
animals (both male and female) in control, LD, MD, and HD groups, respectively.
A white precipitate, possibly related to the alkaline urine was observed on Day 31
in urine samples from three HD females. The sediment had a microscopic
appearance of amorphous granular material consisting of round, oval and
irregularly shaped refractile bodies. The origin and toxicological significance of
the granular material is unknown.
Gross Pathology
Dilation of the colon was observed in 2/3 HD males.

Major Findings
In males and females in the HD group, absolute and relative (to body weight)
liver weights were increased by approximately 10-30% compared to control
values. Also absolute and relative kidney weights were increased by
approximately 8-9% in HD males. All of the changes were not statistically
significant and no histological correlates corresponded with the increased liver
and kidney weights.
Mean absolute and relative (to body weight) adrenal weights were increased by
10 to 40% in MD and HD males and in females at all PF-03709270 dose levels.
In HD animals increased adrenal weights were associated with cortical
hypertrophy. Also absolute and relative thymus weights were decreased by 26%
to 72% compared to control values in MD and HD males and females. The
decreased thymus weights correlated with histological findings of lymphoid
depletion in the thymus. The increased adrenal weights and decreased thymus
weights are consistent with treatment-related stress.
No liver or kidney histopathology was reported.
GI tract: In the jejunum and, to a lesser extent, the ileum, minimal mucosal
hyperplasia was noted in HD animals. The effects were subtle and likely reflected
a slight increase in cell loss from villi and increased proliferation of crypt
epithelium.
Adrenal Glands and Thymus: Decreased cortical hypertrophy in HD animals
and lymphoid depletion in HD males (minimal to marked) and females (moderate
to marked) was consistent with a treatment-related stress response.
Toxicokinetics: See Section 5.4

5.5.2. General Toxicology; Additional Studies
Study title/ number: 14-Day Oral Gavage Toxicity Study of PF-03709270 with and
(b) (4)
without Probenecid in Rats with a 14-Day Recovery Period/ Study No: 18IT001417503-02






In male and female rats administered 800 mg/kg PF-03709270 with and without
probenecid, histopathology findings included accumulations of seromucinous
secretions along with degeneration of the nasal epithelium and slight osteolysis
of turbinate bones. The nasal findings were reduced for incidence and severity
after the recovery period and may have been related to nasal reflux exposure to
gavage fluids.
Histopathology findings in the large intestine of male and female rats receiving
800 mg/kg/day PF-03709270 with or without probenecid included infiltrates of
mixed inflammatory cells and hyperplasia of the glandular epithelium. The large
intestine findings were fully reversible after the recovery period.
Concomitant administration of 200 mg/kg/day probenecid with 800 mg/kg/day
PF-03709270 did not substantially change PF-03709270-related findings.

Feed Consumption

Hematology

Clinical Chemistry
Urea Nitrogen: Statistically significantly lower urea nitrogen levels in serum
were observed in males and females in Groups 4 (800 mg/kg PF-03709270)
and Group 6 (800 mg/kg PF-03709270:200 mg/kg probenecid) at the end of

recovery period on Day 30, urea nitrogen levels were similar in all groups.
Creatinine: Serum creatinine was statistically significantly increased in Groups
5 (100 mg/kg PF-03709270: 200 mg probenecid) and 6 in males and females at

32% increased, and in females creatine levels were approximately 9% and 6%
increased respectively in Groups 5 and 6 on Day 15. On Day 30 after the
recovery period, creatine levels were similar in all groups.

Urinalysis

Gross Pathology

Renal impairment generally results in increased circulating levels of both urea
nitrogen and creatinine. In this case urea nitrogen levels were reduced in the
groups receiving he highest doses of PF-03709270. Reductions in urea nitrogen
might indicate that less is being produced by the liver. Given the reversibility of
the findings and in the absence of histological correlates in the liver or kidney,
the toxicological relevance of the findings is not clear.
Urine specific gravity was significantly higher for females in Group 6 (1.050)
compared to the mean control value (1.025) at the end of dosing on Day 15.
However, a similar effect was not observed in males in Group 6 or in the other
treatment groups on Day 15 and specific gravity values were similar in all
groups for both sexes at the end of the recovery period on Day 29.
No gross pathology findings were considered to be related to administration of
PF-03709270 or probenecid or the combination.

Table 47. Observations and Results (Study No.: 09GR119)
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
In the HD group, 10/25 pregnant female mice died or were prematurely
euthanized between GD 11 and GD 16 prior to the scheduled termination. The
incidence of mortality was statistically significantly increased in the HD group
compared to the vehicle control group. Death was generally preceded by
decreased motor activity, signs of respiratory distress, abdominal distention,
mild to severe dehydration, and hunched posture. At necropsy, each mouse
had gaseous distention of the stomach and/or the intestines. The deaths was
attributed to PF-03709270.
Clinical Signs
Clinical signs were observed in HD females including signs of respiratory
distress (rales, dyspnea, gasping, open mouth breathing, and bradypnea),
abdominal distention, decreased motor activity, cold to touch, mild to severe
dehydration, pale and/or dark red appearance to one or more body parts

occurred primarily in the HD females that died or were prematurely euthanized.
PF-03709270-related clinical signs were not observed in LD or MD females.

Table 50. Observations and Results (Study No.: 08GR040)
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
Deaths considered to be related to PF-03709270 administration included one
HD female euthanized on GD 10 due to excess body weight loss and one HD
female found dead on GD 19.
Clinical Signs
PF-03709270-related clinical signs in most HD females consisted of alopecia,
stained fur, hunched stance, and noisy respiration. In the MD group, the only
treatment-related clinical sign was noisy respiration in 2 animals.
Body Weights
Statistically significant PF-03709270-related reductions in maternal body weight
and body weight gain were noted in the MD and HD groups. In the HD group,
body weight gain over the dosing period (GD 6-18) was reduced by 42% and
mean body weights were significantly reduced from GD 8 to GD 21 by 4-14%
compared to control values. The effect was less pronounced in the MD group
where body weight gain over the dosing period (GD 6-18) was significantly
reduced by 17%, and mean body weights were significantly reduced from GD
14 to GD 21 by 3-6%. In the LD group, body weight gain over the entire
treatment period (GD 6-18) was greater than that noted in the control group.
Feed Consumption
PF-03709270-related decreases in food consumption were noted in the MD and
HD groups with significant 12% and 30% reductions over the treatment period
for the two dose groups respectively. In the LD group a statistically significant
decrease in food consumption was noted from GD 7-9 (11% reduction
compared to control), however, food consumption over the entire treatment
period was comparable to controls.
Necropsy findings
No PF-03709270-related gross pathology findings were observed. Gravid uterus
Cesarean Section Data weights were significantly decreased in the MD and HD groups, and in the same
groups, non-significant PF-03709270-related increases in the number of early
resorptions and post-implantation losses and decreases in the number of viable
fetuses were noted. Also, mean fetal body weights were significantly reduced by
11% in the HD group (5.09 g) compared to the mean control value (5.72 g).
There were no treatment-related effects on any Cesarean section parameters in
the LD group.
Necropsy findings
External Alterations: The only reported external malformation was an
Offspring
omphalocele in a single LD fetus.
Visceral Alterations: None of the visceral malformations were statistically
significantly increased for litter or fetal incidence in the PF-03709270-treatment
groups compared to control values. Two malformations that did not occur in the
vehicle control group occurred in single fetuses in the MD (single fetus with situs
inversus) and the HD groups (single fetus with retroesophageal aortic arch).
There were no PF-03709270-related increases in visceral variations.
Skeletal Alterations: No skeletal malformations were reported. Two skeletal
variations, unossified cervical centrum and unossified metatarsal, were
statistically significantly increased for litter incidence in the HD group compared
to the vehicle control group.

Body Weights

Major Findings
No significant differences in mean body weights were observed for any of the
PF-03709270 treatment groups. In HD dams, there were statistically significant
decreases in body weight gain over the gestation intervals of GD 7 to GD 10
(reduced 133% compared to control values), GD 20 to GD 23 (reduced 83%
compared to control values), and for the entire dosing period from GD 7 to GD
20 (reduced 60% compared to control values). In the MD group, a statistically
significant decrease in body weight gain was noted over the gestation interval
of GD 20 to GD 23 (reduced 50% compared to control values) and for the
entire dosing period GD 7 to 20 (reduced 36% compared to control values). In
the LD group, body weight gains were significantly decreased over the entire
dosing period from GD 7-20 (reduced 28% compared to control values).
Feed Consumption
Average maternal food consumption in the MD and HD groups was statistically
significantly reduced daily from GD 8-22 and over the intervals of 8-10, 11-13,
14-16, 17-20, and 8-20. In the LD group, food consumption was significantly
reduced daily from GD 13-22 and over the intervals of 8-10, 14-16, 17-20, and
8-20. Average daily food consumption was significantly reduced in all the PF03709270 treatment groups over the dosing period (GD 8 to GD 20) with dosedependent reductions in daily food intake of 15%, 36% and 44% compared to
control values for the LD, MD, and HD groups, respectively. For the GD 23 to
29 interval, food consumption was similar in all groups.
Necropsy findings
No maternal necropsy findings were considered related to PF-03709270
Cesarean Section Data administration. In the MD and HD groups, late resorptions were increased
compared to control values with statistical significance achieved for the HD
group. Also, post-implantation loss was significantly increased and the number
of viable fetuses, and gravid uterine weights were significantly reduced in the
MD and HD groups compared to control values. Mean fetal body weights were
significantly reduced by approximately 9% and 7% in the MD and HD groups
respectively with mean values of 39.75, 39.50, 36.30, and 37.09 grams for the
control, LD, MD, and HD groups, respectively.
Necropsy findings
External Alterations: No external malformations were considered related to
Offspring
administration of PF-03709270. Two external malformations were reported:
exencephaly in one vehicle control fetus and omphalocele in one MD fetus.
Visceral Alterations: No visceral malformations were reported. Multiple visceral
variations occurred with similar incidences in all groups.
Skeletal Malformations: There were no PF-03709270-related skeletal
malformations. Malformations (fused frontal, nasal, rib, and sternebra; absent
interparietal, supraoccipital, and thoracic arch; hemicentric thoracic centrum;
and misshapen parietal) were either seen only in the concurrent control group
or at incidence levels comparable to or below the concurrent control group.
Skeletal Variations: Multiple skeletal variations were observed but only one
variation was increased for incidence in a dose-dependent manner. The litter
incidence of unossified forepaw phalanx was statistically significantly increased
in both the MD group (litter incidence of 72.2%) and HD group (litter incidence
of 84.6%) compared to the LD (litter incidence of 23.5%) and control (litter
incidence of 21.1%) groups. This variation may have resulted from maternal
toxicity and is consistent with the reduced fetal body weights observed in the
MD and HD groups in this study.

The Office of Clinical Pharmacology (Division of Infectious Disease Pharmacology and Division of

Pivotal or supportive evidence of
The pivotal evidence of effectiveness for sulopenem in patients
effectiveness
with uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTI) comes from one
Phase 3 trial (IT001-301).
General dosing instructions
The proposed dosing regimen is one bilayer tablet (500 mg
sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid) administered orally with
food twice daily for 5 days. Probenecid increases the plasma
exposures of sulopenem while decreasing its renal clearance.
Because of the importance of urine drug concentrations in the
treatment of uUTI, use of probenecid in combination with
sulopenem etzadroxil may not be appropriate for the proposed
indication. Nonclinical PK/PD studies also suggest the proposed
dosage regimen may not be optimal.

(intrinsic and extrinsic factors)

mL/min due to reduced effectiveness. Use is also not
recommended in subjects on hemodialysis due to the unknown
impact of hemodialysis on the disposition of sulopenem.
Labeling
The contents and format of the proposed labeling language are not
aligned with the current guidance and will be revised.

6.2. Summary of Clinical Pharmacology Assessment
6.2.1. Pharmacology and Clinical Pharmacokinetics
Table 65. Summary of the Pharmacokinetic Properties of Sulopenem
Absorption
Sulopenem etzadroxil is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem, the microbiologically-active
moiety, following oral administration. Only the pharmacokinetic profile of sulopenem is discussed further
because sulopenem etzadroxil is not detected in plasma following oral administration. The absolute
bioavailability of sulopenem following administration of a single dose of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil
and 500 mg probenecid as the oral bilayer tablet under fasted conditions was 40%. Peak plasma
concentrations are achieved within 1 h under fasted conditions and 2 h under fed conditions. A high fat
meal increased the oral bioavailability of sulopenem to 64%.
Distribution
% bound to human plasma protein
10.7%
Volume of distribution (L)a
75 L (following intravenous administration) and 134 L (apparent
Vd after oral administration)
Elimination
The half-life of sulopenem is approximately 1.2 hours.
Metabolism
Sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed after oral administration to sulopenem in the intestines and in
systemic circulation. Sulopenem and two inactive metabolites formed by β-lactam cyclic amide bond
hydrolysis (M1a and M1b) are the major circulating entities. Sulopenem, M1a and M1b accounted for
32%, 21.8% and 43.6%, respectively, of circulating radioactivity in the mass balance study. No
metabolism of sulopenem was observed in vitro with recombinant CYP or UGT enzymes.
Excretion
Following oral administration of a 2000 mg dose of [14C] sulopenem etzadroxil, 85.1% of the radiolabeled
dose was recovered in urine (44.3%) and feces (40.8%) as unchanged sulopenem and metabolites.
Sulopenem accounted for 26.9% and 3.1% of the administered dose in urine and feces, respectively.

6.2.2. General Dosing and Therapeutic Individualization
General Dosing
The Applicant’s proposed dosage regimen is one bilayer tablet (containing 500 mg sulopenem
etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid) administered orally twice daily for 5 days based on the
expectation that as a β-lactam, sulopenem should exhibit time dependent killing. However,
data from the Applicant’s nonclinical PK/PD studies suggest that sulopenem’s activity against
uropathogens may be concentration dependent, which would imply that the proposed dosage
regimen is not optimal. If sulopenem’s activity is indeed concentration dependent, a higher
dose would be expected to be more efficacious than the proposed dosage regimen.
Therapeutic Individualization
No clinically significant differences in the PK of sulopenem were observed based on age,
gender, or body weight.

100
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Hepatic Impairment
The effect of hepatic impairment on the PK of sulopenem was not studied. However, because
sulopenem does not undergo significant hepatic metabolism or biliary excretion, hepatic
impairment is not expected to impact the PK of sulopenem.
Renal Impairment
The sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid fixed-dose combination is not recommended in patients
with CLcr ≤60 mL/min and patients on hemodialysis.
The dedicated renal impairment study showed AUC values of sulopenem for subjects with mild,
moderate and several renal impairment were 2.0-, 3.0- and 7.4-fold higher, respectively, than
the corresponding exposure in subjects with normal renal function after receiving a single 1000
mg oral dose of sulopenem etzadroxil. These increases in sulopenem plasma exposure
paralleled a progressive decrease in sulopenem renal clearance with worsening renal
impairment. However, because sulopenem has a short half-life (~1 h), the cumulative amount
of sulopenem recovered in urine over a 24 h period was comparable across renal function
groups. Although the effect of probenecid on sulopenem exposure was not evaluated in this
study, probenecid’s functionality as an OAT3 inhibitor is attenuated in the setting of renal
impairment, and thus is not expected to yield significant increases in sulopenem exposures in
subjects with renal impairment. The effects of kidney failure (CLcr <15 mL/min) and
hemodialysis on the PK of sulopenem were not studied.
Given the proposed uUTI indication, renal impairment has implications for both safety and
efficacy. The safety assessment for subjects across renal function groups indicated that no
additional treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were observed in the various renal
impairment groups compared with subjects with normal renal function. The AUC observed in
subjects with severe renal impairment was comparable to the AUC associated with the
maximally tolerated dose (MTD) in single ascending doses (SAD) studies, and ~28% higher than
the AUC observed for the MTD in multiple ascending doses (MAD) studies. Nonetheless, given
sulopenem’s short half-life and the proposed treatment duration of 5 days, 500 mg sulopenem
administered with 500 mg probenecid is expected to be safe in subjects with severe renal
impairment. This was confirmed in the Phase 3 uUTI trial, where no additional TEAEs were
observed in subjects with severe renal impairment (See Section 8.2).
Based on the available safety information, the fixed-dose combination is not recommended in
patients with CLcr <15 mL/min and patients on hemodialysis because the safety of sulopenem
has not been studied in these subpopulations.
In the Phase 3 uUTI trial, the efficacy of sulopenem was lower in subjects with CLcr ≤60 mL/min
compared to subjects with CLcr >60 mL/min (See Section 8.1.2). This decreased response to
sulopenem may be partly due to the reduced renal clearance of sulopenem (and subsequently,
lower urine sulopenem concentrations especially early in the dosing interval) in subjects with
CLcr ≤60 mL/min. Therefore, the fixed-dose combination is not recommended in patients with
CLcr ≤60 mL/min due to sulopenem’s reduced effectiveness in this subpopulation.

6.3. Comprehensive Clinical Pharmacology Review
6.3.1. General Pharmacology and Pharmacokinetic Characteristics
Information pertaining to the general pharmacology and pharmacokinetic characteristics of
sulopenem are summarized in Table 66. Relevant clinical pharmacology information is also
summarized for sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid in Table 66.
Table 66. General Pharmacology and Pharmacokinetic Characteristics
Characteristic
Summary
Mechanism of Action
Sulopenem etzadroxil is an oral prodrug that is rapidly cleaved to
release the active compound, sulopenem. Sulopenem belongs to the
penem (β-lactam) class of antibacterial drugs. Sulopenem inhibits
bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to essential penicillin-binding
proteins (PBP).
Probenecid is a uricosuric and renal tubular blocking agent that
inhibits the OAT3-mediated excretion of sulopenem, thereby
providing increased plasma concentrations of sulopenem.
Active Moieties
Sulopenem
QT Prolongation
At a concentration of 40 times or greater than that achieved after a
single 500 mg dose, sulopenem does not prolong the QTc interval to
any clinically relevant extent.
Bioanalysis
Multiple LC-MS/MS assays were developed and validated to
determine concentrations of sulopenem in human plasma and urine.
All bioanalytical methods met the requirements for accuracy,
precision, sensitivity, and specificity.

dosing regimen for uUTI
administration of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with 500 mg

Based on a population pharmacokinetic analysis, model predicted

respectively.
Of note, the model-predicted sulopenem AUC and Cmax for Phase 3
uUTI patients are based on composite PK data from subjects
reported as having received the fixed-dose bilayer tablet in either the
fed or fasted state. Fed status was poorly defined in the Phase 3
study and food intake was not reported for all subjects. Because
food increases bioavailability and food intake was variable,
delineating the influence of infection on sulopenem exposures is
confounded by this lack of uniformity in study drug administration.

6.3.2. Clinical Pharmacology Questions
Does the clinical pharmacology program provide supportive evidence of effectiveness?
The primary evidence of efficacy of sulopenem in the treatment of uUTI was provided by one
Phase 3 trial (IT001-301). In accordance with the FDA guidance on drug development for the
treatment of uUTI, the Applicant evaluated sulopenem urine concentrations in a subpopulation
of patients enrolled in the Phase 3 trial. Based strictly on comparison of the mean urine
103
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
concentrations from uUTI patients to the proposed susceptible breakpoint of 0.5 µg/mL, the
Applicant asserts that sulopenem urine concentrations exceed this threshold concentration for
at least 80% of the dosing interval. However, no formal target attainment analyses were
conducted based on urinary concentrations to support this assertion or illustrate that adequate
sulopenem concentrations are achieved at the site of action.
Is the proposed dosing regimen appropriate for the general patient population for which the
indication is being sought?
The proposed oral dosing regimen for adults is 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with 500 mg
probenecid (one bilayer tablet as a fixed-dose combination) administered twice daily for 5 days
for the treatment of uUTI caused by susceptible microorganisms proven or strongly suspected
to be non-susceptible to a quinolone. This dosing regimen may not be appropriate because only
a subset of the population in the Phase 3 uUTI trial met the predefined margin for
demonstration of efficacy relative to ciprofloxacin, which is further corroborated by nonclinical
PK/PD findings.
Sulopenem Etzadroxil Dosing
As with other β-lactam antibacterials, the efficacy of sulopenem was expected to be driven by
the duration of time that plasma concentrations exceed MIC (i.e., T > MIC). To support the
proposed dosage regimen for the treatment of uUTI, the Applicant conducted PK/PD studies in
a murine thigh infection model. These studies were intended to: 1) delineate the relevant
PK/PD index for sulopenem, and 2) estimate the magnitude of this index required for various
microbiologic endpoints (i.e., bacterial stasis, 1-log, and 2-log CFU/mL reduction in bacterial
burden). Per the Applicant’s interpretation of the data from these studies, sulopenem’s activity
was characterized as time dependent. Therefore, a 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil in
combination with 500 mg probenecid every 12 hours was expected to achieve the T > MIC
target associated with antimicrobial activity over the range of epidemiological MIC90 values
observed for target pathogens. However, the Clinical Pharmacology team’s assessment of the
nonclinical PK/PD studies determined that there was insufficient evidence for the use of
T > MIC as the relevant index for sulopenem. Although not definitive, the overall data trend
suggested that sulopenem exhibits concentration-dependent killing against uropathogens (for
details, see response to the question regarding clinical pharmacology information to support
the proposed breakpoint in this section). If sulopenem’s activity is indeed concentration
dependent as suggested by these studies, the proposed dosing regimen of 500 mg sulopenem
etzadroxil administered twice daily (in combination with 500 mg probenecid) may be
suboptimal. A higher dose of sulopenem etzadroxil would be expected to yield higher urine
concentrations of sulopenem and thus be more efficacious for the treatment of uUTI.
Probenecid Dosing
Because the bilayer tablet includes probenecid, a marketed drug, and the Applicant relied on
information described in the FDA-approved labeling for the listed drug, the probenecid
104
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
component of the formulation was bridged to a commercial probenecid tablet. To this end, the
Applicant illustrated that probenecid plasma exposures were comparable following
administration of the bilayer tablet and probenecid, USP tablet (an FDA-approved generic drug
version of the reference listed drug, Benemid) in Study IT001-105.
Probenecid lacks antimicrobial activity; instead, it increases plasma exposures of β-lactams by
decreasing the renal clearance of these drugs. As an adjuvant to β-lactam therapy, the
recommended daily dose of probenecid is 2000 mg administered in divided doses. For the uUTI
drug development program, probenecid dose selection was informed by Studies A8811018 and
IT001-101, two Phase 1 studies which evaluated the effect of probenecid doses of 250 mg, 500
mg, and 1000 mg on sulopenem exposure. In Study IT001-101, sulopenem AUCs following
administration of sulopenem etzadroxil with either 250 mg or 500 mg probenecid were
comparable. In both Studies A8811018 and IT001-101, increasing the dose of probenecid from
500 mg to 1000 mg of probenecid (i.e., a 2-fold increase in dose) resulted in only an additional
1.3 to 1.4-fold increase in sulopenem AUC. The Applicant noted that this additional fold
increase in exposure would not result in a clinically relevant increase in T > MIC at MICs of 0.5
(b) (4)
µg/mL and 1 µg/mL
Therefore, 500 mg probenecid was expected to be sufficient.
In Study IT001-102, it was determined that simultaneous administration of a single 500 mg dose
of probenecid with sulopenem etzadroxil results in higher plasma sulopenem exposures than
either staggering the administration of sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid, or administering
probenecid as 2 divided doses. Based on these findings, 500 mg probenecid was selected for coformulation with sulopenem etzadroxil.
When administered as a single 500 mg dose, probenecid increased the plasma AUC of
sulopenem by ~1.3 to 1.4-fold compared to administration of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil
alone. Additionally, multiple dose administration of 500 mg probenecid with 500 mg sulopenem
etzadroxil decreased renal clearance of sulopenem by 1.9-fold and increased sulopenem AUC
by 1.8-fold under fed conditions (See Appendix 16.3). The cumulative amount of sulopenem
recovered in urine over a 24 h period was comparable in the presence or absence of
probenecid. However, because probenecid increases plasma exposures of sulopenem at the
expense of diminished renal clearance, its use for the treatment of uUTI may not be
appropriate if sulopenem’s activity is concentration dependent (as suggested by nonclinical
PK/PD studies). Instead, concurrent use of probenecid may promote subtherapeutic urine
concentrations of sulopenem and thus contribute to treatment failure.
Sulopenem Etzadroxil With Probenecid Dosing
The proposed dosing regimen for the treatment of uUTI was evaluated in the Phase 3 uUTI trial,
IT001-301, in which adult females with signs and symptoms of uUTI were randomized to receive
either 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with 500 mg probenecid as a fixed-dose combination or
ciprofloxacin. The primary study endpoint of overall response (a composite of clinical and
microbiological response) was evaluated in 2 separate patient populations: patients who
presented with a quinolone-susceptible pathogen at baseline (MMITTS), and patients who
105
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
presented with a quinolone-resistant pathogen at baseline (MMITTR). In the MMITTR
population, sulopenem showed superiority to ciprofloxacin in the treatment of uUTI. However,
in the MMITTS population, sulopenem failed to demonstrate noninferiority to ciprofloxacin
(See Section 8). Failure to meet the noninferiority margin in the MMITTS population may be
indicative of suboptimal dosing of sulopenem etzadroxil as suggested by the nonclinical PK/PD
studies. Furthermore, because probenecid may decrease urinary concentrations of sulopenem,
its use for a uUTI indication may be inappropriate.
Is an alternative dosing regimen or management strategy required for subpopulations based
on intrinsic patient factors?
No clinically significant differences in the PK of sulopenem were observed based on age, gender
or body weight based on popPK modeling. Hepatic impairment is also not expected to impact
the PK of sulopenem. However, use of the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid fixed-dose
combination tablet is not recommended in subjects with CLcr ≤60 mL/min due to safety and
efficacy concerns in this subpopulation (as described below).
Hepatic Impairment
The effect of hepatic impairment on the PK of sulopenem was not studied. In vitro, sulopenem
was not metabolized by recombinant CYP or UGT enzymes. Additionally, the mass balance
study (Study A8811006) indicated that biliary excretion does not play a role in sulopenem
elimination. In the Phase 3 uUTI trial, 20 subjects in the sulopenem arm of the study had a
history of liver disease and the incidence of adverse events (AEs) in this subset of subjects (30%)
was comparable to that of the general population (25%). In the Phase 3 cUTI trial, 29 subjects
with a history of liver disease were identified and in this study, a higher percentage (i.e., 38%)
of patients receiving sulopenem experienced adverse events compared to the overall study
population (15%). However, given the small number of subjects with hepatic impairment and
possible variability in severity of hepatic impairment in the cUTI trial, the safety implications of
this difference in the incidence of adverse events are unknown. Based on the totality of
available information, hepatic impairment is not expected to significantly impact the PK of
sulopenem. Therefore, the proposed dose is expected to be safe in patients with hepatic
impairment.
Renal Impairment
In the mass balance study, following oral administration of a 2000 mg dose of [14C]sulopenem
etzadroxil, approximately 26.9% of total radioactivity was recovered in urine as unchanged
sulopenem. Based on population PK modeling of data from all Phase 3 trials, a 2-fold increase in
AUC was observed with decreasing CLcr following administration of the bilayer tablet. However,
multiple confounders may preclude reliable estimation of the effect of renal impairment on
sulopenem exposure using population PK modeling (See Appendix 16.3). Ultimately, renal
impairment was not associated with an increased incidence of adverse events in the Phase 3
uUTI trial.
106
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
In the dedicated renal impairment study (Study A8811009), following administration of a 1000
mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil, sulopenem plasma AUC0-inf increased 2.0-, 3.0- and 7.4-fold
for subjects with mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively, compared with
subjects with normal renal function. However, these higher exposures were not associated with
a higher incidence of TEAEs in subjects with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment
compared to subjects with normal renal function. Notably, PK in patients with CLcr <15 mL/min
and the effect of dialysis were not assessed in the renal impairment study.
The renal impairment study did not evaluate the effects of coadministration of probenecid on
sulopenem exposure in the various renal function groups. According to the referenced
probenecid labeling, the effects of probenecid as an OAT3 inhibitor are diminished in the
setting of chronic renal impairment (particularly when estimated glomerular filtration rate is
≤30 mL/min) due to functional decline of tubular secretion. Therefore, coadministration of
probenecid is not expected to increase sulopenem exposure to a significant extent in the
setting of severe renal impairment and renal failure. The single 1000 mg dose of sulopenem
etzadroxil used in the renal impairment study is expected to be administered as divided doses
of 500 mg twice daily for the treatment of uUTI. Because the AUC of sulopenem increased
approximately dose proportionally within the sulopenem etzadroxil dose range of 400 to 2000
mg in SAD studies, the estimated sulopenem AUC for a 500 mg dose in subjects with severe
renal impairment is approximately 24.0 µg·h/mL. This exposure is comparable to that of the
MTD (4000 mg) in SAD studies (i.e., 26.9 µg·h/mL). The MTD in MAD studies was 1200 mg
sulopenem etzadroxil in combination with 1000 mg probenecid BID, which was associated with
an AUC of 18.8 µg·h/mL. Although this AUC is ~28% lower than the anticipated AUC for a 500
mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil in subjects with severe renal impairment, the proposed dose
is expected to be safe in subjects with severe renal impairment given sulopenem’s short halflife even in the setting of severe renal impairment (i.e., 2.75 h) and the short treatment
duration of 5 days.
As indicated in the FDA guidance on drug development for the treatment of uUTIs, urinary
exposures are important for the efficacy of drugs intended for the treatment of uUTI. Subgroup
efficacy analyses for the MMITTR population in the Phase 3 uUTI trial showed a lower response
rate in subjects with CLcr ≤60 mL/min in both the sulopenem and ciprofloxacin arms (See
Section 8.1.2). The underlying causes of reduced efficacy in subjects with CLcr ≤60 mL/min
could be multifactorial, with failure to achieve adequate drug exposures in urine as a
contributing factor. In the Phase 3 uUTI trial, Day 1 urine concentrations were evaluated in 117
subjects in the sulopenem arm. Of these, only 7 subjects had CLcr ≤60 mL/min. Study results
suggested that compared to subjects with normal renal function, subjects with severe renal
impairment (CLcr <30 mL/min) exhibited significantly lower sulopenem urine concentrations
across the entire 6 h urine collection period as shown in Figure 1. Sulopenem urine
concentrations in patients with CLcr 30 to ≤60 mL/min were also low for the first 2 h collection
interval, and increased thereafter.

Due to the limited number of subjects with urine PK data who had CLcr ≤60 mL/min (and
especially those with severe renal impairment, where N=1), it is unclear if these observations
are representative of the expected difference in sulopenem urine concentrations when
compared to subjects with normal renal function. Nonetheless, if the efficacy of sulopenem is
concentration dependent, the slower renal clearance (and consequently, lower urine
concentrations of sulopenem especially early in the dosing interval) in subjects with moderate
and severe impairment may have contributed to the reduced efficacy rate observed in this
population.
Based on the totality of information, the proposed dose is expected to be safe in patients with
mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment. Because subjects with CLcr <15 mL/min and
subjects on hemodialysis were excluded from the renal impairment study, the safety of
sulopenem in this population cannot be ascertained. Additionally, since the drug product is
supplied as a fixed-dose combination, dosage reduction (if needed) would not be feasible for
such patients. From an efficacy perspective, the proposed dose appears to be less efficacious in
subjects with CLcr ≤60mL/min. Furthermore, administration of a higher dose in this population
may be infeasible, especially in patients with CLcr <30 mL/min, whose sulopenem plasma
exposure following a 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil is expected to approximate that of
the MTD in single and multiple ascending dose studies.
Because of the above-stated safety and efficacy concerns, administration of the 500 mg
sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid fixed-dose combination tablet is not recommended
in patients with CLcr ≤60 mL/min and in patients on hemodialysis.

Are there clinically relevant food-drug or drug-drug interactions, and what is the appropriate
management strategy?
Yes, food intake increases the bioavailability of sulopenem and may moderately improve the
tolerability of sulopenem. Therefore, the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet
should be administered with food. No clinically relevant drug-drug interactions (DDIs) were
observed with sulopenem etzadroxil, sulopenem or probenecid.
Food Effect
Following administration of the to-be-marketed sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet
formulation to healthy adult volunteers, AUCinf and Cmax increased 48% and 45%, respectively,
with a high fat meal (800-1000 calories; 50% fat) compared to fasted conditions (Table 67).
