The Applicant proposed that the bilayer tablet should be taken with food
.
The Applicant’s rationale for this recommendation is that food increases the oral bioavailability
of sulopenem and based on the results of the Phase 3 uUTI trial, the incidence of diarrhea is
significantly decreased with food intake. Although food intake was reported in the Phase 3 uUTI
study, the type of food consumed and caloric contents were not recorded. Furthermore, the
timing of food intake and definition of fed state were not clearly defined. Based on the
available information, the incidence of treatment-emergent diarrhea was comparable under
fed (7.1%) and fasted conditions (7.4%) as summarized in Table 68. Nonetheless, administration
of study drug with food appeared to decrease the mean duration of treatment-emergent
diarrhea from 5.6 days to 3.7 days. The lack of a notable difference in the incidence of diarrhea
is consistent with the safety findings from the dedicated food effect study, IT001-105, where
the incidence of GI-related TEAEs following administration of the bilayer tablet were identical
(7.1%) in the fed and fasted states; however, no diarrhea was reported under either fed or
fasted conditions.

Of note, food did not appear to impact efficacy in the Phase 3 uUTI trial. Administration of the
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet in the fed or fasted states resulted in
comparable overall response rates of 65.2% and 66.3%, respectively, at the TOC visit for the
entire microbiologically-evaluable population. This was consistent with efficacy results in the
MMITTR population, where efficacy rates were reported as 65.4% in the fed state and 59.4% in
the fasted state.

Drug-Drug Interactions
Summary of In Vitro Studies
In vitro studies indicated that sulopenem is a substrate of OAT3, and sulopenem etzadroxil is a
substrate of P-gp and inhibitor of CYP3A4/5, P-gp, BCRP, OAT1 and OAT3. No clinical evaluation
of sulopenem etzadroxil as a OAT1/3, CYP3A4/5, BCRP and P-gp inhibitor was performed by the
110
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Applicant. Given that sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed upon oral administration and
was undetected in plasma in the mass balance study (Study A8811006), the potential for
clinically relevant DDIs with OAT1/3 is considered to be low. Because sulopenem etzadroxil is
administered orally, it has the potential to inhibit CYP3A4/5, BCRP and P-gp in the gut. The
sulopenem etzadroxil IC50 for inhibition of CYP3A4/5 could not be calculated within the
concentration range studied in vitro, and was estimated to be >150 µM. Although the IC50
values for BCRP (IC50=20.4 µM) and P-gp (IC50=1.91 µM) are likely to be exceeded by more than
10-fold in the GI tract following administration of a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil,
the Applicant’s in vitro stability and release studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil is
rapidly degraded in simulated intestinal fluid. Therefore, sulopenem etzadroxil’s inhibition of
BCRP and P-gp is expected to be transient. Similarly, regardless of the magnitude of the in vitro
IC50 for CYP3A4/5 inhibition, sulopenem etzadroxil’s effect as a CYP3A4/5 inhibitor is also
expected to be transient and not result in a clinically significant DDI with CYP3A4/5 substrates.
Probenecid is a known OAT3 inhibitor, and was found to be a substrate and inhibitor of BCRP in
vitro. No clinical evaluations of probenecid as a BCRP substrate and inhibitor were performed.
The in vitro IC50 of probenecid as a BCRP inhibitor was 814 µM, resulting in an Igut to IC50 ratio of
10, which is the threshold for characterizing an orally administered drug as a BCRP inhibitor in
the 2020 FDA In Vitro DDI Guidance. However, because of probenecid’s low aqueous solubility
(0.06 mg/mL), the probability of clinically significant BCRP-mediated DDIs with probenecid is
low. Furthermore, the relevance of the interaction between probenecid and BCRP substrates or
inhibitors may not be clinically meaningful. For instance, coadministration of cyclosporine (an
inhibitor of BCRP) with eltrombopag (a BCRP substrate) did not have clinically meaningful
implications (Aslanis et al. 2018). However, clinically significant interactions with BCRP
substrates have typically been reported where multiple transporter pathways are responsible
for the disposition of the substrate drug (Allred et al. 2011).
Summary of Clinical DDI Studies
Effect of P-gp Inhibitors on Sulopenem Pharmacokinetics:
Because sulopenem etzadroxil was identified as a P-gp substrate in vitro, the Applicant
conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the effect of P-gp inhibitors on sulopenem exposure
using oral itraconazole. In Study IT001-103, administration of a clinical dose of 200 mg
itraconazole (2 x 100 mg capsules) daily for 3 days in the fasted state, followed by concomitant
administration of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid on Day 4 in the fed state did not result in a
clinically significant increase in sulopenem exposure. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is
required for coadministration with P-gp inhibitors.
Effect of Antacids and Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPI) on Sulopenem Pharmacokinetics:
Results of in vitro solubility studies indicated that sulopenem etzadroxil is a Biopharmaceutical
Classification System Class IV drug (i.e., low permeability and low solubility) that does not
exhibit pH-dependent solubility within a pH range of 1.2 to 6.8. Based on this information,
111
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
coadministration of gastric pH modifiers would not be expected to impact sulopenem’s
exposure. However, per the Applicant, in vitro stability studies indicated that sulopenem
etzadroxil was unstable in simulated gastric fluid (containing pepsin) but stable in simulated
enzyme-free intestinal fluid. Therefore, gastric pH modifiers were predicted to decrease
sulopenem etzadroxil’s vulnerability to acid degradation and thus increase the bioavailability of
sulopenem. Given that the stability of sulopenem etzadroxil was evaluated in gastric fluid in the
presence of pepsin, it is unclear that its degradation was precipitated exclusively by low gastric
pH.
The Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study using pantoprazole, a PPI, and aluminum
hydroxide, an antacid, in Study A8811018. Administration of 40 mg pantoprazole for 3 days,
followed by coadministration with sulopenem etzadroxil on Day 4 under fasted conditions did
not significantly impact sulopenem exposure. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is necessary for
coadministration with a PPI.
Administration of a single dose of 600 mg aluminum hydroxide with sulopenem etzadroxil
under fasted conditions decreased AUC0-last and Cmax by less than 20%. According to the FDA
guidance on conducting DDI studies with gastric-acid reducing agents, PPIs present the worst
case scenario for pH-dependent DDIs due to their long-lasting effects on gastric pH. Thus, a
negative finding from a dedicated study with a PPI, as observed in this study, indicates a lack of
pH-dependent DDI. Therefore, no dosage adjustment is required for coadministration with an
antacid.
Effect of Sulopenem-Etzadroxil/Probenecid on Valproic Acid Pharmacokinetics:
Concomitant administration of carbapenem antibacterial drugs and valproic acid has been
associated with clinically significant reductions in serum valproic acid concentrations by an
unknown mechanism, resulting in a loss of seizure control. Because sulopenem (a thiopenem) is
structurally similar to carbapenems, the Applicant conducted a DDI study (Study IT001-104)
with valproic acid using the sulopenem-etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet, a standalone
sulopenem immediate release (IR) tablet and IV sulopenem. In this study, multiple dose
administration of 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with valproic acid decreased valproic acid AUC0tau and Cmaxss by approximately 25% and 19%, respectively. Similarly, coadministration of 1000
mg IV sulopenem with valproic acid also resulted in reductions of valproic acid plasma AUC0-tau
and Cmaxss of 33% and 28%, respectively. However, when administered concomitantly with
sulopenem etzadroxil and probenecid, less than 10% reductions in valproic acid plasma
exposures were observed. These results indicate that probenecid negates the reduction in
valproic acid plasma concentrations caused by sulopenem. These findings were corroborated in
the Applicant’s Phase 3 cUTI study, (Study IT001-302) in which one subject in the sulopenem
arm was receiving concomitant valproic acid treatment. Following the IV sulopenem treatment
phase of the study (i.e., Days 1-5), valproic acid plasma/serum levels decreased to 21000 ng/mL
(in serum) from a baseline of 54800 ng/mL (in plasma). However, following the switch to oral
step-down therapy with sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, valproic acid levels recovered to
50100 ng/mL (in plasma) and 50600 ng/mL (in serum) at the end of treatment visit.

{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
(b) (4)

the net effect of
coadministering sulopenem-etzadroxil/propenecid with valproic acid is a clinically insignificant

Does the clinical pharmacology information support the proposed breakpoint?
No, the clinical pharmacology information provided to support the proposed susceptibility
breakpoint is insufficient.
PK/PD index and target determination for sulopenem were conducted using a murine thigh
infection model. As with other β-lactams, the PK/PD driver of sulopenem’s efficacy was
expected to be %T > MIC. However, the Applicant’s dose fractionation studies failed to illustrate
definitively that T > MIC best correlates with sulopenem’s antibacterial activity. One study
report provided by the Applicant suggested AUC/MIC as the relevant efficacy determinant while
another indicated that it was T > MIC. All the same, the Applicant assumed T > MIC as the
relevant index for sulopenem. On this basis, the Applicant determined T > MIC target values (for
various microbiological endpoints) using the dataset generated from the dose fractionation
studies, which is unsupported by current practice (See Section 16.3).
A series of information requests were communicated to the Applicant to address
inconsistencies in the study reports, convey expectations for the conduct and analysis of
nonclinical PK/PD studies, and obtain any additional information available for review. Over the
course of these communications, the Applicant provided additional insight on their approach to
PK/PD index selection, revealing a flawed analysis which focused solely on select study results.
The Applicant also reanalyzed the existing nonclinical PK/PD dataset in a manner more
consistent with current convention. The data from the reanalysis was not definitive, but
suggested that sulopenem exhibits pathogen-dependent PK/PD properties. Specifically, data for
studies conducted with K. pneumoniae indicated that sulopenem exhibits concentrationdependent killing. This is illustrated in the 3 panels of Figure 2 for one strain of K. pneumoniae,
where change in bacterial density is plotted as a function of T > MIC, AUC/MIC, and Cmax/MIC,
respectively. Based on the magnitude of the coefficient of determination (r2), Cmax/MIC
appears to best correlate with reduction in bacterial burden, followed by AUC/MIC. Data for
E.coli suggested that AUC0-24h/MIC may be the relevant efficacy determinant against E. coli,
followed by Cmax/MIC. This interrelatedness of AUC/MIC and Cmax/MIC (which are both
concentration-dependent indices) in bacterial killing is not uncommon. On the other hand, for
some Gram-positive pathogens, sulopenem appeared to exhibit time-dependent killing.
Because the relevant PK/PD index for antibacterial drugs is typically pathogen independent, this
discordance may be reflective of the complexities of sulopenem’s PK/PD properties or point to
experimental errors.

of target attainment analyses are unreliable. Therefore, target attainment analyses cannot be

7.2. Review Strategy
The clinical and statistical reviewers evaluated sulopenem’s efficacy and safety for the
indication of uUTI based mainly on the data generated from Study 301. Supplementary safety
data were obtained from Studies 302 and 303 in cUTI and cIAI, respectively. In addition to
confirming the efficacy and safety analyses conducted by the Applicant, the clinical and
statistical reviewers also conducted analyses that more closely followed the original statistical
analysis plan.

8. Statistical and Clinical Evaluation
8.1. Review of Relevant Individual Trials Used To Support Efficacy
8.1.1. IT001-301 for Treatment of Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection
Trial Design
IT001-301 (also referred to as Study 301 in this review) was a Phase 3, multi-center, doubleblind, randomized trial designed to compare the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of oral
sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid with that of oral ciprofloxacin for the treatment of uUTI.
The primary objective of this study was to compare the overall response (clinical and
microbiological combined response) of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid versus oral
ciprofloxacin for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infection (uUTI) in adult women
at the primary timepoint of TOC at Day 12 (±1 day).
Eligible women with uUTI were randomized 1:1 to receive either:



A bilayer tablet with sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg/probenecid 500 mg twice daily for 5 days
and placebo ciprofloxacin capsules twice daily for 3 days or
Oral ciprofloxacin 250 mg capsules twice daily for 3 days and placebo sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid tablets twice daily for 5 days.

Randomization was conducted using a permuted block method with an Interactive Web
Randomization System.
This was a double-blind, double-dummy study. Over-encapsulated ciprofloxacin capsules were
used.
Study visits included screening, Days 1, 3, 5 (±1 day) end of treatment (EOT), Day 12 (±1 day)
TOC, and Day 28 (±2 days) final visit (FV).
Inclusion criteria were as follows:


Female patients ≥18 years of age with ≥24 hours and ≤96 hours of urinary symptoms
attributable to a urinary tract infection



The microbiological modified intent-to-treat (MMITT) population (discussed in further detail
below) was to only include patients with uUTIs caused by Enterobacterales and/or S.
saprophyticus (study uropathogens)

Patient-Determined Clinical Response
The patient was considered a clinical success at a given timepoint if the first three conditions in
the definition of overall response were met. All other patients not meeting the success criteria
were to be considered as failures unless data were unavailable to determine a success or
failure. In this case, an indeterminate response was assigned. Deaths due to reasons other than
the uUTI would also be considered as indeterminate responses.
Statistical Analysis Plan
Two independent primary analyses answering separate research questions in the ciprofloxacinsusceptible population and the ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible (resistant) population were
incorporated into the design and analysis of the study. In the ciprofloxacin-susceptible
population, sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid and ciprofloxacin were compared for noninferiority, while in the ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible population, sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid was assessed for superiority over ciprofloxacin. The study protocol was
reviewed under a special protocol assessment agreement.
Analysis Populations
The intent-to-treat (ITT) population comprised all randomized patients regardless of whether
the patients received study drug.
The modified ITT (MITT) population was to include all patients in the ITT population who
received at least a single dose of study medication and had the disease under study, defined as
having 2 of the 4 baseline uUTI symptoms and pyuria in the baseline urinalysis.
The microbiological modified intent-to-treat (MMITT) population included all MITT patients
with a positive study entry urine culture within 48 hours prior to first dose, defined as ≥105
colony forming units (CFU)/mL of a uropathogen (Enterobacteriaceae or Staphylococcus
saprophyticus only) and no more than 2 species of microorganisms with ≥105 CFU/ml.
The Susceptible MMITT (MMITTS) population included all MMITT patients with a baseline
uropathogen susceptible to the comparator drug, ciprofloxacin (ciprofloxacin MIC ≤1 mg/L),
and no baseline pathogen non-susceptible to ciprofloxacin.
The Resistant MMITT (MMITTR) population included all MMITT patients with a baseline
uropathogen non-susceptible (defined as MIC ≥2 mg/L) to the comparator drug, ciprofloxacin.
Interim Analysis
Two interim analyses for sample size re-estimation were planned when response data at TOC
were available for approximately 33% and 66% of the patients (approximately 450 and 900
123
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
patients, respectively). For the susceptible population, the sample size re-estimation was based
on the blinded overall outcome and evaluability rate (i.e., percentage of the ITT population in
the MMITT population).
In the resistant population, a conditional power analysis for the superiority hypothesis in the
MMITTR population was conducted when 66% of patients had been enrolled (unblinded interim
analysis). If the conditional power was <40% or ≥80%, no change to the sample size would be
made. If the conditional power was 40% to <80%, the sample size for MMITTR population
would be calculated based on the observed overall success rates in each treatment group and
increased to a maximum number. However, the maximum number was not specified. No
adjustment to the overall alpha level was needed. The sample size re-estimations were
conducted by an independent, unblinded statistician. A Data Monitoring Committee (DMC)
would make recommendations based on the analysis results.
Statistical and Clinical Reviewers’ Comment: The Applicant made changes to the planned
analysis after the unblinded interim analysis was conducted. This is discussed below under
protocol amendments.
Efficacy Analysis
The proportion of successes was defined using the following formula: number of
successes/(number of successes + number of failures + number of indeterminates).
For the superiority test in the MMITTR population, a two-sided 95% CI for the observed
treatment difference in success rates was determined using the Miettinen and Nurminen
method without stratification. If the lower bound of the 95% CI was greater than 0%, the null
hypothesis would be rejected and superiority of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid to
ciprofloxacin would be concluded. According to the post-hoc tables submitted on 4/27/2021,
the p-value was calculated using a Chi-squared test.
Statistical Reviewer’s Comment: The method for calculating a p-value was not provided in the
SAP, protocol, or study report. It appears that the Applicant reported p-values from a Chisquared test using a 3-category outcome (success/failure/indeterminate) for some of their
analyses. As the outcome is considered a binary outcome (success/combined failure and
indeterminate) for the primary analysis, we report p-values calculated using a Chi-squared test
with a 2-category outcome.
For the susceptible (MMITTS) population, a one-sided non-inferiority test was performed at the
2.5% level of significance using the same Miettinen and Nurminen method without
stratification with a -10% non-inferiority margin.
For the overall response, patients were defined as an indeterminate if any data needed to
determine whether a patient was a success or failure were missing, unless the available data
showed the patient to be a failure. In the analysis, these patients were considered as not having
a successful outcome.
124
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Secondary and additional efficacy analyses, including per patient microbiological response, per
pathogen microbiological response, investigator-determined clinical response, and patientdetermined clinical response were conducted using the same methods as in the primary
efficacy analyses.
Sample Size Calculation
Sample size calculations were conducted separately for the resistant population and susceptible
population. For the superiority test in the MMITTR population, 105 patients per arm would
provide 90% power given a two-sided alpha level of 0.05 and a 66% and 43% overall success
rate in the sulopenem and ciprofloxacin groups, respectively. For the non-inferiority test in the
MMITTS population, the sample size determination of 441 patients per arm was based on the
method of Farrington and Manning, assuming a non-inferiority margin of 10%, a power of 90%,
a one-sided alpha level of 0.025, and a 70% treatment success rate.
Assuming that 22% of the patients would have resistant pathogens and 83% of randomized
subjects would meet the criteria for the MMITT population, the sample size for this study was
1364 randomized subjects.
Protocol Amendments
There were 2 protocol amendments, dated 6/7/2018 and 1/6/2020. Amendment 1 occurred
prior to the start of the study. Amendment 2 occurred after the unblinded interim analysis and
replaced the statement “If the conditional power is <40%, the superiority hypothesis in the
MMITTR population will not be tested at the end of the study” with “If the conditional power is
<40%, no change to the sample size will be made.” This was to clarify that if the conditional
power at the interim analysis was <40%, the superiority hypothesis in the MMITTR population
would still be tested at the end of the study.
Statistical and Clinical Reviewers’ Comment: Of note, the results of the unblinded interim
analysis were presented to the DMC on 10/10/2019. Therefore, the Applicant already knew
that the conditional power was <40% when they submitted Amendment 2 on 1/6/2020
resulting in the change to conduct superiority hypothesis testing regardless of the conditional
power. This leads to concerns that the Applicant was changing the planned analysis based on
the results of the unblinded interim analysis.
The first version of the SAP was finalized on 9/30/2019 prior to the unblinded interim analysis.
The second version of the SAP was finalized on 3/11/2020, well after the unblinded interim
analysis was conducted. This version of the SAP affected the Analysis Population and
Microbiologic Response which impacted the primary endpoint of Overall Response. These
changes are discussed here.

125
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Use of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to Determine Whether Subjects Would be Assigned to
the Susceptible (MMITTS) or Nonsusceptible (MMITTR) Analysis Population
Iterum changed how discrepancies in antibacterial drug susceptibility between the
local/regional laboratory and central laboratory would be addressed. This change is notable as
the ciprofloxacin susceptibility status of the baseline pathogen defines whether a subject is in
the MMITTS or MMITTR population. In the revised SAP, Iterum used PCR to identify mutations
in the gyrA gene to adjudicate the ciprofloxacin susceptibility status. Although resistance to
ciprofloxacin may be mediated by mutations in the bacterial gyrA gene, there are other gene
mutations which are also associated with quinolone-resistant isolates (e.g., parC, parE) as well
as plasmid-mediated resistance genes which would be missed using the testing conducted by
the Applicant. In addition, bacterial mutations, if present, may not translate to functional
quinolone resistance. As a result, phenotypic susceptibility results are more reliable.
Statistical, Clinical, and Clinical Microbiology Reviewers’ Comment: The Division does not
agree with Iterum’s choice to use PCR to determine ciprofloxacin-susceptibility. Instead, the
Division maintains that the phenotypic results from the central laboratory should be used in
cases where there is a discrepancy between the local and central laboratory in the ciprofloxacinsusceptibility status. Subjects with a baseline ciprofloxacin nonsusceptible isolate from either a
central lab culture or from a central lab confirmatory identification should be included in the
MMITTR population.
Change in the Definition of Microbiological Response
In the Applicant’s revised SAP, the definition of microbiological response, which is a component
of the primary endpoint (overall response), was revised to determine if the isolate on the
follow-up culture matched the baseline organism (Table 71). The Applicant added a footnote
(delineated in red print below) to the following table defining microbiological response:

126

Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}

determined “regardless of susceptibility” and the added footnote does not impact the definition
of eradication. This could be interpretated as only changing a subject from persistence to
indeterminate.
8.1.2. Study Results
Compliance With Good Clinical Practices
This study was conducted in compliance with Good Clinical Practice guidances.
Financial Disclosure
The Applicant certified that none of the investigators for Trial 301 had any disclosable financial
interests or arrangements with the Applicant.
Patient Disposition
The trial was conducted between August 23, 2018 and January 20, 2020. A total of 1802
subjects from 114 study sites from three countries (USA, Ukraine, and Russia) were screened
for enrollment. A total of 131 subjects failed screening. The most common reason for screening
failure, occurring in 66 subjects, was failure to meet urine dipstick requirements as per inclusion
criterion #3.
A total of 1671 patients from 108 study sites were randomized (835 to sulopenem, 836 to
ciprofloxacin). Two sites that included 81 patients from the US (48 in the sulopenem group and
33 in the ciprofloxacin group) were excluded from the Applicant’s ITT population for the
efficacy analyses (Site 202: 68 patients; Site 218: 13 patients) because the Applicant considered
the data unreliable (i.e., the Applicant claimed that there were questionable microbiological
results by pulse-field gel electrophoresis and concerns about PK data). These exclusions are
discussed below.
The remaining 1590 patients included 787 in the sulopenem group and 803 in the ciprofloxacin
group. Approximately 97% of these patients completed study drug treatment, while 3%
discontinued treatment prematurely. The primary reasons for discontinuation of treatment
were adverse events and “patient request.” The Applicant’s disposition of patients is reported
in Table 72. Note that the only exclusions from the MITT population, other than the exclusion of
patients from Sites 218 and 202 by the Applicant, were due to not receiving treatment.
Approximately 18% of the patients were included in the MMITTR population and approximately
50% of patients were in the MMITTS population.

Statistical, Clinical and Clinical Microbiology Reviewers’ Comment: We do not agree with
Iterum’s decision to exclude Site 202 from the efficacy analysis. Regarding the clusters of
subjects with related pathogens, these clonal relationships may exist in UTIs in the community.
In addition, most patients were not in one of these four clusters. Regarding the artificial
intelligence drug compliance software, the FDA inspector found evidence that the software
results were likely not interpreted correctly. Some of the subjects initially may have spit out the
dose during recording because of difficulty swallowing the pills or difficulty with the phone app.
However, many of these subjects confirmed that they were able to eventually take the
scheduled dose which was well-documented in the source records. Regarding the finding of
some subjects with no measurable drug level, it is important to note that this was a minority of
subjects. The late decision to exclude this site is also questionable especially since it was after
the unblinded interim analysis. Overall, the Division did not find sufficient reason to exclude Site
202.
The Applicant provided additional analyses using the original SAP and included Site 202
following a request by the FDA on 4/27/2021 (SN#0037). Table 73 shows the analysis
populations using the original SAP and including Site 202 but excluding Site 218. More subjects
were included in the resistant and susceptible groups based on the original SAP as compared
with using the revised SAP.

Protocol Violations/Deviations
Major protocol deviations were related to inclusion/exclusion criteria (N=8) and study
medication (N=1; dosed incorrectly for all 10 doses, resulting in taking ciprofloxacin once a day
instead of twice a day). Major protocol deviations were reported for three subjects in the
sulopenem group and six subjects in the ciprofloxacin group (including the 1 subject taking
ciprofloxacin once a day, instead of twice a day) in the MMITT population. In the MMITTR
population, only 2 major deviations were reported (related with inclusion/exclusion criteria in
the ciprofloxacin group).

Table 78 shows the Applicant’s results as reported in their initial study report, as well as the
updated results from the Applicant using the original definition of microbiological response to
determine overall response and the original definition of the MMITTR population. The major
difference between these two analyses are that subjects with urine cultures that grew >103
CFU/mL of the baseline uropathogen were considered as having an overall nonresponse in the
second analysis (using the original SAP), regardless of susceptibility and the determination of
whether the baseline and post-baseline organism were the same by whole genome sequencing.
Note that the overall response rate for sulopenem decreased by an absolute difference of
11.3%. The treatment difference is smaller in the second analysis (using the original SAP) as the

Data Quality and Integrity
We have found no potential issues concerning the submitted data quality that raise questions
about the efficacy results. Anomalies were found with Site 218, as discussed above and below
(see Sections 4.1 and 8.3 for additional details). However, the Division identified several issues
with the Applicant’s analysis of Study 301 which occurred after an unblinded interim analysis
which call into question the reliability of the results and include the following: (1) revision to
the SAP that changed the definition of the microbiological response and overall response
endpoint for Study 301, (2) revision to the SAP to include use of PCR to define the patient
susceptibility populations, (3) the late exclusion of clinical study Site 202 and (4) Iterum’s
revision to the analysis plan to allow for superiority testing in the MMITTR population after they
were notified by the DMC that the conditional power was <40% at the unblinded interim
analysis which, based on the original pre-specified plan, would not have resulted in testing for
superiority in the MMITTR population. The Division acknowledges that there may be additional
issues with the conduct of these 3 studies that we have not yet identified given the prior
questionable changes to the SAP and exclusion of Site 202 after the unblinded interim analysis
of Study 301.

Additional Analyses Conducted on the Individual Trial
Interim Analyses
As noted earlier in this review, two interim analyses for sample size re-estimation were planned
to be conducted in Study 301 when response data at TOC were available for approximately 33%
and 66% of the patients (approximately 450 and 900 patients, respectively). Blinded sample size
re-estimations for the MMITTS non-inferiority assessment were to be conducted at both
interim analyses and an unblinded sample size re-estimation using conditional power for the
MMITTR superiority assessment was to be conducted at the second interim analysis. However,
the interim analyses were delayed such that the two interim analyses were conducted at the
same time.
The results from the interim analyses for the MMITTS population and unblinded analysis for the
conditional power assessment of the MMITTR population were presented to the DMC on
October 10, 2019. The non-inferiority sample size re-estimation for the MMITTS population at
the second interim analysis resulted in a recommendation to add up to 828 patients to the
study. The Applicant chose to increase the sample by as many as 400 subjects.
138
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
The conditional power from the unblinded interim analysis for the resistant population was less
than 40%. Because of this low conditional power, the sample size was not changed for the
resistant population. As noted above, based on the SAP in place at the time of the interim
analysis, the final analysis of the MMITTR population was not to be conducted if the conditional
power was <40%. However, this text was removed from the SAP after the interim analysis. Note
that though it does not appear that this requirement is needed to control the Type I error,
there is concern that the SAP was changed based on the results of the unblinded interim
analysis.
The original unblinded interim analysis results when approximately 66% of the subjects were
enrolled showed only a minimal effect of sulopenem over ciprofloxacin for overall response
(see Table 84). The Applicant was notified by the DMC that: “The conditional power with the
revised sample size for MMITTR is below 40%. So there isn’t a need for any sample size
calculation for the superiority test.”1 After being notified of this finding, the Applicant changed
the microbiological response definition. To demonstrate the large impact this change had on
the study results, the second analysis in this table reports the results using this altered endpoint
on the same subjects who were included in the interim analysis. The sulopenem response rate
increased 20.7% while the ciprofloxacin response rate increased by 3.1%, and the difference
between the sulopenem and ciprofloxacin response rates changed from 8.3% to 25.9%.
Additional changes to the analyses were made after the interim analysis, including the change
to the MMITTR definition and the exclusion of Site 202 from the analysis. The third row
considers these changes on the group of subjects from Study 301 available at the interim
analysis. These changes in the revised SAP increased the difference in the response rates
between sulopenem and ciprofloxacin to 31.4%. As stated above, we did not agree with the
Applicant’s interpretation of the changes to the SAP and exclusion of Site 202 after the
outcome of the interim analysis was known by the Applicant.

8.1.3. Assessment of Efficacy Across Trials
Along with the results from the uUTI resistant and susceptible populations, the Applicant
conducted two additional Phase 3 trials, one in complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI) and
one in complicated intra-abdominal infection (cIAI). The results of these studies are discussed
here.
Study 302-cUTI
Study 302 was a Phase 3, multi-center, double-blind, randomized trial designed to compare the
efficacy, tolerability, and safety of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem with that of IV
ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin/clavulanate for the treatment of cUTI.
Subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive either IV sulopenem 1000 mg once daily for at least 5
days (5 doses) followed by sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg co-administrated with oral probenecid
500 mg twice daily to complete 7-10 total days of treatment or ertapenem IV 1000 mg once
daily for at least 5 days (5 doses) followed by oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg or amoxicillinclavulanate 875 mg twice daily to complete 7-10 total days of therapy. Duration of treatment
could be extended up to a total duration of 14 days for patients with bacteremia at baseline.
The primary efficacy endpoint was overall response (resolution of symptoms and clearance of
the baseline uropathogen) at Day 21 (TOC). The primary analysis population was the
microbiological modified Intent-to-Treat population (MMITT), defined as subjects who received
at least a single dose of study medication, had the disease under study (having 2 of the 5
baseline cUTI symptoms), and had a positive study entry urine culture within 48 hours prior to
the first dose and no more than 2 species of microorganisms identified in the study entry urine
culture with ≥105 CFU/mL, except in the situation where 1 of the organisms cultured from the
urine was also isolated from blood cultures drawn at baseline. A positive urine culture was
defined as ≥105 CFU/mL of a uropathogen (Enterobacterales only, susceptible to sulopenem
[MIC ≤1] and ertapenem [MIC ≤0.5]). Patients with a study pathogen isolated from baseline
blood cultures were included in the MMITT population regardless of the patient’s baseline
urine culture result.
As in Study 301, the Applicant’s efficacy results were based on definitions of microbiological
responses using the same footnote for “Persistence” (See the section of “Protocol
Amendments” in Study 301). We requested the reanalysis of the data based on the definitions
without using PCR data. The results from the two analyses from the initial report and from the
updated report were consistent.
The two treatment groups were comparable with respect to demographic characteristics. The
majority of subjects were females (about 55%). The mean age was about 59 years (range: 18 to
94 years). The majority of subjects had acute pyelonephritis (57.1% sulopenem; 56.9%
ertapenem); E. coli was the most common organism isolated (76.1% on sulopenem; 78.6% on
ertapenem).

142
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
As noted in Table 88, this study failed to show noninferiority using a 10% NI margin. Sulopenem
was significantly worse than the active comparator, ertapenem.

Study 303-cIAI
Study 303 was a Phase 3, multi-center, double-blind, randomized trial designed to compare the
efficacy, tolerability, and safety of IV sulopenem followed by oral sulopenem with that of IV
ertapenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole or amoxicillin/clavulanate for the
treatment of cIAI.
A total of 674 subjects were randomized (1:1) to receive either IV sulopenem 1000 mg once
daily for at least 5 days (5 doses) followed by sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg coadministered
with oral probenecid 500 mg twice daily to complete 7-10 total days of treatment or ertapenem
IV 1000 mg once daily for at least 5 days (5 doses) followed by oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg and
metronidazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily to complete 7-10 total days of
therapy. Duration of treatment could be extended up to a total duration of 14 days for patients
with bacteremia at baseline. The primary efficacy endpoint was clinical response at the TOC
visit (Day 28).
The two treatment groups were comparable with respect to demographic characteristics. The
majority of subjects were male (about 53.5%). The mean age was about 54 years (range: 18 to
90 years). The number of subjects with cIAI caused by appendicitis with perforation or
periappendiceal abscess was similar (47.5%); E. coli was the most common organism isolated
(75.9% on sulopenem; 77.4% on ertapenem).
The primary efficacy endpoint was clinical response at the TOC visit. The analysis population
was the MMITT population (MMITT), which included all randomized patients who received at
least a single dose of study medication, had the disease under study, had at least 1 Gramnegative study pathogen (aerobic or anaerobic organisms) identified at study entry within 48
hours prior to the first dose of study drug and up to 24 hours after the first dose, regardless of
isolate susceptibility and regardless of other organisms identified in the culture.
The results are shown in Table 89. After initial unblinding of the study, imbalances in outcome
by treatment were identified by the Applicant, such as lower efficacy with sulopenem
compared to the active comparator in subjects with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, more failures
due to surgical interventions in the sulopenem arm, lower success rates in subjects receiving
only IV sulopenem compared to only receiving IV ertapenem. Therefore, the Applicant
conducted a post-hoc analysis by re-examining and re-analyzing the data. We do not agree with
143
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
the Applicant’s post-hoc analysis after the study data were unblinded. This study failed to show
noninferiority using a 10% margin, either based on the primary analysis or the post-hoc
analysis.

8.1.4. Integrated Assessment of Effectiveness
Study 301 demonstrated that in patients with ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible uUTI, sulopenem
was superior to ciprofloxacin in overall response (combined microbiological response and
clinical response) at the TOC visit with a difference of 15.3% (95% CI: 4.3%, 25.8%) and a p-value
of 0.0062, according to the original statistical analysis plan and including data from clinical Site
202.
Of note, sulopenem failed to demonstrate noninferiority to ciprofloxacin in the ciprofloxacinsusceptible population of this trial. As the cUTI (Study 302) and cIAI (Study 303) trials did not
meet the pre-specified noninferiority margins, there is a lack of other evidence of efficacy to
support the single successful trial in uUTI. In fact, sulopenem was statistically inferior to the
comparator in the ciprofloxacin-susceptible population of Study 301 and in the cUTI Study 302.
Additionally, the Division identified several issues with the Applicant’s analysis of Study 301
which occurred after an unblinded interim analysis which call into question the reliability of the
results and include the following: (1) revision to the SAP that changed the definition of the
microbiological response and overall response endpoint for Study 301, (2) revision to the SAP to
include use of PCR to define the patient susceptibility populations, (3) the late exclusion of
clinical study Site 202 and (4) Iterum’s revision to the analysis plan to allow for superiority
testing in the MMITTR population after they were notified by the DMC that the conditional
power was <40% at the unblinded interim analysis which, based on the original pre-specified
analysis plan, would not have resulted in testing for superiority in the MMITTR population. The
Division acknowledges that there may be additional issues with the conduct of these 3 studies
that we have not yet identified given the prior questionable changes to the SAP and exclusion
of Site 202 after the unblinded interim analysis of Study 301.

8.2. Review of Safety
8.2.1. Safety Review Approach
The primary safety analysis was conducted on the data derived from the Phase 3 uUTI Study
301 as this is the indication sought by the Applicant in this NDA. Additional analyses were
144
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
conducted on the combined Phase 3 study population which includes safety data from Studies
301, 302 (cUTI), and 303 (cIAI). The Phase 1 studies conducted by the Applicant and Pfizer as
well as the Phase 2 studies conducted by Pfizer did not provide significant additional safety
data; data from these studies are summarized at the end of Section 8.2.4.
8.2.2. Review of the Safety Database
Overall Exposure
The safety database for sulopenem (Table 90) includes 825 subjects who received sulopenem
for the treatment of uUTI and an additional 1030 subjects in controlled Phase 3 studies who
received sulopenem for other indications. In Study 301, subjects were randomized to receive
oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid for 5 days or oral ciprofloxacin for 3 days which matched
the actual median duration of treatment in each arm. In Study 302, the median total duration
of treatment (IV and oral) was 10 days in each arm of which the median duration of oral
treatment was 4 days. In Study 303, the median total duration of treatment (IV and oral) was 9

Adequacy of the safety database:
The safety database is acceptable. There were over 800 patients exposed to sulopenem for the
treatment of uUTI in Study 301 who received the indicated dose and duration. The subjects in
Studies 302 and 303 provide additional safety information.
8.2.3. Adequacy of Applicant’s Clinical Safety Assessments
Issues Regarding Data Integrity and Submission Quality
The Applicant’s safety database includes subjects from Study 301 who were enrolled at Sites
202 (68 subjects) and 218 (13 subjects). These two sites were closed by the Applicant because
(b) (7)(A)
of concerns of misconduct.
The Applicant excluded subjects from
both sites from the efficacy database but included them in the safety database. In addition, the
incidence of TEAEs reported from sites in Ukraine was much lower compared to sites in the
United States and Russia (Section 8.2.7).
M.O. Comment: The Applicant’s rationale for excluding Site 202 from the efficacy analysis was
that there were four clusters of patients with closely related isolates by PFGE and there was
concern for intentional medication nonadherence based on artificial intelligence compliance
software and no measurable drug levels in several of the subjects with available PK data. We did
not agree that these issues justified removing all subjects from Site 202 from the efficacy
analyses and decided to include these subjects in our analyses. Of note, the adverse event
profile among subjects from Site 202 did not differ from the overall study population. Regarding
Site 218, there were no TEAEs reported from this site, but as there were only 13 subjects
enrolled at this site, the impact on the safety findings is limited. However, these 13 subjects
from Site 218 were removed from the Agency’s safety database. The lower rate of TEAEs from
Ukraine is likely a result of differing patient attitudes and investigator reporting behaviors.

Categorization of Adverse Events
AEs were accurately classified as treatment-emergent if they occurred at or after the first dose
of study drug. The Applicant used the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities, version 21.0
for all Phase 3 studies. Coding of verbatim terms to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory
Activities preferred terms was generally acceptable.
Routine Clinical Tests
In Study 301, complete blood count with differential and serum chemistries, including liver
enzymes, were checked at baseline and at TOC (Day 12). Urinalysis and urine culture were
obtained at baseline, Day 3, EOT (Day 5), TOC, and Day 28. Vital signs were checked at baseline,
EOT, and TOC.
M.O. Comment: The routine clinical tests were acceptable.

M.O. Comment: Review of these subjects’ narratives revealed the following:


Given the short duration of treatment, the deaths related to cancer are not related to the
study drug.



Subject IT001-303/
was a 76-year-old woman with a history of left bundle branch
block and ischemic heart disease who was treated with IV and PO sulopenem following
surgery for cholecystitis and intraabdominal abscess. On Day 11, she was found pulseless.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was unsuccessful, and she died. This death is unlikely to be
related to the study drug given the patient’s age and history of heart disease.



Subject IT001-303/
was an 88-year-old woman who was treated with IV
sulopenem following surgery for gangrenous appendicitis with peritonitis. On Day 3, she
developed hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and cerebral failure and was started
on mechanical ventilation. She died on Day 5. The autopsy showed hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy. The direct cause of death was reported as cardiovascular failure. This
death is unlikely to be related to the study drug as the patient had preexisting cardiac
disease based on the hypertrophic myocardium found at autopsy.



Subject IT001-303/
was a 77-year-old woman with a history of cardiovascular
disease and diabetes mellitus who was treated with IV sulopenem following surgery for
complicated cholecystitis. On Day 4, the subject experienced a sudden loss of consciousness
with hypotension and was diagnosed with a stroke (CVA). She quickly worsened and died the
same day. The autopsy showed ischemic stroke. This death is unlikely to be related to the
study drug given the prior risk factors of cardiovascular disease and diabetes mellitus.



Subject IT001-303/
was a 74-year-old woman with a history of hypertension who
was treated with IV and PO sulopenem following surgery for gastric ulcer perforation and
peritonitis. She completed her course of sulopenem on Day 11 and was deemed a clinical
success at EOT and at Day 21. She died at home on Day 28 and no further information was
available. The cause of death is unknown, but could have been due to cardiac arrest, stroke,
or pulmonary embolism. This death is unlikely to be related to the study drug as it occurred
several days after the last dose.



Subject IT001-303/
was a 64-year-old man with history of hypertension who was
treated with IV ertapenem following surgery for gangrenous cholecystitis with perforation,
local peritonitis, and subhepatic abscesses. On Day 3, he developed acute respiratory
dysfunction and heart failure and died the next day. No autopsy was performed. This death

in the study are less likely to be related to the study drug. After review of the subject narratives,
the following SAEs are notable:


Angioedema: Subject
was a 54-year-old woman who developed swelling of the
face 20 minutes after taking the first dose of sulopenem. Dyspnea started 10 minutes later.

The subject did not seek medical attention, but instead went to a pharmacy and took an

within 3 hours. It appears likely that the SAE of angioedema was related to the sulopenem.

Pyelonephritis and urosepsis: Subject
was a 46-year-old woman who was treated
with sulopenem x 5 days for a P. mirabilis uUTI. At the TOC visit (Day 12) she had no uUTI
symptoms and the urine culture was negative. However, on Day 17 she presented with fever,
flank pain, and dysuria. She was found to have an obstructing kidney stone with
hydronephrosis and acute kidney injury. A repeat urine culture grew P. mirabilis. She was
treated with non-study antibacterial drugs and percutaneous nephrostomy. At the Day 28
visit she had no further symptoms. The kidney stone was the likely cause for the recurrent
infection; the study drug was unlikely to be related.



Diarrhea and pneumonia: Subject
was an 81-year-old woman who was treated
with ciprofloxacin x 5 days for uUTI. On Day 9 she presented with altered mental status and
cough; she was diagnosed with a pneumonia and was hospitalized. She was treated with
non-study antibacterial drugs (cefepime, vancomycin, azithromycin, and cefdinir). The
pneumonia was considered resolved by Day 13. She developed diarrhea on Day 14 and was
hospitalized on Day 16 with volume loss and pre-renal acute kidney injury likely secondary to
the diarrhea. The diarrhea and acute kidney injury later resolved. The pneumonia was
unlikely to be related to the study drug. It is possible the antibacterial drugs for the
pneumonia as well as the ciprofloxacin for the uUTI led to the diarrhea.

M.O. Comment: Regarding subjects who experienced an SAE in the integrated Phase 3 safety
population:


The imbalance between the treatment arms is mostly accounted for by the imbalance in the
SOC of infections and infestations (Table 96). Within this SOC, the PTs of abdominal abscess
and urinary tract infections account for much of the imbalance.



Review of the narratives for abdominal abscess, appendiceal abscess, and liver abscess (all
from Study 303 in cIAI) revealed that most occurred after treatment was completed.



Review of the narratives for urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, and cystitis (almost all
from Study 302 in cUTI) revealed that all occurred after treatment was completed.



Regarding these SAEs due to infections, these events are not directly attributable to the
study drug, but likely rather reflect either treatment failure or a complication of the primary
infection. However, it is difficult to make that determination with the available data.

Vital Signs
Review of the vital sign data from Studies 301, 302, and 303 did not reveal any significant
differences between the treatment arms.
Electrocardiograms
Electrocardiograms were not collected in Studies 301, 302, or 303 as there was adequate data
regarding sulopenem and cardiac conduction from the Phase 1 program. See the QT subsection
below for further information.
QT
On 06 Sept 2017, FDA notified Iterum that data from the Phase 1 Study A7371007 were
adequate to serve as a substitute for a thorough QT study and therefore Iterum did not need to
conduct a dedicated thorough QT study. The following is a summary of the QT Interdisciplinary
Review Team review from 2017.
Study A7371007 was a randomized, investigator- and subject-blinded, sponsor-unblinded,
placebo-substitution, sequential cohort, crossover design, single escalating dose study of IV
sulopenem. A total of 26 healthy subjects were randomized to treatment in 2 cohorts. Each
164
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
cohort had 3 crossover periods and consisted of 12 subjects each. Each subject received a single
IV dose of either placebo or sulopenem (400 mg, 800 mg, 1600 mg, 2400 mg, and 2800 mg IV
infusion over 1 h) in each dosing period. The 2800 mg IV infusion over 1 hour resulted in a mean
Cmax of 109.7 µg/mL and a ΔΔQTcF of 0.07 ms with 90% CI of -4.20 to 4.34 ms. The QT
Interdisciplinary Review Team concluded sulopenem does not prolong the QTc interval. Of
note, the Cmax for the oral 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil and 500 mg probenecid tablet is in the
range of 1.6-1.9 µg/mL which much lower than the 2800 mg IV dose which did not prolong the
QT interval.
Analysis of the heart rate, PR interval, and QRS interval data from Study A7371007 did not
reveal any notable findings.
Immunogenicity
Not applicable for this NDA.
Summary of Phase 1/2 Clinical Studies
The Applicant and Pfizer conducted 24 Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies of sulopenem with both IV
and oral formulations that exposed a total of 2006 subjects to sulopenem (Table 90). Review of
the Phase 1 studies revealed the following safety signals: diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain,
headache, dizziness, rash, and abnormal urine odor. One subject receiving oral
sulopenem/probenecid experienced mild angioedema of the face and lip and discontinued
study drug. All these safety signals were also identified in the Phase 3 program. In the Pfizerconducted Phase 2 studies, there were 4 subjects with fatal SAEs; 3 received sulopenem and 1
received comparator. Review of the narratives for these subjects revealed that 2 of the 3
deaths among the sulopenem-treated subjects were related to underlying malignancy. The
other death in the sulopenem arm was related to a myocardial infarction and pneumonia which
were unlikely to be related to the study drug.
M.O. Comment: The Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies do not reveal additional safety signals related
to sulopenem.
8.2.5. Analysis of Submission-Specific Safety Issues
No specific safety issues were identified prior to review of this NDA. However, as diarrhea was
noted to be a common TEAE for which there was a notable imbalance between the treatment
arms, further analyses of diarrhea events were conducted and are summarized in this
subsection. In addition, a discussion of liver enzyme elevations is provided above in the
subsection labeled “Laboratory Findings.”

arm and 21 (2.6%) in the ciprofloxacin arm in Study 301. The severity of the diarrhea events is

M.O. Comment: The average duration of diarrhea was longer by about one day in sulopenem

diarrhea longer than 5 days; all but 2 were in the sulopenem arm. Subjects who took the study

doses with food. The review team will consider whether the labeling should recommend taking
the drug with food to reduce the duration of diarrhea. In summary, diarrhea is a common, but
not serious, safety finding for oral sulopenem.

M.O. Comment: The incidence of TEAEs in the overall population was 24.8% in the sulopenem
arm and 13.9% in the ciprofloxacin arm while the incidence of diarrhea was 12.4% in the
sulopenem arm and 2.5% in the ciprofloxacin arm. Subjects with Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, those
with BMI >30, and those in the United States were more likely to have a TEAE compared to the
overall population. Among these groups, the difference in the incidence of TEAEs between the
arms was mostly accounted for by diarrhea as it was in the general population. Review of the
demographic data shows that most subjects with Hispanic/Latino ethnicity and BMI >30 were
enrolled in the United States. The higher rates of TEAEs and diarrhea in these subjects may be
due to different physiological responses based on ethnicity or obesity or could be related to
differences in AE reporting by country/site. An example of likely reporting differences is that the
rate of TEAEs in Ukraine was notably lower than in Russia or the United States and there were
no TEAEs of diarrhea reported from Ukraine.
8.2.8. Specific Safety Studies/Clinical Trials
There were no dedicated safety studies for this NDA.
8.2.9. Additional Safety Explorations
Human Carcinogenicity or Tumor Development
In the Phase 3 integrated safety population, there were 5 subjects with a TEAE in the neoplasms
SOC, 4 in the sulopenem arm and 1 in the comparator arm. These cases were discussed in the
deaths and significant adverse events subsections above. Review of these subjects found that
most cases were related to preexisting cancer.
168
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
M.O. Comment: Given the short duration of treatment, it does not appear that any of the cases
of cancer were related to the study drug. Overall, there is no clinical evidence that sulopenem is
carcinogenic.
Human Reproduction and Pregnancy
Pregnant women were excluded from all clinical studies of sulopenem. However, there was one
pregnancy reported in a patient who received sulopenem in the integrated Phase 3 safety
population. The subject had a negative local urine pregnancy test at screening, but the central
laboratory test was reported positive 3 days later. The study drug (oral sulopenem/probenecid
for uUTI) was stopped at that time. The subject had an uneventful pregnancy and delivered a
healthy infant 8 months later.
M.O. Comment: There are insufficient data to draw any conclusions regarding the effects of
sulopenem on human reproduction and pregnancy.
Pediatrics and Assessment of Effects on Growth
There are no data on the safety of sulopenem in pediatric patients less than 18 years of age.
The Sponsor submitted an agreed initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) on 21 February 2018. The
label for probenecid includes a contraindication for children under the age of 2 years. After
consultation with the pediatric team in the Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health, no
apparent scientific basis for this pediatric contraindication was found. As a result, no pediatric
contraindication will be added to the sulopenem/probenecid label.
Overdose, Drug Abuse Potential, Withdrawal, and Rebound
Sulopenem does not have known drug abuse potential.
8.2.10. Safety in the Postmarket Setting
Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
Sulopenem is not approved for use in any country.
Expectations on Safety in the Postmarket Setting
If approved, the oral tablet formulation of sulopenem may be used off-label to treat uUTI
caused by quinolone-susceptible pathogens and for stepdown therapy for other infections such
as cUTI and cIAI. There are no distinct safety concerns regarding this possible off-label use, but
the Phase 3 studies for cUTI and cIAI did not meet their primary efficacy endpoints.
8.2.11. Integrated Assessment of Safety
The safety data for sulopenem in the treatment of uUTI were derived from Study 301 which
evaluated 5 days of oral sulopenem compared to 3 days of oral ciprofloxacin. The subjects in
169
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Study 301 were all adult women. Additional safety data were reviewed from Study 302 in cUTI
and Study 303 in cIAI which included use of both the IV and oral formulations of sulopenem.
The Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies confirmed the safety findings of the Phase 3 studies. The
collective safety issues identified from these sources will be summarized in this section.
Two subjects taking oral sulopenem/probenecid experienced angioedema involving the face
and one also had associated dyspnea. One subject was enrolled in Study 301 and another in
one of the Phase 1 studies. Both subjects stopped the study drug due to the angioedema
events. Both subjects took antihistamine drugs and neither experienced any sequelae from
these events. Regardless, angioedema associated with dyspnea suggests involvement of the
airway which could be life-threatening. Hypersensitivity is included as a warning in the
proposed labeling.
Gastrointestinal adverse events, including diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain, were common
among subjects taking oral sulopenem/probenecid. In Study 301, 17% of sulopenem subjects
experienced a GI adverse event compared to 8% of ciprofloxacin subjects. In particular,
diarrhea was a prominent adverse event associated with sulopenem with 12% experiencing at
least one event of diarrhea. However, the diarrhea and other GI adverse events were generally
mild and not treatment-limiting. The duration of diarrhea appeared to be reduced when
sulopenem was taken with food. GI adverse events and diarrhea will be noted in section 6 of
the labeling and the review team will consider recommending that sulopenem be taken with
food to reduce the incidence and/or duration of diarrhea.
Elevations in ALT were more common among sulopenem subjects compared to ciprofloxacin
subjects in Study 301. This was also noted in the integrated Phase 3 population which included
Studies 302 and 303. In Study 301, the elevations in ALT were generally less than 5x the upper
limit of normal. There were no cases of Hy’s Law in Study 301. However, there was a subject in
Study 302 who met Hy’s Law criteria on Day 5, but subsequently had normal liver enzyme tests.
The Sponsor reports the cause of the liver test elevations was a drug-drug interaction between
(b) (4)
valproic acid and sulopenem.
. Elevated transaminases will be noted in section 6 of the
labeling.
Other nonserious adverse events that occurred uncommonly, but more frequently among
sulopenem subjects compared to the comparator subjects include dizziness, rash, abnormal
urine odor, and vulvovaginal yeast infection. All these adverse reactions will be included in
section 6 of the labeling.
Overall, the safety issues with oral sulopenem/probenecid do not preclude approval; the known
risks of sulopenem can be managed by appropriate labeling.

8.3. Statistical Issues
One Phase 3 study is included in this NDA for the indication of treatment of uUTI. We have
identified the following statistical issues related to this study.
170
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Late Change of SAP
After the unblinded interim analysis in October 2019, the conditional power was noted to be
less than 40% in the MMITTR (ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible) population. On March 11, 2020,
the SAP was changed to revise the definitions of the MMITT populations and microbiological
response based on PCR and antibacterial susceptibility data. The Division did not agree with
these changes. Instead, the Division analyzed efficacy based on the original SAP. Although the
study results remained significant, they were not as significant as initially reported.
Late Decision of Removing Study Site 202
Sites 202 and 218 were removed from the efficacy analyses by the Applicant. Site 202 was
removed due to unreliable laboratory results. Site 218 was removed due to the concern of
study misconduct. For Site 218, the Division agreed with the removal. However, for Site 202,
the Division did not find sufficient justifications for its removal. Therefore, Site 202 was
included in the Division’s efficacy analysis.
As noted, these changes were made after the unblinded interim analysis for the resistant
population and led to a larger treatment effect with a more significant p-value as compared to
the Division’s analysis using the original SAP.

8.4. Conclusions and Recommendations
This NDA contains one Phase 3 clinical trial in uUTI (Study 301) for the proposed indication. The
Applicant also submitted the data from one Phase 3 study in cUTI (Study 302) and one Phase 3
study in cIAI (Study 303) as supportive information. The Division has the following conclusions:
When using the original, agreed-upon SAP and including Site 202 we found there was a lower
level of statistical significance for the difference in overall response rate by treatment arm in
the ciprofloxacin-resistant (MMITTR) population than was initially reported (p>0.001 vs.
p<0.00001) in Study 301.
Regarding the lack of other evidence of efficacy, we note that in Study 301, significantly inferior
results were observed in the overall response rate for sulopenem compared to ciprofloxacin in
the ciprofloxacin susceptible (MMITTS) population. In addition, significantly inferior results for
sulopenem were observed in the complicated urinary tract infections trial (Study 302) and there
was a lack of noninferiority of sulopenem in the complicated intra-abdominal infections trial
(Study 303).
From a safety perspective, there is an adequate safety database for oral
sulopenem/probenecid. Identified safety issues include hypersensitivity reactions, elevated
liver enzymes, and GI adverse reactions. Overall, the safety issues with oral
sulopenem/probenecid do not preclude approval; the known risks of sulopenem can be
managed by appropriate labeling.

171
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
The Division recommends that the NDA receive a Complete Response given the lack of
substantial evidence of effectiveness and that the Applicant consider the following future steps:
1. Re-evaluate the proposed dose/dosing regimen given the issues associated with PKPD/target attainment.
2. Conduct a second Phase 3 uUTI study to provide additional evidence of effectiveness.
3. Use a more relevant comparator given the current standard of care, such as nitrofurantoin.

9. Advisory Committee Meeting and Other External Consultations
No advisory committee meeting was held, and no external consultations were obtained as
there were no issues that needed input from external experts.

Human PK Studies in Healthy Volunteers
Single Ascending Dose
Study A8811001 was a single ascending dose study to characterize the PK, safety, and
tolerability of two sulopenem oral prodrugs, PF-03678685 and PF-03709270 (i.e., sulopenem
etzadroxil) in healthy adult volunteers. Eighteen male subjects aged 21 to 52 years with a mean
body mass index (BMI) of 24.0 kg/m2 were enrolled and randomized to 2 cohorts to receive one
of the two sulopenem oral prodrugs or placebo according to the schematic in Table 118.

All doses were administered following an 8 h fast; subjects were required to refrain from eating
or drinking anything except water for another 4 h post-dosing. Sulopenem prodrugs were
administered as oral powders (supplied as 100 mg, 300 mg, and 500 mg dose strengths) for
reconstitution. Dose escalations within each cohort were based upon available preliminary
safety, tolerability, and PK from previous dosing periods. Whole blood and plasma PK samples
were collected pre-dose and at pre-specified times post-dose for measurement of sulopenem,
sulopenem prodrugs and formate (a by-product of prodrug hydrolysis) using validated liquid
chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) methods. Pharmacokinetic
assessments included: Cmax, Tmax, area under the curve (AUC) and t1/2.
Per the Applicant, this study was expected to inform the selection of an appropriate sulopenem
prodrug for future studies. Both prodrugs were well-tolerated and there were no study
discontinuations due to adverse events (AEs). One subject in the sulopenem etzadroxil cohort
was no longer willing to participate and withdrew from the study after receiving single doses of
400 and 1000 mg in Periods 1 and 2, respectively. Following Period 1, all subjects from the PF03678685 cohort were discontinued from the study because exposures of sulopenem from the
400 mg dose were considered too low to warrant further study. Because PF-03678685,
sulopenem etzadroxil and formate were not detected in whole blood or plasma samples at any
dose level, PK parameters are only summarized for sulopenem (Table 119).

Single and Multiple Ascending Dose
Study A8811003 was a PK, safety, and tolerability study of single and multiple ascending doses
of sulopenem etzadroxil that also evaluated the effect of probenecid on sulopenem exposure.
Seventy-two healthy male adult subjects were planned for enrollment into 6 cohorts
(N=12/cohort). Dose escalation was contingent upon the absence of serious AEs and doselimiting intolerance. The planned dosing schemes for Cohorts 1 through 6 are summarized in
Table 121 and Table 122. Subjects in the multiple dose cohorts were dosed for 10 days using a
sulopenem etzadroxil powder in bottle formulation at dose strengths of 600 mg and 2000 mg.

All doses were administered under fasted conditions. Blood samples were collected pre-dose
and at pre-specified times post-dosing for measurement of sulopenem, formate and 2ethylbutyric acid. Pharmacokinetic assessments included: Cmax, Tmax, AUC0-inf, AUC0-last, AUC0-tau,
Rac and t1/2. A 24 h urine collection was also performed for subjects in the multiple dose cohorts
on Day 6. Blood and urine samples were assayed using validated LC-MS/MS methods.
Reviewer’s Comment: In addition to the release of sulopenem, hydrolysis of the sulopenem
etzadroxil prodrug ester bond yields formate and 2-ethylbutyric acid as by-products.
Ultimately, 11 male healthy volunteers aged 22-48 years (mean = 30.6 years) were enrolled in
Cohort 1, where 2 of 5 study discontinuations were due to treatment-emergent adverse event
(TEAEs). Each subject in this cohort reported at least 1 TEAE, with diarrhea being most
frequently reported. Single doses of 2000 mg and 4000 mg were considered well-tolerated
while doses of 6000 mg and 8000 mg were poorly tolerated due to a greater frequency and
severity of AEs. Twenty-four healthy volunteers aged 23-51 years (twenty-three males and one
female), were enrolled in Cohorts 2 and 3, three of whom discontinued the study due to AEs.
Overall, 12 of the 24 subjects in Cohorts 2 and 3 reported at least 1 adverse event. As with the
single ascending dose portion of this study, diarrhea was the most frequently observed AE,
occurring in 18 (75%) of subjects. Due to the prevalence and severity of treatment-related
gastrointestinal AEs observed in Cohort 2 (where sulopenem etzadroxil 2000 mg twice daily
[BID] was administered), Cohorts 4 through 6 of this study were not enrolled. Multiple dose
administration of 1200 mg sulopenem etzadroxil with 1000 mg probenecid (Cohort 3) was
better tolerated than multiple doses of 2000 mg sulopenem etzadroxil.

Following oral administration of single doses of 2000 mg to 8000 mg, AUC increased in an
approximately dose proportional manner while Cmax increased less than dose proportionally
(Table 123). Mean sulopenem exposures in Cohort 3, where subjects received 1200 mg
sulopenem etzadroxil with 1000 mg probenecid BID were moderately higher than exposures
observed in Cohort 2 following administration of 2000 mg sulopenem etzadroxil BID (Table 62).
The terminal half-life of sulopenem was ~1.44 h with probenecid and 1.27h in the absence of
probenecid. Interindividual variability was moderate (18 to 26%) for both AUC and Cmax on Days
1 and 10 with and without probenecid. Mean accumulation ratios were below 1 for both
Cohorts 2 and 3 due to an inexplicable reduction in both AUC and Cmax on Day 10 compared to
Day 1. This reduction was less pronounced when sulopenem etzadroxil was administered with
probenecid (6%) versus without (30%).
The 24-hour urinary excretion accounted for approximately 16 to 17% of the total parent dose
(i.e. active sulopenem component) in both Cohort 2 and 3. In the presence of probenecid, CLr
decreased by ~65% compared to administration of sulopenem etzadroxil alone. Formate was
unquantifiable at any dose levels evaluated in this study and concentrations of 2-EBA were
below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) at most time points.

Absolute Bioavailability and Food Effect
Study IT001-105 was an open label, single-center, four sequence, three period study to assess
the safety, tolerability, and absolute bioavailability of the to-be-marketed sulopenem etzadroxil
and probenecid bilayer tablet in the fed and fasted state. This study also evaluated the PK,
safety, and tolerability of two other sulopenem formulations: an oral powder-in-bottle (PIB)
sulopenem etzadroxil formulation and intravenous (IV) sulopenem. Additionally, this study was
used to bridge the probenecid layer of the bilayer tablet and commercial probenecid by
comparing the PK of probenecid following administration of the bilayer tablet to that of
188

Reference ID: 4829902

{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
probenecid, USP tablet (an FDA-approved generic drug version of Benemid). Shown in Table
125 are the details of drug administration in each cohort of the study.
Table 125. Treatment Sequence of the Four Cohorts in Study IT001-105

Reviewer’s Comment: Per the Applicant, the objective of including Cohort 2 was to investigate
the effect of a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil on the PK of sulopenem when
separated by a 7-day washout period. Given the decrease in sulopenem exposure following
multiple dose administration of sulopenem etzadroxil (in Study A8811003), this evaluation was
deemed necessary to determine whether a period effect may explain this observation. However,
it is the reviewer’s opinion that given sulopenem’s short half-life, the dosing regimen indicated
for Cohort 2 is insufficient to address the stated question.
Per the Applicant, the proposed dosing regimen for Study Period 2 of Cohort 4 was intended to
evaluate any potential food effect on the PK of IV sulopenem. Given that food does not impact
the absorption of parenteral administration, no food effect is expected.
Both oral sulopenem etzadroxil formulations contain 366 mg of the sulopenem active
component. For this reason, 366 mg IV sulopenem was used to assess the absolute
bioavailability of the oral formulations. Drug administration across cohorts proceeded as
described below:





Period 1 - After an overnight fast of at least 10 h, subjects received their assigned single
dose treatments and continued fasting for at least 4 h post-dosing.
Period 2 - Following a 7-day washout, subjects were readmitted into their assigned cohorts
to receive the same treatments as indicated for Period 1. With the exception of Cohort 2, all
other cohorts were provided a standard high-fat breakfast (~800-1000 kCal total, 50% fat)
30 min before dosing. Subjects in Cohort 2 received their assigned treatment under the
same fasted conditions outlined for Period 1.
Period 3 - Following another 7-day washout period, subjects were readmitted into their
assigned cohorts. Cohorts 1-3 received 366 mg sulopenem IV infused over 1 h while Cohort
4 received 1000 mg sulopenem IV infused over 3 h in combination with a 500 mg oral
probenecid tablet.

168 h. All toilet papers that came into contact with feces was also collected. Subjects were
discharged before Day 7 if either ~90% of the administered radioactivity was recovered from
urine and feces, or 24 h urine and fecal samples from 2 consecutive collections each had
radioactivity levels amounting to ~1% of the total administered radioactivity.
Analytical Methods
Quantitation of sulopenem in plasma was performed using a validated LC-MS/MS method with
an LLOQ of 25.0 ng/mL and upper limit of quantification of 5,000 ng/mL. Radioanalysis of
plasma and urine sample was conducted using liquid scintillation counting (LSC) for at least 5
min or 100,000 counts. For radioanalysis of feces, samples were combusted and analyzed by
LSC. Oxidation efficiency was evaluated daily by analyzing a commercial radiolabeled standard
both directly in scintillation cocktail and by oxidation. Acceptance criteria were combustion
recoveries of 95 to 105%. The sensitivity of detection of radioactivity was 100 dpm.
For metabolite profiling, plasma samples were pooled per the Hamilton method (i.e. across
timepoints for each subject). For urine, samples were pooled from 0-48 h for each subject and
for feces, fecal homogenates containing the highest levels of excreted radioactivity (i.e. samples
obtained between 0-120 h) were pooled per subject for analysis. Metabolite quantification was
performed by measuring the areas of individually separated high-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) peaks by HPLC with radio-detection. Identification of the metabolites
from HPLC column eluent was performed by mass spectrometry.
Results
PK parameters for sulopenem and total radioactivity were determined from plasma
concentration-time data. Quantitation of metabolites in biological matrices was expressed as
percentage of dose in urine and feces, and percentage of sample for plasma. The mean of total
recovered radioactivity was 85.1% (range 80.2 to 95.0%), most of which was recovered within
the first 72 h (Table 70). Although the mean total recovered radioactivity was <90%, both urine
and fecal samples from 2 consecutive collections had radioactivity levels approximately less
than 1% of the total administered dose for all subjects. The percentages of radioactivity
recovered in urine and feces were similar, i.e., 44.3% vs. 40.8%, respectively (Table 132).
