Reviewer’s Comment: By 48 h, 43% of total radioactivity was recovered in urine. Within the first
48 h, fecal recoveries were highly variable; 2 subjects had unusually low fecal recoveries
(mean = 3.13%) compared to the other 2 (mean = 31.2%). No dosing or sampling issues were
reported that could explain these observations.
The prodrug, sulopenem etzadroxil, was undetected at any timepoint. The proposed
biotransformation pathway of the prodrug is provided in Figure 5. Based on AUC0-last,
sulopenem accounted for 32% of circulating plasma total radioactivity (Figure 6) and the mean
observed terminal half-life of sulopenem in plasma was 1.1 h. Quantifiable levels of
radioactivity were observed in plasma through 96 h post-dose. However, this collection interval
was insufficient to estimate the terminal half-life of total radioactivity in plasma. Aside from
sulopenem, major circulating metabolites were the 2 diastereomers, M1a and M1b, accounting
for 21.8% and 43.6%, respectively. These inactive metabolites are formed by hydrolysis of the
sulopenem β-lactam ring (Figure 5). Sulopenem was the major metabolite recovered in urine,
accounting for 26.9% of the administered dose (based on 0-48 h pooled urine). In feces,
sulopenem only accounted for 3.1% of administered dose (based on 0-120 h pooled feces). In
feces, the majority of metabolites are proposed to be derived from sulfoxide reduction by gut
microbial activity. In urine, M1a and M1b accounted for 7.4% and 2.5%, respectively, of the
administered dose.
Reviewer’s Comment: In vitro studies evaluating the stability and release of sulopenem in
human blood, and simulated gastric and intestinal fluids provided the following key
observations:


In human blood, sulopenem concentrations did not exceed ~30% of sulopenem etzadroxil
input, indicating possible biotransformation in blood.



Sulopenem etzadroxil was slowly degraded in simulated gastric fluid containing pepsin;
however, this did not produce detectable concentrations of sulopenem, suggesting the
formation of other degradants.



In enzyme-free simulated intestinal fluid, sulopenem etzadroxil was stable. However, in
simulated intestinal fluid containing porcine pancreatin, sulopenem etzadroxil was rapidly
degraded.



It was observed that in porcine small intestinal fluid, sulopenem etzadroxil was rapidly
degraded, and sulopenem was undetectable.

Although these studies did not elucidate the structural identity of the other degradants from
the prodrug, the observations lend some additional insight on the fate of sulopenem etzadroxil
and sulopenem. The low percentage of plasma radioactivity attributable to sulopenem may be
explained in part by substantial and rapid degradation of the prodrug both by gastric enzymes
and in blood.

Renal Impairment
Study A8811009 was an open-label, 2-way crossover study which evaluated the PK, safety, and
tolerability of IV sulopenem and oral sulopenem etzadroxil in subjects with varying degrees of
renal function. Mass balance studies indicated that renal clearance accounted for ~50% of total
sulopenem excretion. Because of the apparent importance of renal clearance and the likelihood
that sulopenem will be administered in patients with renal impairment, this study was
necessary to determine the impact of renal impairment on the PK of sulopenem.
The study was designed to enroll 8 subjects per renal function group (except for the severe
renal impairment cohort, where N=5). Subjects were selected based on their estimated CLcr
based on the Cockcroft Gault equation and were classified as follows:





Group 1: Normal Renal Function (CLcr >80 mL/min)
Group 2: Mild Renal Impairment (CLcr >50 and ≤80 mL/min)
Group 3: Moderate Renal Impairment (CLcr ≥30 and ≤50 mL/min)
Group 4: Severe Renal Impairment (CLcr <30 mL/min)

Reviewer’s Comments: The Applicant’s classification of renal function groups was based on the
1998 FDA Guidance on Pharmacokinetics in Patients with Impaired Renal Function – Study
Design, Data Analysis, and Impact on Dosing and Labeling. Reclassification of renal function
groups according to the 2020 version of the guidance displaces 4 subjects from the mild to the
moderate impairment group. Notably, subjects with kidney failure, classified as having CLcr <15
mL/min were omitted from this study.
Subjects were required to have stable renal function, defined as having 2 serum creatinine
values obtained within 7-14 days which differed by ≤20% (for subjects with renal impairment)
and ≤25% for subjects with normal renal function. Subjects in Groups 1 through 4 participated
in 2 treatment periods with dosing in these periods separated by a washout period of 14 days.
Subjects fasted for 8 h before and 3 h after dosing. On Day 1 of each treatment period, subjects
received a single dose of study drug as follows:



Period 1: 800 mg sulopenem 1.5h IV infusion, except in Group 4, where only 1 subject was
administered 800 mg and all others received 200 mg sulopenem 1.5 h IV infusion.
Period 2: 1000 mg (2 X 500 mg) sulopenem etzadroxil immediate release (IR) tablets.

Reviewer’s Comment: An interim analysis of PK data from 1 subject in the severe impairment
group during the IV dosing period indicated higher sulopenem exposures than predicted. To
maintain IV exposures within the Applicant’s observed maximally tolerated dose (MTD) for IV
dosing, the protocol was amended to administer 200 mg sulopenem for the remaining severely
renally impaired subjects.
Subjects with normal renal function who received any prescription drugs, vitamins, and dietary
supplements within 7 days or 5 half-lives (whichever was longer) prior to the first dose of study
drug were excluded. Renally impaired subjects on any immunosuppressive drugs (including
cyclosporine, tacrolimus and sirolimus) and drugs known to affect estimation of CLcr (including
cimetidine, trimethoprim and cibenzoline) were also excluded.

PK Sampling and Assessments
Plasma samples for assessment of sulopenem PK and metabolites were collected pre-dose and
at pre-specified times post-dosing. Urine samples were also obtained pre-dose and at intervals
of 0-6, 6-12 and 12-24 h post-dose. The following PK parameters were calculated: AUC0-24,
AUC0-last, AUC0-inf, Cmax, Tmax, Vz, Vz/F, CL/F, CL, CLr, CLnr t1/2, and Ae24. Plasma protein-binding
was not determined in this study. A one-way ANOVA model with group as a fixed effect was
used to compare log-transformed AUCinf, AUClast and Cmax for mild, moderate, and severe renal
impairment groups to the normal renal function group.
Reviewer’s Comment: Because the plasma protein binding of sulopenem is 11%, changes in
protein binding resulting from impaired renal function are expected to be low. Therefore, use of
total concentrations is appropriate.
Results
Study Population
With the exception of race and renal status, overall mean demographic characteristics were
similar across renal function groups. Seventeen male and twelve female subjects aged 38 to 78
years with a mean BMI of 27.7 kg/m2 were enrolled in this study and a majority of the subjects
(86.2%) were White. One subject in the severe impairment group discontinued the study after
Period 1 (i.e., following administration of IV sulopenem) due to AEs, leaving twenty-eight PK
evaluable subjects.
Protocol Deviations
Twelve subjects did not have metabolite assays performed and three subjects (two in the
normal renal function group and one in the severe impairment group) did not save all urine for
processing.
Reviewer’s Comment: Overall, the implications of these protocol deviations are considered to be
minor. Consistent with the observations from the single ascending doses (SAD) and multiple
ascending doses (MAD) studies, concentrations of 2-EBA and formate were below LLOQ at most
timepoints in subjects for whom metabolites were evaluated.
The Applicant did not specify which intervals of urine collection may have been impacted by the
lapses in urine collection and analysis. The reviewer’s analysis of raw urine PK data for the 2
subjects from the normal renal function group with incomplete urine collection yielded no
indication of which (or how many) urine samples were impacted by the protocol deviation.
Exclusion of urine PK data from these subjects had only a modest effect, which was an increase
in the estimated mean urine concentration for the 0-6 h collection interval from 177.45 µg/mL
to 201.2 µg/mL.

Pharmacokinetics
Following administration of a single 1000 mg oral dose of sulopenem etzadroxil, AUC of
sulopenem increased 7.4-fold in subjects with severe renal impairment compared to those with
normal renal function, and Cmax increased 2.9-fold (Table 133). Sulopenem half-life increased
with worsening renal function, but remained short (i.e. 2.8 h) in subjects with severe renal
impairment. Sulopenem etzadroxil was well-tolerated and the incidence of AEs was comparable
across renal function groups.
Reviewer’s Comment: The bioavailability of sulopenem in this study increased progressively
from 22% with normal renal function to 35% in subjects with severe renal impairment. The
mechanism underlying this increase is unknown, but may be due to gastroparesis (delayed
gastric emptying) observed in severe renal impairment and more commonly, in end-stage renal
disease (Kumar 2021). Because sulopenem is poorly soluble (Biopharmaceutical Classification
System Class IV), slowed gastric emptying may provide additional time and opportunity for drug
dissolution and thus result in absorption of a larger proportion of the administered dose.
It has been reported that renal impairment results in downregulation of renal OAT transporter
expression and function (VanWert et al. 2010) and the probenecid USPI notes that probenecid
may not be effective when GFR ≤30 mL/min. Because probenecid requires functional OAT
transporters to exert its effect, chronic renal impairment diminishes probenecid’s effectiveness
as an OAT3 inhibitor. Therefore, concomitant administration of probenecid with sulopenem
etzadroxil is not expected to further increase sulopenem exposures in subjects with severe
renal impairment. The single 1000 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil used in the renal
impairment study is intended to be the total daily dose for the treatment of uUTI administered
500 mg BID for a total duration of 5 days. Given that sulopenem exposures increase
approximately dose proportionally (within the dose range of 400 mg to 2000 mg),
administration of a 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil in subjects with severe renal
impairment is anticipated to yield a sulopenem AUC0-inf of ~23995 ng·h/mL. The AUC0-inf at the
MTD of 4000 mg from SAD studies is 26900 ng/mL. In MAD studies, dose escalation beyond the
starting 2000 mg BID dose of sulopenem etzadroxil was infeasible due to the occurrence of
severe adverse events at higher doses. 1200 mg sulopenem etzadroxil in combination with
1000 mg BID probenecid appeared to be well tolerated and yielded moderately higher
exposures than the 2000 mg BID sulopenem etzadroxil regimen. Day 10 AUCtau for 1200 mg
sulopenem etzadroxil plus 1000 mg was 18800 ng·h/mL, which is 28% lower than the exposure
anticipated for 500 mg in subjects with severe renal impairment. Given sulopenem’s short halflife even in the setting of severe renal impairment (i.e., 2.75 h) and the short treatment
duration of 5 days, the proposed dose is expected to be safe in subjects with severe renal
impairment. However, because sulopenem PK has not been evaluated in subjects with CLcr <15
mL/min or subjects on dialysis, the sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer tablet cannot be
used in this population.

Successful treatment of urinary tract infections is expected to be contingent upon the
achievement of adequate concentrations of study drug in urine (Gilbert 2006). Thus, in patients
with renal insufficiency, sufficiently high urine concentrations may be difficult to achieve.
Where sulopenem is concerned, the cumulative amount excreted in urine following a single
oral dose was generally comparable across the renal function groups studied (Table 133).
Reviewer’s Comment: CLr decreases with decreasing renal function, thus the rate of sulopenem
elimination is expected to be fastest with normal renal function and slowest with severe renal
impairment. This may result in variable sulopenem concentrations across urine collection
intervals, which may have implications for efficacy. However, for a short half-life drug like
sulopenem, regardless of the differences in sulopenem concentrations at the various urine
collection intervals, the resulting amount of sulopenem recovered is similar across renal function
groups. Of note, the higher 24 h urine recovery of sulopenem in the severe impairment was
driven by a single outlier whose urine recovery was 365000 µg; exclusion of this subjects brings
the Ae24 to 126877 µg, which is in closer agreement with the values observed in other renal
function groups.
Clinical Drug-Drug Interactions
Study IT001-102 was a Phase 1, randomized, open-label single-dose, 4-way crossover study to
evaluate the effect of gallic acid, tannic acid, and probenecid on the plasma PK of sulopenem.
Sulopenem was administered as the etzadroxil prodrug in a PIB formulation. Probenecid is an
OAT3 inhibitor commonly used in this capacity to increase the plasma exposures of β-lactam
antibiotics. Gallic acid and tannic acid are phenolic compounds that are structurally similar to
probenecid and suggested to also inhibit OAT3.
Thirteen healthy male and female subjects were enrolled in this study. The 4 treatment periods
were as follows:



Period 1 – 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil alone
Period 2 – Sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg + probenecid 500 mg

{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}



Period 3 - Sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg + gallic acid 400 mg
Period 4 - Sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg + tannic acid 400 mg

A 3-period probenecid sub-study was also conducted in 12 additional male and female subjects
in which a single 500 mg dose of sulopenem etzadroxil PIB was administered with probenecid.
The treatment periods were as follows:



etzadroxil dosing

Tmax, CL/F and t1/2. The mean difference between test and reference treatments, geometric
mean ratios and their 90% CIs were determined.
Results
No prior medications were reported and concomitant medications were limited to
administration of over-the-counter Tylenol severe cold and flu to treat a viral syndrome in one
subject. All treatments were well tolerated and of the 3 discontinuations from the primary
study, none were due to AEs. An approximately 33% increase in sulopenem AUC was observed
when administered with 500 mg probenecid, which exceeds the 5% increase observed with
gallic acid (Table 134). Inexplicably, sulopenem exposure with coadministration of tannic acid (a
precursor to gallic acid) resulted in a ~12% reduction in sulopenem AUC. Results of the
probenecid sub-study indicate that the maximum benefit of probenecid is observed with
simultaneous administration of sulopenem etzadroxil (Table 135).

Study IT001-101
Study IT001-101 was a Phase 1, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, multiple dose
study of two sulopenem prodrugs (PF-04064900 and PF-03709270) with and without
probenecid (under fed and fasted conditions) or gallic acid (under fasted conditions). The study
objectives included:







To evaluate the safety and tolerability of sulopenem prodrugs following multiple dose
administration
To evaluate the effect of food on PK, safety, and tolerability of the sulopenem prodrugs
To characterize the PK of sulopenem and its prodrugs when coadministered with
probenecid
To estimate the relative oral bioavailability of the sulopenem prodrugs
To evaluate the effect of different doses of probenecid when co-administered with a single
dose of sulopenem etzadroxil
To evaluate the effect of gallic acid on the PK of sulopenem when coadministered with
sulopenem etzadroxil

Two hundred and forty healthy adult male and female subjects aged 20-60 years with CLcr
ranging from 91 to 156 mL/min were randomized to 5 treatment groups as indicated in Table
74. Of these, 192 subjects where enrolled in Treatment Groups 1-4 and 48 subjects were
enrolled in Treatment Group 5. For both prodrugs, an oral powder in bottle formulation was
used.
Blood samples were obtained pre-dosing and at pre-specified times post-dosing to assess
sulopenem and sulopenem prodrug PK parameters. Urine samples were also obtained pre-dose
and post-dosing on Days 2 and 7 of treatment for assessment of sulopenem urine PK. On Day 1,
urine was collected at 2 h intervals through 12 h post-dosing, and at 6 h intervals on Day 7
through 24 h post-dosing. For plasma, parameters of interest included: Cmax, Tmax, AUClast,
AUCtau on Days 1 and Day 7, t½ and Rac. For urine, Ae24 and CLr were calculated.
Reviewer’s Comment: Given that sulopenem etzadroxil (PF-03709270) was the prodrug selected
for marketing, and probenecid was the OAT3 inhibitor of choice for the to-be-marketed
formulation, the study results will focus on observations made following administration of this
prodrug in the presence and absence of probenecid. Additionally, because food effect and
bioavailability were determined under IT001-105 for the to-be-marketed formulation, the effect
of food on sulopenem exposure will not be covered under the review of this study.

Study IT001-103
Study IT001-103 was a Phase 1, 2-period, 4-sequence, parallel study to evaluate the effects of
multiple dose administration of itraconazole (a P-gp inhibitor) on the PK of sulopenem in
healthy adult subjects. The rationale for this study is that in vitro, sulopenem etzadroxil was
identified as a P-gp substrate. This review focuses on the two study cohorts wherein the to-bemarketed bilayer tablet was used.
Thirty-two adult male and female subjects were enrolled in the cohorts of interest. Drug
administration was as follows:



Period 1 - Single 500 mg sulopenem etzadroxil/500 mg probenecid bilayer tablet under fed
(Cohort 2) and fasted (Cohort 3) conditions
Period 2 – Following a washout period of 3 days, 200 mg of itraconazole (2 X 100 mg oral
capsules) was administered once daily for 4 days in the fasted state for both Cohorts 2 and
3. On Day 4, itraconazole was coadministered with a single oral dose of the bilayer tablet
under fed (Cohort 2) and fasted (Cohort 3) conditions.

Blood samples for PK assessment were obtained pre-dosing and at pre-specified times through
12 h post-dosing. Plasma PK parameters such as AUC0-t, AUCextrap, AUC0-inf, Cmax and t1/2 were
summarized descriptively. The Cmax and AUCs of sulopenem in the bilayer tablet administered
alone in the fasted and fed states, respectively, were compared to the exposures achieved in

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
the presence of itraconazole using a paired t-test for the natural-log transformed Cmax and
AUCs.
Reviewer’s Comment: The itraconazole dose (200 mg) used in this study provides adequate
exposure for P-gp inhibition. Because sulopenem etzadroxil is rapidly hydrolyzed to sulopenem
after oral administration, a clinically significant drug-drug interaction (DDI) with P-gp inhibitors

Results
Sulopenem was generally well tolerated. One subject in Cohort 3 (where the bilayer tablet was

Study IT001-104
Study IT001-104 was a Phase 1, open-label, 2-period, 3-sequence, parallel study designed to
evaluate the effects of multiple-dose administration of IV sulopenem, sulopenem
etzadroxil/probenecid bilayer oral tablet or sulopenem etzadroxil oral tablet on the steadystate PK profile of valproic acid in healthy adult subjects. The rationale underpinning this study
is the observation that carbapenems may decrease the plasma concentrations of valproic acid.

Reviewer’s Comment: The significant reduction in sulopenem AUC and Cmax observed with the
administration of aluminum hydroxide appears to be driven by lower sulopenem exposures with
concomitant administration of the antacid for 1 subject. The Applicant does not offer an
explanation for the lower exposures observed for sulopenem etzadroxil + aluminum hydroxide in
this subject. When data from the subject are excluded from the analysis, the reduction in AUC
and Cmax improve to 7% and 14%, respectively. According to the FDA guidance on evaluating
gastric pH-dependent drug interactions, results of an interaction study with a proton-pump
inhibitor (PPI) present the worst-case scenario for pH-dependent DDIs due to the long-lasting
effect of this class on gastric pH. Therefore, a negative result with a PPI, as is the case here, is
indicative of a lack of pH-dependent DDI.
The main goal of the probenecid portion of the study was to inform probenecid dose selection
for use in combination in a fixed-dose tablet. The doses evaluated (500 mg and 1000 mg) are
consistent with the standard doses of probenecid generally recommended for coadministration
with β-lactams to improve their plasma exposures. Both sulopenem AUC and Cmax increased
approximately 1.4-fold with a 2-fold increase in the dose of probenecid (Table 145). The
amount of sulopenem recovered in urine over 12 h decreased by 9% with a 2-fold increase in
the dose of probenecid.

Metabolism
CYP450 and UGT Reaction Phenotyping
The metabolic stability of sulopenem in the presence of human recombinant UGTs (UGT1A1,
1A3, 1A4, 1A6, 1A9, 2B7 and 2B15) and CYPs (1A2, 2A6, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4 and 3A5) at
concentrations of 1 and 10 µM in Study Iterum-03-09Aug2019. No metabolism was observed
when sulopenem was incubated with recombinant UGT or CYP enzymes. For unspecified
reasons, the Applicant states that in vitro metabolism of sulopenem could not be characterized
sufficiently using human liver microsomes or hepatocytes. No in vitro metabolism studies were
conducted for sulopenem etzadroxil because it is expected to be rapidly hydrolyzed to the
active sulopenem moiety.
Reviewer’s Comment: The review team postulates that the inability to illustrate in vitro
metabolism of sulopenem using human liver microsomes or hepatocytes is because sulopenem
may be susceptible to non-CYP and UGT-mediated biotransformations in these in vitro test
systems. Thus, the Applicant’s use of recombinant CYP and UGT enzymes elucidates the
involvement (or lack thereof) of these enzymes in the disposition of sulopenem.
In Vitro Drug-Drug Interaction Studies
CYP Inhibitory and Induction Potential
Studies DM2006-070429-029 and 17081086ITX evaluated the inhibitory potential of sulopenem
and sulopenem etzadroxil on pooled human liver microsomal activity of CYP1A2, CYP2B6,
CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4/5. Sulopenem was found to not be a direct or timedependent inhibitor of CYP isoforms tested up to 150 µM. Sulopenem etzadroxil was found to
be a time-dependent inhibitor of CYP3A4/5, but an IC50 could not be calculated within the
concentration range studied, and was estimated to be >150 µM. The potential of sulopenem to
induce the activities of CYPs 1A2, 2B6 and 3A4 were evaluated in Study 17081087ITX using
pooled human hepatocytes. No induction of enzyme activity was observed using sulopenem
concentrations of 0.07 to 150 µM. The induction potential of sulopenem etzadroxil was not
evaluated.
Transporter Studies
Studies 17081088ITX and Iterum-02-08-Mar2019-A1 evaluated sulopenem and sulopenem
etzadroxil both as substrates and inhibitors of human BSEP, P-gp, MRP2, MATE1, MATE2-K
OAT1, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1 and OCT2 transporters. Bidirectional permeability was
evaluated using MDCKII or HEK293 cells expressing the respective uptake transporters.
Sulopenem was a substrate of OAT3 with over 34-fold accumulation in cells expressing OAT3
and inhibitor of OAT1 with IC50>150 µM. Sulopenem was neither a substrate or inhibitor of
BCRP, P-gp, BSEP, MRP2, MATE1, MATE2-K, OAT1B1B1, OAT1P1B3, OCT1 or OCT2. Sulopenem
etzadroxil was a substrate and inhibitor of P-gp (IC50=1.91 µM) and BCRP (IC50=20.4 µM), and an
inhibitor of OAT1 (IC50=93.6 µM) and OAT3 (IC50=34.8 µM). However, inhibition of OAT1 and

Identification of PK/PD Index of Sulopenem
The pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) index of sulopenem was evaluated with
dose-fractionation in a murine thigh infection model using 2 strains each of E. coli, K.
pneumoniae, S. pneumoniae and S. pyogenes with sulopenem minimum inhibitor concentration
(MIC) in the range of 0.0078 – 1 µg/mL. Immunosuppressed mice were used in studies involving
E. coli while all other dose-fractionation studies were conducted in immunocompetent mice.
Sulopenem total daily doses in the range of 3.125 – 200 mg/kg/day were administered
according to q3h, q6h, q12h and q24h dosing regimens 24h post-inoculation of murine thigh
muscles to delineate the PK/PD driver of sulopenem’s antibacterial activity. Accompanying PK
studies were conducted for sulopenem single doses of 4.69, 18.75, 75 and 300 mg/kg. Because
protein binding of sulopenem in mouse plasma was determined to be 0.01 and concentration
independent, adjustment of PK parameters for protein binding was negligible. The correlation
of AUC/MIC, Cmax/MIC, and T > MIC to the PD data (i.e., change in log10 CFU) was determined by
non-linear least-squares regression analysis using a Hill-type model. Based on the coefficient of
determination (r2), results presented for S. pneumoniae in Figure 8 suggest that AUC/MIC is the
PK/PD index that best correlated with sulopenem’s antibacterial activity.

Reviewer’s Comment: Although the Applicant’s Summary of Clinical Pharmacology described 2
sets of nonclinical PK/PD studies, the original NDA submission provided only an abbreviated
nonclinical PK/PD study report (for Study 810-00081) which offered limited information on
PK/PD index and target determination in a murine thigh infection model. Therefore, an IR (dated
02/11/2021) was issued to the Applicant, seeking clarification on which of the studies described
in the Summary of Clinical Pharmacology was used to inform PK/PD targets for probability of
target attainment (PTA) analysis. In response to this IR, the Applicant provided an unpublished
manuscript, an abstract presented at 2 scientific conferences and laboratory notebook pages.
Per the Applicant, information contained in the report for Study 810-00081, abstract and
laboratory notebook pages were integrated into the unpublished manuscript. Therefore, the
manuscript served as the Applicant’s primary source of information for the identification of a
PK/PD index and target for sulopenem.
Per the reviewer’s assessment, the integrity of PK and PD information provided by the Applicant
is questionable due to discrepancies in the data and results summarized in the Study 810-00081
report, abstract and unpublished manuscript. Key issues identified by the reviewer include: a)
incongruity of the best PK/PD index for sulopenem suggested by Study 810-00081 and the
unpublished manuscript, b) differences in values of PK parameters reported in the abstract
compared to the unpublished manuscript, and c) inconsistencies in the methodology described
within the unpublished manuscript. Study report 810-00081 briefly outlined dose-fractionation
studies conducted with a single isolate each of K. pneumoniae and S. pneumoniae in a murine
thigh infection model. In this report, T > MIC was identified as the relevant PK/PD driver for
sulopenem’s activity, which is consistent with the known PK/PD driver for other penem (i.e. βlactam) antibacterial drugs. Although data from Study 810-00081 were purportedly integrated
into the unpublished manuscript, results presented in the manuscript conclude that AUC/MIC
(and not T > MIC) is the relevant PK/PD driver. The Applicant’s explanation for these
contradicting observations is that both concentration and T > MIC are relevant to sulopenem’s
activity. Additionally, inconsistencies in the values of PK parameters summarized in the abstract
compared to the manuscript render the PK data unreliable. Ultimately, a dearth of details,
questionable data and ambiguities regarding study methodology and PK/PD analyses render the
results of the nonclinical PK/PD studies uninterpretable. Because raw data from these studies
were not available, the reviewer was unable to conduct independent analyses to confirm
T > MIC as the PK/PD driver of sulopenem’s antibacterial activity.

Population PK Analysis
Review Summary
The Applicant’s population PK (PopPK) analysis reasonably describes the time-concentration
profiles of sulopenem in healthy subjects and subjects with uUTI. Parameters for clearance
were estimated with acceptable relative standard errors (RSE) less than 20%. There was no
notable bias in goodness-of-fit (GOF) plots and the visual predictive check (VPC). The ETA
shrinkages for PK parameters for clearance and volumes of distributions are modest (25% to
57%). The PopPK model is acceptable to be used to derive the summary exposure parameters
(AUCtau, Cmax) for healthy and uUTI infected patients. Limitations of the popPK model were
noted in describing covariate effects (such as renal function, food status, and formulations).
These should be carefully considered when interpreting the model derived covariate effects
and using the model for simulations for target attainment analysis.

some oral doses. This was described using an absorption model with two parallel chains of

estimated to 2540 µg/h and 77.9 µg/mL. V1, V2, and V3 were estimated to 12.6 L, 7.40 L and
4.49 L, respectively.
Inter individual variability (IIV) for TM, V1, V2 and V3 were 16.1%, 20.2%, 25.3% and 21.2%,
respectively. The IIV for the parameters related to absorption were 23.0%, 71.1% and 189% for
mean transit time for first transit chain (MTT1), number of transit compartments for first transit
chain (NTR1) and the fraction of dose going into the fast or slow absorption chain, respectively.
The inter occasion variability estimated for MTT1 was 26.0%.
The bioavailability (F) of sulopenem etzadroxil was estimated to 21.2%. Food increased F by
32.6% for the PIB and monolayer tablet formulation, and 47.2% for the bilayer tablet. Food
prolonged absorption and MTT1 by 63.0% for the monolayer tablet and PIB formulation. PIB
formulation also showed a faster overall absorption as compared to mono- and bilayer tablet,
20.1%. There was also a statistically significant effect on F following multiple oral dosing
without probenecid, predicting a 24.7% lower F on day 7.
Administrating IV sulopenem and oral sulopenem etzadroxil with probenecid reduced TM by
32.4% at probenecid dose ranging from 250-500 mg and with 52.0% at the higher probenecid
dose (1000 mg). Probenecid was also found to be a covariate on the volumes of distributions
(reducing the volumes by 12.2%). Creatinine clearance (CLcr) had an impact on TM, resulting in
8.35% decrease in TM for every 10 ml/min change in CLcr. Refer to Applicant’s PopPK report,
Table 9 and 10 (parameter estimates of the Phase 1 popPK model), Figures 10, 11, 12, 13 (GOF
plots), and Figure 14 and Figure 15 (prediction corrected VPC plots).

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Reviewer’s Comment: The Phase 1 PopPK model adequately describes the observed PK data for
healthy subjects. The GOF plots do not show any notable bias and the VPC plots by dose groups
showed a good agreement between the predicted and the observed data, as well as capturing
the variability of the observed data. For further model building, the Applicant fixed the transit
compartment parameters (i.e., MTT1, NTR1, NTR2) and the effect of probenecid, and food with
the estimates from the Phase 1 model and re-estimated the rest parameters with pooled data
including Phase 3 data.
Final PopPK model: The structural model of the final model is the same as Phase 1 PopPK
model. Phase 3 patient data were added to the model development and additional covariate
relationships were examined in a stepwise procedure. In addition to the structural covariates
included in Phase 1 model, the final model includes body weight as a covariate on V1, V2, and
V3 with allometric scaling with exponent of 1, and sex was included for TM. Separate residual
variability for the Phase 3 studies was included and a Phase 3 study effect was estimated for
MTT1. The parameter estimates for the final covariate model are listed in Table 151.

Reviewer’s Comment: In general, the Applicant’s final PopPK model acceptably describes the
observed PK data collected from Phase 1 and Phase 3 studies. Most PK parameters were
estimated with acceptable precision (%RSE <20%) and IIVs were estimated with %RSE <50%. ETA
shrinkages for TM, V1, V2, and V3 were modest (25%, 57%, 48%, and 49%). The GOF plots by
route of administration did not show any obvious bias. The VPC plots showed that the model
predictions are in agreement with the observed concentrations for both Phase 1 and Phase 3
studies. Therefore, the reviewer agrees that this model can be used to derive the summary
exposure metrics such as AUC and Cmax for the study populations.
Body weight, and sex minimally impact sulopenem exposure and these impacts are not
considered clinically meaningful. With decreasing CLcr from 116 to 48 mL/min, there is a 2- fold
increase in sulopenem AUC0-12h following a 500 mg bilayer tablet. The model predicted
magnitude of CLcr impact is somewhat smaller than those observed in the dedicated RI study. In
the RI study, sulopenem AUCinf increased in subjects with mild, moderate, and severe renal
function by 210%, 350% and 740% after a single oral dose of 1000 mg sulopenem etzadroxil,
and 170% (mild RI) and 250% (moderate RI) after an 800 mg IV dose. Note that a different
formulation (tablet without probenecid) was used in the RI study from the proposed formulation
(bilayer tablet with probenecid). The impacts of renal impairment on probenecid and the
associated impact on sulopenem exposures were not incorporated in the Applicant’s PopPK
model.
The complexity of the structural model and the potential interactions between intrinsic/extrinsic
factors that are correlated to each other (i.e., renal function, food effects, and formulations
(with or without probenecid) make it difficult to interpret the model-estimated covariate effects.
Therefore, this limitation should be carefully considered when this model is used for simulations
for target attainment analysis. One example is food effect. The model-derived food effect on
bilayer tablets is mainly driven by the data from the food effect study (IT001-105) which showed
231
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
a significant food effect (approx. 50% higher exposure vs. fasted). While most subjects (90.7%)
from Phase 3 studies were recorded as in a fed status during dosing, the model predicted
exposures for Phase 3 subjects are generally lower than those observed in healthy subjects with
fed status and more close to those observed in fasted status. It is not clear whether the lower
exposures observed in the Phase 3 studies are due to the inherent PK difference between
patients (uUTI, cUTI) vs. healthy subjects, or the way food status was recorded in the Phase 3
studies (i.e., inaccurate record of food status, or the consumed food ([planned] meal/snack)
different from those (high-fat meal) consumed in Study IT001-105.
Because of the deficiencies in the determination of PK/PD targets noted by the Clinical
Pharmacology reviewer (See Appendix 16.3), the Applicant’s target attainment analysis could
not be evaluated by the reviewer. In the Phase 3 efficacy trial (IT001-301) supporting the
proposed indication, PK samples were collected in a subset (n=118) of intent-to-treat (ITT)
population (n=787). Therefore, the exposure-response for clinical efficacy/safety was not further
evaluated by the reviewer.

16.5. Clinical Microbiology
16.5.1. In Vitro Information
16.5.1.1. Mechanism of Action
Sulopenem is a penem antibacterial drug that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to
penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). A competitive binding assay was conducted with 3H-penicillin
in E. coli strain W-7 that showed sulopenem (CP-65,207) had the highest affinity for PBP2, with
concentrations as low as 0.004 µg/mL (Figure 14) (Gootz 1989). It has also shown that the
relative order of affinity towards PBPs of sulopenem in E. coli was PBP2>PBP1A > PBP1B >
PBP4>PBP3>PBP5/6. Additionally, it was determined through a hydrolysis study that CP-65207
was highly stable to some cephalosporinases, including plasmid-encoded enzymes TEM-1, SHV1, and PSE-2.

{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Figure 14. Autoradiograph of Competitive Binding of Unlabeled CP-65,207 Versus 3HPenicillin G
for E. coli W-7 PBPs

16.5.1.2. Bactericidal Activity
The bactericidal activity of sulopenem was demonstrated in several time-kill studies. Sulopenem
exhibited bactericidal killing in one study (Uppsala 2018-10-11), at concentrations ≥4X the MIC
against E. coli and K. pneumoniae isolates (Table 155).
Table 155. Strains Used in Uppsala Time-Kill Study and Sulopenem MIC Values

Abbreviations: MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration

Bactericidal activity was seen at ≥4X the MIC against ARU 829 (E. coli ESBL+) and ARU 835 (K.
pneumoniae ATCC 43816) and at ≥8X the MIC against ARU 768 (E. coli ATCC 25922) and ARU
827 (K. pneumoniae ESBL+) (Figure 15).

16.5.1.3. Mechanisms of Resistance
The development of resistance to sulopenem was evaluated in spontaneous mutation
frequency studies using two E. cloacae isolates and in serial passage studies using clinical
isolates of E. coli and K. pneumoniae.
In a spontaneous mutation frequency study, colonies were isolated at a frequency of 1 X 10-8
with a ≤2-fold increase in MIC from the parent strain. In the serial passage mutation studies,
MIC values increased 16-fold during 15 serial passages in two out of the three tested E. coli
isolates and were unchanged for the third isolate. MIC values increased 8-fold during serial
passage for one of the two K. pneumoniae isolates tested, and MIC values increased from 0.5 to
256 µg/mL for the other isolate.
243
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Similar to other carbapenems, resistance to sulopenem occurs primarily due to enzymatic
inactivation by carbapenemases, but also can be caused by β-lactamase production, efflux
pump expression, and changes in porins and/or PBPs (Papp-Wallace et al. 2011; Papp-Wallace
2019).
16.5.1.4. Interaction With Other Antimicrobials
Interactions of sulopenem with nine other antimicrobial agents were evaluated in a
checkerboard assay using four E. coli and two K. pneumoniae isolates (JMI final report 17-ITR-01
Part 3). The antimicrobial drugs that were tested in combination with sulopenem were
amoxicillin, aztreonam, ceftriaxone, doxycycline, gentamicin, levofloxacin, nitrofurantoin,
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and vancomycin (Table 157). No instance of antagonism was
observed in vitro between sulopenem and other antibacterial drugs against tested E. coli and K.
pneumoniae isolates. Only, two instances of synergy were observed, both with trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, against E. coli ATCC 35218 (TEM-1) and E. coli 937054 (ESBL, CTX-M-15).
Table 157. Summary of the Minimum and Maximum FICI Values Observed During Checkerboard
Testing of Sulopenem With a Variety of Agents Against E. Coli and K. Pneumoniae

Abbreviations: FICI, fractional inhibitory concentration index.

16.5.1.5. In Vitro Spectrum and Activity
In vitro susceptibility testing was performed to determine the MIC by following the Clinical
Laboratory Standard Institute guidelines (CLSI M07, M11, and M100). Sulopenem demonstrated
in vitro activity against aerobic and anaerobic gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria in
profiling, surveillance, and clinical studies. The in vitro MIC50/90 values (inhibits the growth of
≥50% and ≥90% of the isolates) were determined for sulopenem in all studies but this review
only focuses on relevant uUTI pathogens from 3 recent surveillance studies and a single uUTI
clinical study (IT001-301).
The activity of sulopenem was evaluated in a large collection of clinical isolates (UTI and IAI
infection sources) from the US, Europe, and Canada. The first study was conducted by testing
873 aerobic clinical isolates collected from 2013-2015 (International Health Management
Associates [IHMA]; Study IHMA_2757); the second study was conducted by testing 1,918
aerobic clinical isolates collected from 2016-2017 (JMI; Study 17-ITR-05); and a third
244

{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
surveillance study was conducted by testing 3,126 aerobic clinical isolates collected from 2016
in Canada (the Health Sciences Centre; CANWARD 2016).

Sulopenem exhibited in vitro activity against Enterobacterales including uUTI-relevant

cross-resistance.

16.5.2.1. Systemic Infection Models
Summaries of the in vivo activities of sulopenem and its prodrug, sulopenem etzadroxil dosed
orally (PO) or subcutaneously (SC) are presented below:
Study RR 810-00093: Briefly, CF1 mice (n=10) were infected via an intraperitoneal (IP) challenge
with 3.5 x 107 CFU/mouse of K. pneumoniae 53A1109 isolate. This is an ESBL-producing strain
that contains the TEM-1, OXA-9, multiple SHVs and AmpC β-lactamase genes with a sulopenem
MIC value of 0.25 µg/mL. Compounds in this study were dosed PO or SC at 0.5- and 4.0-hours
post-infection to determine the protective dose for 50% of the tested animals (PD50).
Sulopenem failed when dosed PO (PD50 >50 mg/kg) but was efficacious when dosed SC, with a
PD50 of 3.4 mg/kg, as shown in Table 168. Prodrug sulopenem etzadroxil dosed orally exhibited
a PD50 of 9.0 mg/kg in this model.
Study RR 810-00093: CF1 mice (n=10) were infected via an IP challenge with 1.3 x 102
CFU/mouse of S. pneumoniae 02J1095. This is a macrolide-resistant, penicillin-tolerant strain
with sulopenem MIC value of 0.25 to 0.5 µg/mL. Compounds were administered at 0.5- and 4hr post-infection. Sulopenem failed when dosed PO (PD50>50 mg/kg) but was efficacious when
dosed SC, with a PD50 of 4.3 mg/kg (Table 168). Sulopenem etzadroxil dosed orally exhibited a
PD50 of 6.3 mg/kg.
Study RR04-25-2006: CF1 female mice (n=8) were infected via IP injection with 3.5 x 102
CFU/mouse of S. pneumoniae 02J1095 strain with sulopenem MIC value of 0.25 to 0.5 µg/mL.
Compounds were administered at 0.5- and 4-hr post-infection. When dosed PO, sulopenem
failed with a PD50 of >50 mg/kg but was efficacious when dosed SC (PD50 6.3 mg/kg) as shown
in Table 168. Sulopenem etzadroxil demonstrated an oral PD50 of 12.5 mg/kg.
Table 168. Efficacy (PD50 in mg/kg) of Sulopenem, Sulopenem Etzadroxil and Comparators
Against Murine Systemic Infections

Abbreviations: PD50, 50% of protective dose

16.5.2.2. Pulmonary Infection Models
The in vivo activity of sulopenem and its prodrug was evaluated in mouse pulmonary infection
models caused by different gram-positive organisms in two studies: RR 810-00093 and RR-0501-2006.
257
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
Study RR 810-00093: Briefly, CF-1 mice were infected via the intranasal route with 1.3 x 106
CFU/mouse of S. pneumoniae 02J1095 (macrolide-resistant, penicillin-tolerant strain with
sulopenem MIC value of 0.25 to 0.5 µg/mL). Mice were treated twice per day for two days
starting 18 hours post-infection. Sulopenem demonstrated a PD50 of >50 mg/kg when dosed
PO, whereas, the PD50 was 13.9 mg/kg when dosed SC in this model (Table 169). Sulopenem
etzadroxil had a PD50 of 12.5 mg/kg when dosed PO.
Table 169. Efficacy (PD50 in mg/kg) of Sulopenem, Sulopenem-Etzadroxil and Comparators
Against Murine Pulmonary Infections

Abbreviations: PD50, 50% of protective dose

Study RR-05-01-2006: A second study was conducted to evaluate the activity of sulopenem and
the prodrug. Mice were infected with 1.04 x 106 CFU/mouse via intranasal infection with S.
pneumoniae 02J1095. Compounds were dosed twice per day for two days starting 18 hours
post-infection. Sulopenem PD50 values were 14.3 and >50 mg/kg for when dosed PO and SC,
respectively. Sulopenem etzadroxil had an oral PD50 of 16.4 mg/kg in this model.
16.5.2.3. Gerbil Otitis Media Models
The in vivo activity of sulopenem, and the prodrug sulopenem-etzadroxil was investigated in a
gerbil model of otitis media caused by H. influenzae Rd/AH5-3 strain (β- lactamase-negative,
ampicillin-resistant with sulopenem MIC value of 0.015 to 0.06 µg/mL). Briefly, gerbils were
infected via direct injection into the middle ear with 1.25 x 107 CFU/gerbil; therapy was initiated
18 hr post-infection and continued three times daily for two days. In this model, sulopenem
failed when dosed PO with a PD50 of >50 mg/kg but was efficacious when administered SC with
a PD50 of 4.3 mg/kg (Table 170). Sulopenem etzadroxil had an oral PD50 of 4.5 mg/kg.

16.5.3. Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics Studies
(For a detailed review of the PK/PD studies, PTA analysis, and Monte-Carlo simulation, please refer
to the Clinical Pharmacology section 6.3.2 of this unireview)
To evaluate the PK/PD relationship for sulopenem, a mouse thigh infection study was
conducted using clinical isolates of S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, E. coli and K. pneumoniae with
different resistant phenotypes. Based on preclinical data, the Applicant states that fT > MIC was
the PK/PD target that best correlated with efficacy. However, the FDA Clinical Pharmacology
reviewer found significant issues related to the data presented for the PK/PD studies and the
data suggest that the PK/PD target index for sulopenem is predicted to be Cmax/MIC based on
plasma concentration.
Clinical Microbiology Reviewer’s Comments: Although the Applicant stated that T > MIC is the
PK/PD target for sulopenem that best correlates with efficacy, the FDA Clinical Pharmacology
reviewer found significant issues related to the data presented for the PK/PD studies.
16.5.4. Clinical Study For Sulopenem: uUTI
The Applicant conducted a single Phase 3 clinical study (IT001-301) to determine the safety and
efficacy of a 5-day course of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid against a 3-day course of
oral ciprofloxacin for the treatment of adult female patients (≥18 years of age) with uUTI.
Additionally, supporting safety data for sulopenem were submitted from two different failed
Phase 3 clinical studies conducted for complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI; IT001-302) and
complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI; IT001-303). The three Phase 3 clinical trials are
summarized in Table 171. However, this review focuses primarily on the uUTI trial (IT001-301).
Clinical Microbiology Reviewer’s Comments: The study results in this section were largely taken
from the Applicant’s analyses and were used to assist in review of the clinical microbiology data
for an initial assessment of possible susceptibility test interpretive criteria/breakpoints. The
Clinical Microbiology reviewer defers to the Statistical reviewer for analysis and comment on the
Agency’s assessment of the efficacy results as noted in Section 8.1 of this unireview.

In Study 301, the microbiological modified intent-to-treat (MMITT) population comprised all
subjects who had at least one or a maximum of two baseline urinary bacterial pathogen(s)
identified from urine with ≥105 CFU/mL. A total of 830 (sulopenem arm, dosed BID for five days)
and 829 (ciprofloxacin arm, dosed twice daily for three days) patients were included in the
modified intent-to-treat (MITT) population. The primary endpoint for the study was the overall
response (clinical and microbiological success) on Day 12 (±1 day) at the test-of-cure (TOC) visit.
Bacterial urinary pathogens were identified from microbiological culture from acceptable urine
specimens collected at baseline, and subsequent visits.
Among the ITT population, uUTIs were predominantly caused by E. coli (56.0% in sulopenem
treatment group and 58.4% in ciprofloxacin treatment group), K. pneumoniae (6.5% in
sulopenem treatment group and 6.0% in ciprofloxacin treatment group), and P. mirabilis (2.2%
in sulopenem treatment group and 2.1% in ciprofloxacin treatment group).

16.5.4.1. uUTI Phase 3 Clinical Study, SURE 1: IT001-301
Methods for Microbiological Collection, Culture, and Identification
Microbiological Sampling
For microbiological culture and analysis, mid-stream clean-catch urine specimens were
collected from patients into a sterile container at Screening (Baseline), Day 3, Day 5 (EOT), Day
12 (TOC), Day 28, and for any study-related visits. All specimens were sent to the local
Microbiology laboratory or the regional Microbiology Laboratory (Covance) within 24 hours
after collection. In addition, an aliquot of screening/baseline urine samples were also sent to
central Microbiology laboratory, International Health Management Associates for the US sites
only.
For the US sites, Covance served as the regional Microbiology Laboratory where isolates were
stored in duplicate and where quantitative urine culture, identification and susceptibility testing
were performed at all visits. The Central Microbiology Laboratory, IHMA conducted studyspecific quantitative urine culture, identification and susceptibility testing/custom MIC and
urine Gram stain/reading at Screening/Baseline only. IHMA also stored duplicates of isolates at
-80°C and performed re-identification and susceptibility testing of isolates received from
Covance.

susceptible to the comparator drug, ciprofloxacin (defined as MIC ≤1 mg/L), and no baseline
pathogen phenotypically resistant to ciprofloxacin.
MMITTR: The MMITTR patients were those MMITT patients with a baseline uropathogen
resistant to the comparator drug, ciprofloxacin (defined as MIC ≥2 mg/L).

16.5.4.2. Emergence of Resistance During Therapy
Impact of Treatment on the Distribution of Susceptibility to the Treatment Regimen
In this study, no post baseline isolate was observed with a sulopenem MIC that had increased
by ≥4-fold relative to a baseline isolate of the same genus and species. However, there was one
patient that was reported to have an MIC increase of ≥16-fold during therapy. Patient 129-1001
was a 73-year-old woman that had a baseline E. coli with an MIC of 0.015 µg/mL and an E. coli
with an MIC of 0.25 µg/mL was identified at TOC. The baseline isolate with the lowest MIC was
compared to the TOC isolate as it was having a ≥4x MIC change and was investigated for further
analysis. It was revealed that the patient also had an E. coli at baseline with the same whole
276
Version date: October 12, 2018
Reference ID: 4829902

NDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 213972}
{sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid}
genome sequence with an MIC of 0.25 µg/mL. All three E. coli isolates were susceptible to
ertapenem and the patient had fully resolved all uUTI symptoms at the TOC visit. Furthermore,
this indicated that a sub-population of the same bacterial species with different MIC values may
have been present at baseline.
Treatment with sulopenem had very little impact on the distribution of MIC’s between the pretreatment and post-treatment isolates. Overall, the MIC50/90 values were 0.03/0.06 µg/mL and
0.03/0.12 µg/mL against pre-treatment and post-treatment isolates, respectively.

Correlation of microbiological success to MIC values of baseline E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P.
mirabilis isolates
In the uUTI clinical study, the microbiological success in relation to MIC values of baseline E.
coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis isolates from the sulopenem treatment group the in
MMITT (MMITTR and MMITTS) population at the TOC visit are summarized below:






Among 437 baseline E. coli isolates with an MIC range of 0.015 to 1.0 µg/mL, the overall
microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 76.4%. The highest sulopenem MIC that
correspond to microbiological success was 0.25 µg/mL and 3/5 (60%) isolates were
eradicated. Only one baseline E. coli isolate with a sulopenem MIC of 1 µg/mL was available
but persisted. No baseline isolate with MIC values at ≥2 µg/mL was available. The MIC50/90
was 0.03/0.06 µg/mL against all E. coli isolates from both surveillance and clinical studies.
Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL would be reasonable and will cover most E. coli
population.
Among 48 baseline K. pneumoniae isolates with an MIC range 0.015 to 8.0 µg/mL, the
overall microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 77.1%. The highest sulopenem MIC that
correspond to favorable microbiological eradication was 0.12 µg/mL and 7/8 (87.5%)
isolates at this MIC were successfully eradicated. No baseline isolate was available with MIC
values between 0.25 to 2.0 µg/mL. However, only 2 baseline isolates with MIC values 4 and
8 µg/mL were available but eradicated. The MIC50/90 was 0.03/0.12 against all K.
pneumoniae isolates from both surveillance (US and Europe) and clinical studies. Therefore,
a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL would also be reasonable and would cover most K.
pneumoniae.
Among 17 baseline P. mirabilis isolates with an MIC range of 0.03 to 0.25 µg/mL, the overall
microbiological eradication rate at TOC was 82.4%. The highest sulopenem MIC that
correspond to microbiological success was 0.25 µg/mL and 10/10 (100%) isolates at this MIC
were successfully eradicated. No baseline isolate was available at MIC values ≥0.5 µg/mL.
Against P. mirabilis isolates from both surveillance and clinical studies, the MIC50/90 was
between 0.12/0.25 to 0.25/0.5µg/mL. Therefore, a susceptible BP of 0.25 µg/mL would also
be reasonable and would cover most P. mirabilis.

In summary, the overall microbiological success was observed in patients with baseline isolates
of E. coli and P. mirabilis that had MIC values of ≤0.015 to 0.25 µg/mL. No baseline E. coli isolate
at MIC 0.5 µg/mL was available but a single isolate at MIC 1.0 µg/mL was available with
microbiologic failure. No baseline P. mirabilis isolate with MIC ≥0.5 µg/mL was available. The
overall microbiological success was observed in patients with baseline K. pneumoniae isolates
that had MIC values of ≤0.015 up to 0.12 µg/mL. No baseline K. pneumoniae isolates with MIC
values between 0.25 to 2 µg/mL were available, however, only two isolates at MIC 4 and 8
µg/mL were available with overall success outcome.
Therefore, the Clinical Microbiology team recommends revised sulopenem S/I/R MIC BPs of
≤0.25/0.5/≥1.0 µg/mL against Enterobacterales (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and P. mirabilis only).
The corresponding disk diffusion zone diameter BPs have been calculated by following CLSI

We agree with the inclusion of E. coli, K. pneumoniae and P. mirabilis in the first list pathogens
of 12.4 Microbiology section of the sulopenem labeling. However, inclusion of pathogens in the
second list has been modified based on the relevance of uUTI indication and of having an in
vitro MIC90 of ≤0.25 µg/mL. The recommendation is that the following organisms could be
included in the second list: Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Streptococcus agalactiae, Citrobacter
freundii, Citrobacter koseri, Enterobacter cloacae species complex, Klebsiella aerogenes,
Klebsiella oxytoca, Proteus vulgaris, Providencia alcalifaciens, and Providencia stuartii.
